teile.einleitung: A thunderstorm is a weather event with lightning and thunder, often accompanied by heavy rain, wind and sometimes hail. What you mostly hear shortly after a flash of lightning is the thunder. Thunderstorms are impressive, but can also be dangerous.
wichtigste: In a thunderstorm there is lightning and thunder.
You mostly hear the thunder shortly after the lightning.
Thunderstorms form in tall, towering thunderclouds.
A bolt of lightning is a huge electrical discharge.
In Switzerland, most thunderstorms occur in summer.
In a thunderstorm you take shelter in a house or car.

abschnitte.text: Thunderstorms form when warm, damp air rises quickly. As it rises, it cools and a tall, dark **thundercloud** forms, which experts call cumulonimbus. This cloud can grow over ten kilometres tall. At the top it is often flat like an anvil.

In the cloud, grains of ice and drops of water collide and become electrically charged. If the voltage gets too great, it discharges as **lightning**. A bolt can flash inside the cloud, between clouds or between cloud and ground. The air in the lightning channel becomes about 30,000 degrees hot for a moment, hotter than the surface of the sun.

**Thunder** is produced because the strongly heated air expands explosively. Light is much faster than sound, so you see the lightning first. Sound travels about one kilometre in three seconds. If you count the seconds between lightning and thunder and divide by three, you know roughly how many kilometres away the thunderstorm is.

In Switzerland, thunderstorms occur mainly from May to September, often in the afternoon or evening after hot days. Especially many flashes of lightning are counted in **Ticino** and on the southern edge of the Alps. Thunderstorms sometimes bring hail, gusts of storm and heavy rain, which can lead to floods. MeteoSwiss warns of severe thunderstorms with warning levels.

In a thunderstorm you are safe in buildings and in cars, because the metal shell of the car conducts the current around the outside. Outdoors you should avoid summits, ridges, single trees and water. Anyone caught outside crouches down in a hollow with feet together. A **lightning conductor** on the roof leads lightning safely into the ground.

begriffe.erklaerung: The technical name for the tall, dark thundercloud.
A huge electrical discharge in the air.
The bang that is produced by the rapid expansion of the hot air during lightning.
A metal rod with a cable that leads lightning safely into the earth.

gewusst: Across the whole Earth, on average about 40 to 50 flashes of lightning strike per second.
The saying that lightning never strikes the same place twice is not true: tall towers are often hit several times a year.

teile.einleitung: In California stands a tree that has more wood than any other in the world. It is called **General Sherman**. It is a giant sequoia and already over 2000 years old.
wichtigste: General Sherman is the biggest tree in the world, measured by its amount of wood.
It is a giant sequoia.
It is about 84 metres tall.
Its trunk is almost 8 metres across at chest height.
It stands in Sequoia National Park in California, USA.
Its age is estimated at about 2300 to 2700 years.

abschnitte.text: **General Sherman** is not the tallest tree in the world, but the **biggest**, measured by its **amount of wood**. Its trunk contains almost **1500 cubic metres** of wood. It is about **84 metres** tall, as tall as a building with about 25 storeys. At chest height, the trunk is almost **8 metres** across, and right at the bottom even over 11 metres. Many children would have to hold hands to reach around it.

The tree stands in **Sequoia National Park** in **California**, USA. There, many giant sequoias grow in a grove called the **Giant Forest**. It is named after **William T. Sherman**, a general in the American Civil War. Many people visit it every year. A fence protects its roots from too many feet.

The age of General Sherman is estimated at about **2300 to 2700 years**. So it was already growing in the time of the ancient Romans. Giant sequoias are among the **oldest living things** on Earth. They grow only in a small area on the western slopes of the **Sierra Nevada**. There a lot of snow falls in winter, which supplies water in summer.

Giant sequoias have **thick bark**. At the bottom of the trunk it is almost a metre thick. It is fibrous and **burns poorly**. This way the trees survive many **forest fires**. Small fires even help them: the heat opens the cones, and on the bare ground the seeds can sprout.

In Switzerland, too, there are giant sequoias. Since the **19th century**, many have been planted in **parks**, gardens and woods. Some are already very big today and are among the tallest trees in their area. Of course they are still much younger than General Sherman.

gewusst: The seed of a giant sequoia is smaller than a rolled oat flake, even though a giant grows from it.
The tallest tree in the world is a coast redwood, also in California.

teile.einleitung: **Digestate** (in German, “Gärgut”) is what is left over when green waste, slurry or food scraps have been fermented in a biogas plant. It still contains many nutrients and is used as fertiliser.
wichtigste: Digestate is produced by fermentation in biogas plants.
Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium remain largely in the digestate.
Liquid digestate serves as a liquid fertiliser on meadows and fields.
A large part of the nitrogen is present as ammonium.
Spreading close to the ground, for example with a trailing hose, reduces ammonia losses.
Plastic in green waste ends up as a foreign substance in the digestate.

abschnitte.text: In a **digestion plant**, bacteria break down organic material **without air**. This produces **biogas**, mainly methane. What is left over is the digestate. Nutrients such as **nitrogen**, **phosphorus** and **potassium** remain largely intact. The digestate is often separated into a solid and a liquid part, which is called **separation**.

Farmers usually spread the **liquid digestate** as a **liquid fertiliser** on meadows and fields. A large part of the nitrogen is present as **ammonium**. Plants can therefore take it up quickly. Ammonium can, however, escape into the air as a gas, as **ammonia**. If the digestate is spread close to the ground, for example with a **trailing hose**, less is lost. In Switzerland, spreading close to the ground has been required in many cases since 2024.

Digestate usually contributes less to **humus formation** than compost. Part of the carbon has already been removed as biogas. Solid digestate is therefore often left to compost further. In this **after-composting**, it is turned into stable **compost** with access to air. This improves the soil in the long term.

Ordinary **plastic bags** do not belong in the green waste for digestion. They end up in the digestate as **foreign substances** and as **microplastic**, and so on the fields. One advantage of digestion shows with slurry: fermented slurry usually smells less strongly. Many strong-smelling organic acids have already been broken down in the plant.

gewusst: From biogas you can make electricity, heat or even fuel for vehicles.
Many Swiss farms run their own small biogas plants for their slurry.

teile.einleitung: The hazel is a shrub that grows in Swiss woods, at the edges of woods and in hedges. It flowers as early as late winter and is one of the first bloomers of the year. In autumn it bears the popular hazelnuts.
wichtigste: The hazel flowers very early, often as early as January to March.
The male flowers hang as yellow catkins on the twigs.
The female flowers are tiny and have fine red threads.
The wind carries the pollen to other flowers.
Hazelnuts ripen from the end of August into autumn.
The dormouse and the squirrel like to eat hazelnuts.

abschnitte.text: The **hazel** is a shrub with several stems. It flowers very early in the year, often as early as **January to March**. Then it has no leaves yet. Its pollen therefore flies unhindered through the air. For bees it is one of the first sources of food after the winter.

The hazel has two kinds of flowers. The male flowers hang as long, yellow **catkins** on the twigs. They look like little sausages. The female flowers, on the other hand, are tiny and look like **buds**. Only fine **red threads** peep out at the top. From them the nuts develop later.

The hazel is **pollinated by the wind**. It carries the fine yellow pollen of the catkins far away to other flowers. That is why the hazel makes a great deal of pollen. In people with an allergy it can trigger **hay fever**. Because the hazel flowers so early, the hay fever season for them begins as early as winter.

Hazelnuts ripen **from the end of August into autumn** and then fall from the shrub. The edible kernel sits in a **hard, brown shell**. You can open them with a **nutcracker**. Hazelnuts are nourishing and contain a lot of fat.

Many animals eat hazelnuts. **Squirrels** hide them in the ground in autumn and look for their stores again in winter. The **dormouse** (in German, “Haselmaus”, or “hazel mouse”) is even named after the hazel. It likes to eat hazelnuts and has a long **hibernation**. Birds such as the jay and woodpeckers also fetch hazelnuts.

gewusst: Squirrels do not find all the hidden nuts again: new hazel shrubs can grow from the forgotten ones.
A large hazel shrub produces millions of grains of pollen.

teile.einleitung: Every species of animal and plant needs a particular place to live. This typical place to live is called a **habitat**. If it is lost, the species often disappear too.
wichtigste: The habitat is the typical place where a species lives.
The term habitat refers to a single species, the biotope to a community of living things.
The Alpine ibex lives in steep rocky areas in the high mountains.
The beaver needs waters with trees on the bank.
The skylark lives on open meadows and fields.
The loss of habitats is a main cause of species extinction.

abschnitte.text: The **habitat** is the place where a species typically lives. There it finds food, shelter and room for its young. The term always refers to **a single species**. A **biotope**, on the other hand, is the living space of a whole community of living things, for example a pond with all the plants and animals in it.

The **Alpine ibex** lives in **steep rocky areas** in the high mountains, where it climbs skilfully. The **beaver** needs **waters with trees on the bank**, because it fells trees for food and for building its lodge. The **skylark** breeds on the ground on **open meadows and fields**. Each species therefore has very particular demands on its habitat.

The **loss of habitats** is regarded as one of the main causes of the decline of many species. Wetlands are drained, meadows built over and hedges removed. Roads and settlements cut up the areas that are left. Animals can then no longer move from one area to another.

**Wildlife bridges** over motorways connect habitats that are separated by roads. Deer, foxes and other animals can cross safely this way. In spring, **toads** migrate to their **spawning waters**. So that they are not run over, helpers set up **amphibian fences** on some roads and carry the animals across the road in buckets.

gewusst: The Alpine ibex was once wiped out in Switzerland and was reintroduced from 1911.
The word habitat comes from the Latin “habitare”, which means to live.

teile.einleitung: A fertilised meadow (in German, a “Fettwiese”, or “fat meadow”) is a meadow that receives a lot of fertiliser. That is why a great deal of grass grows there, which farmers use as feed for their cows.
wichtigste: A fertilised meadow receives a lot of fertiliser.
It is fertilised with manure and slurry from the cowshed.
A great deal of grass grows on a fertilised meadow.
It can be mown several times a year.
Rather few flower species grow there, for example dandelion and cow parsley.
In Switzerland there are especially many fertilised meadows on the Plateau.

abschnitte.titel: Lots of fertiliser, lots of grass
abschnitte.text: A **fertilised meadow** receives a lot of **fertiliser**. The German word “fett” (fat) means here that the soil is rich in nutrients. As a result the plants grow quickly and densely. There is **a great deal of grass**, which serves as feed for cows. The opposite is the **lean meadow**, which receives little or no fertiliser.

The fertiliser mostly comes **from the cowshed**. **Manure** is a mixture of cow dung and straw. **Slurry** is the liquid fertiliser made of dung, urine and water. Farmers spread it on the meadow with a slurry tanker. This way the nutrients from the feed go back into the soil.

Because the grass grows back so quickly, a fertilised meadow can be mown **several times a year**. The grass becomes hay, aftermath hay or silage for the winter. Sometimes the cows also eat the grass directly on the pasture. In Switzerland there are especially many fertilised meadows on the **Plateau**, where the soil is good and the climate mild.

On a fertilised meadow, **rather few** flower species grow. The fast-growing grasses take the light away from the other plants. Typical is the yellow **dandelion**, which turns whole meadows yellow in spring. The **cow parsley** with its white umbels of flowers also often grows on heavily fertilised meadows.

For butterflies and wild bees, fertilised meadows offer less food than colourful lean meadows. Because of the frequent mowing, many insects also have little time to develop. That is why many farms in Switzerland also leave areas with less fertiliser. This way, besides the plentiful feed, there is also room for flowers and animals.

gewusst: A meadow that is yellow with dandelions almost always shows a lot of fertiliser.
The second cut of grass in the year is called “Emd” in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: In spring, long clusters of bright yellow flowers hang from the **laburnum** (also called golden chain tree, in German “Goldregen”, or “golden rain”). It is a popular ornamental tree in gardens and parks. But as beautiful as it is, all its parts are poisonous.
wichtigste: The laburnum blooms yellow in long, hanging clusters.
It blooms in spring, roughly from April to June.
It is a small tree or large shrub.
It often stands in gardens and parks.
Its fruits look like small bean pods.
All parts are poisonous, the seeds most strongly.

abschnitte.text: The **common laburnum** has bright **yellow flowers**. They hang down in long **clusters**. This looks like falling golden rain, hence the German name. It blooms in **spring**, roughly from April to June. The flowers have the shape of little butterflies, as in peas and beans.

The laburnum is a **small tree** or **large shrub**. It grows a few metres tall. In the wild it grows in the mountains of southern and central Europe, including the south of Switzerland. As an **ornamental tree** it is very popular. That is why it often stands in **gardens**, parks and playgrounds. So poisonous plants can also grow in a garden.

The laburnum belongs to the **legumes**, like beans and peas. After flowering, it forms flat **pods**. In them lie the **seeds**. They look like small beans. The pods often stay hanging on the tree for a long time.

**All parts** of the laburnum are poisonous, the **seeds** most strongly. The poison is called **cytisine**. Children like to play at cooking with the bean-like pods and seeds. That is why they are especially at risk. If you suspect poisoning, in Switzerland you call **Tox Info Suisse** at once, telephone number 145.

gewusst: The laburnum is related to the bean, but unlike it, it is poisonous even when cooked.
The laburnum is among the most common causes of plant poisoning in children.

teile.einleitung: The downy oak is an oak that loves warmth and dryness. In Switzerland it grows mainly on sunny, dry slopes in the Valais.
wichtigste: Young shoots and the undersides of the leaves of the downy oak are finely hairy.
It likes a warm and dry climate.
Its main range lies in southern and south-eastern Europe.
In the Valais it forms larger stands on dry slopes.
There it is increasingly replacing the Scots pine in low-lying areas.
With the sessile oak it often forms hybrids.

abschnitte.text: The **downy oak** gets its name from a fine **down**. **Young shoots** and the **undersides of the leaves** are covered with soft little hairs. The hairs protect the leaves from losing too much water. Like all oaks, the downy oak bears **acorns** as its fruit. Its leaves are lobed and rather small.

The downy oak likes a **warm and dry** climate. Its **main range** lies in **southern and south-eastern Europe**. North of the Alps it grows only in especially warm spots. In very dry places it often grows **low and gnarled**. Then it looks more like a large shrub than a tree.

In Switzerland, the downy oak forms larger stands mainly in the **Valais**. There it grows on dry, sunny slopes of the Rhone valley. Smaller occurrences are also found on warm slopes at the southern foot of the Jura and in Ticino. In their light woods live many warmth-loving insects, for example rare beetles and butterflies.

In the Valais, the **Scots pine** is increasingly being **replaced** by the downy oak in low-lying areas. The pines suffer from the growing dryness, and many die. The downy oak copes better with heat and drought. Researchers follow this development closely, because it shows how woods are changing.

The downy oak often forms **hybrids** with the **sessile oak**. Such trees have features of both species. That is why it is sometimes difficult to say which oak you have in front of you. Experts then look closely at the hairiness of the leaves and shoots.

gewusst: In southern Europe, truffles sometimes grow under downy oaks, living together with the roots of the trees.
In the Valais, on some slopes downy oaks grow right next to vineyards.

teile.einleitung: **Barley** is a cereal that is easy to recognise in the field: long, fine bristles hang from its ears. Barley is one of the oldest crop plants in the world. In Switzerland it is grown mainly as animal feed, but it also goes into soup.
wichtigste: You recognise barley by the long awns on the ear.
People have grown barley for about 10,000 years.
In Switzerland, a lot of barley is fed to animals.
Winter barley is often harvested as early as the end of June or in July.
Barley that has been sprouted and dried is called malt.
Bündner barley soup is a well-known dish from Graubünden.

abschnitte.text: Barley is a **cereal** like wheat, rye or oats. Typical are the **awns**: long, fine bristles on the ear. They look like a beard. When the barley ripens, the ears bend downwards. Barley is one of the **oldest crop plants**: people have grown it for about 10,000 years.

In Switzerland, a large part of the barley is fed to animals, for example to **pigs** and **cattle**. Barley is a good **feed grain**. **Winter barley** is sown as early as autumn and is ripe early in summer. It is often harvested at the end of June or in July, even before wheat. That is why barley is usually the first cereal to be harvested in summer.

Hulled and polished barley grains are called **pearl barley** (in German, “Rollgerste”). It is round and is cooked in soups. Very well known is the **Bündner barley soup** from Graubünden. It contains pearl barley, vegetables and often bacon or meat. On cold days it warms you well.

If you let barley grains **sprout** and then dry them, **malt** is made. Malt is needed, for example, for malt drinks. If you roast barley, it tastes similar to coffee. From it, **barley coffee** is made. It contains no **caffeine**, however, and is therefore also suitable for people who do not drink real coffee.

gewusst: Barley has been grown for about 10,000 years.
Barley coffee tastes similar to coffee, but has no caffeine.

teile.einleitung: The **Green Revolution** is the name for the strong increase in harvests in many countries of Asia and Latin America from the 1960s. New cereal varieties, fertiliser and irrigation made it possible. It helped against hunger, but also had disadvantages.
wichtigste: The Green Revolution began in the 1960s.
New high-yield varieties of wheat and rice had short, sturdy stalks.
The varieties needed mineral fertiliser, irrigation and plant protection.
The rice variety IR8 became known in 1966 as “miracle rice”.
The rice research institute IRRI is in the Philippines.
Falling groundwater and the loss of old landraces are criticised.

abschnitte.text: Old cereal varieties had long stalks. If you fertilised them heavily, the ears became heavy and the stalks bent over. This falling over is called **lodging**. Breeders therefore developed **semi-dwarf varieties** with short, sturdy stalks. The dwarfing genes for wheat came from the Japanese variety **Norin 10**. This way the plants could carry many more grains.

The American **Norman Borlaug** bred new wheat varieties in **Mexico**. For this he received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970. For rice, the **International Rice Research Institute IRRI** in the **Philippines** was important. In 1966 it brought out the variety **IR8**, which became known as “miracle rice”. Countries such as India and Pakistan were able to raise their harvests greatly within a few years.

The new **high-yield varieties** brought big harvests only if they got enough **mineral fertiliser**, **irrigation** and **plant protection products**. That cost money. Farmers with a lot of land and capital therefore often profited more than poor smallholders. As a result, agriculture became more dependent on machines, fertiliser and seed companies.

In the Indian **Punjab**, so much water was pumped up for the fields that the **groundwater level** is falling sharply. Soils and waters were polluted by fertiliser and pesticides. From the point of view of **biodiversity**, it is criticised that the new varieties pushed out many **local landraces**. At the same time, in the view of many experts, the Green Revolution saved millions of people from hunger. The assessment is therefore divided to this day.

gewusst: The term “Green Revolution” was coined in 1968 by an American official.
Norman Borlaug was a trained plant pathologist, that is, an expert on plant diseases.

teile.einleitung: Trees, ferns, grasses and flowers have something in common: they have fine channels for water and nutrients. That is why they are called **vascular plants**. This invention allowed plants to conquer the land and grow tall.
wichtigste: Scientifically, vascular plants are called Tracheophyta.
The xylem carries water, the phloem carries sugar.
Transpiration pull draws the water up into the treetops.
Lignin makes the cell walls woody and the plants sturdy.
Ferns and horsetails spread with spores instead of seeds.
Cooksonia is among the oldest known vascular plants.

abschnitte.text: Vascular plants have two kinds of channels. The **xylem**, also called the wood part, carries **water** and minerals up from the roots. The **phloem**, also called the sieve part, distributes the **sugary sap** from the leaves. It flows in living sieve cells to roots, fruits and buds. Together they form the **vascular bundles**.

How does water get to the top of a tall tree? At the leaves, water is constantly **evaporating**. This pulls the connected threads of water in the channels upwards. This is called **transpiration pull**. The explanation for it is called the **cohesion-tension theory**. It explains the transport of water to heights of over 100 metres.

The substance **lignin** is deposited in the cell walls and makes them resistant to pressure. Only with this could plants grow upright and tall. The water-carrying cells of ferns and conifers are called **tracheids**. They are dead, woody cells with small openings, the pits. In conifers they make up almost all of the wood. The name **Tracheophyta** also comes from the tracheids.

Vascular plants include **ferns**, **horsetails** and clubmosses. They form no seeds, but spread with **spores**. Then there are the **seed plants**, that is, conifers and flowering plants. In all vascular plants, the large, long-lived plant is the **sporophyte**. The other generation is small or greatly reduced. Mosses are not vascular plants, and are called Bryophyta.

One of the oldest known vascular plants is **Cooksonia** from the **Silurian**. It is about **430 million years** old and was only a few centimetres tall. It had forked shoots with spore containers at the ends, but no leaves yet. How leaves arose is explained by the **telome theory** of Walter Zimmermann. According to it, the ends of shoots were flattened and grew together into leaves.

gewusst: The first vascular plants were smaller than a finger.
A tree lifts water over 100 metres high without having a pump.

teile.einleitung: A standard orchard is a meadow with large, old fruit trees whose crowns stand high above the ground. Such orchards shaped the Swiss landscape for a long time and are important habitats.
wichtigste: Standard trees have a long trunk, and the crown starts clearly above head height.
Under the trees, the meadow is mown or grazed.
Much of the fruit from standard orchards is made into cider and juice.
Since the 1950s, the number of standard trees in Switzerland has fallen sharply.
The little owl is a typical owl of old orchards.
In Germany, such orchards are often called “Streuobstwiese”, meaning scattered orchard meadow.

abschnitte.text: With a **standard tree**, the crown only starts far up on a long trunk. Underneath, there is enough room for mowing or for grazing animals. So the land is used twice: **fruit** above, **fodder** for cows or sheep below. In Germany such orchards are often called **“Streuobstwiese”**, because the trees stand loosely scattered.

A large part of the fruit is **cider fruit**. Apples and pears are pressed and made into **sweet cider**, juice or apple wine. In old orchards grow many **old varieties** that you can hardly find in shops. An old Swiss apple variety is the **Berner Rose** from the canton of Bern. Some old varieties are robust against diseases and are therefore valuable for breeding.

Old standard trees have **holes**, dead branches and cracked bark. There, hole-nesting birds, bats and many insects find shelter. The **little owl**, a small owl, is typical. It nests in tree holes and hunts mice and insects in the meadow below. With the loss of orchards, it has become very rare in Switzerland.

Since the **1950s**, a great many standard trees have been felled in Switzerland. Low trees in orchard plantations are easier to harvest and look after. In addition, villages and towns grew into the orchard meadows. Today only a fraction of the former trees remain. The federal government, the cantons and nature conservation organisations therefore encourage the planting of new standard trees.

gewusst: A standard fruit tree can live for many decades and only bear really heavily after some years.
In the old orchards of Switzerland, hundreds of different fruit varieties stand together.

teile.einleitung: On the highest peaks of the Alps it is cold, windy and stony. Even so, plants grow there. This **summit flora** is adapted to the harsh climate. Because of global warming, it is changing greatly right now.
wichtigste: Opposite-leaved saxifrage was found on the Dom in the Valais at about 4500 m.
Glacier crowfoot grows up to over 4000 m, for example on the Finsteraarhorn.
Summit plants usually grow as flat cushions or rosettes.
On the south side of a summit, usually more species grow.
Lichens colonise rocks right up to the highest peaks.
With the warming, plants are moving upwards.

abschnitte.text: The highest-growing flowering plant of the Alps is the **opposite-leaved saxifrage**. It forms small cushions with purple flowers and was recorded on the **Dom** in the Valais at about **4500 m**. The **glacier crowfoot** also grows up to over 4000 m, for example on the **Finsteraarhorn**. It blooms white to pink and grows on silicate scree. Plants above the snow line are called **nival plants**.

Close to the ground it is warmer and less windy than higher up. That is why summit plants usually grow flat as **cushions** or **rosettes**. They look for small snow-free spots and **cracks in the rock**. Even higher, where no flowering plant grows any more, you find **lichens**. They are partnerships of a **fungus and an alga** and tolerate cold and drying out.

On the **south side** of an alpine summit you generally find the most plant species. South slopes get more sun, become free of snow earlier and are warmer. The shady **north side** stays under snow longer. There the time for growing is shorter.

Researchers visited summits whose plants had already been listed in the 19th and early 20th centuries. When **compared with the old species lists**, it turned out that on many summits clearly more species grow today. The plants are moving upwards because of the **warming**. For the summit plants this is dangerous. From below, strongly competitive species move up, and above the summit there is no more room to move away.

gewusst: On the Dom in the Valais, a saxifrage blooms at a height of about 4500 m.
Many alpine summits are richer in species today than a hundred years ago, because plants are moving upwards.

teile.einleitung: Halophytes are plants that can grow on salty soils. For most plants, salt is harmful. Halophytes have developed special tricks to cope with it.
wichtigste: The Greek word “hals” means salt.
Halophytes grow on sea coasts, in salt marshes and at salt lakes.
Glasswort colonises, as a pioneer, the mud of the salt marshes on the North Sea.
Some halophytes give off salt through salt glands in the leaves.
Many are fleshy and dilute the salt with stored water.
In mangroves, the seeds germinate while still on the mother plant.

abschnitte.text: The name **halophyte** comes from Greek: “hals” means salt, “phyton” means plant. Halophytes grow on **sea coasts**, in **salt marshes** and at **salt lakes**. On salty ground, plants have a problem: although the soil is wet, they can take up water only with difficulty. The salty water holds on to the water. This is called **physiological drought**.

abschnitte.titel: Salt marshes on the North Sea
abschnitte.text: On the North Sea coast, between the mudflats and the dyke, lie the **salt marshes**. They are flooded by the sea at high tides. Only salt-tolerant plants can grow there. **Glasswort** is a pioneer: as one of the first plants, it colonises the bare **mud**. It holds the mud in place and so helps new salt marshes to form.

Many halophytes are **fleshy and juicy**. They store a lot of water and so dilute the salt they take up. This is called **salt succulence**. Others have **salt glands** in the leaves. These give off a salt solution that turns to crystals on the leaf. This is known, for example, from **sea lavender** and from some mangroves.

**Mangroves** are trees that stand in salt water on tropical coasts. A special feature is **vivipary**: the seeds germinate while they are still hanging on the tree. The seedling grows there into a long shoot. When it falls off, it can quickly anchor itself in the mud or be carried away by the water.

Salty soils do not form only by the sea. In hot, dry regions, **artificial irrigation** can also make the soil salty. The water evaporates at the surface, and the dissolved salts stay behind and accumulate. On such fields many crops then grow badly. Halophytes are therefore also researched in order to make salinised soils usable again.

gewusst: You can eat glasswort: it is sometimes sold as “sea asparagus”.
On the leaves of some halophytes you can see tiny salt crystals.

teile.einleitung: Some leaves look as if they were made up of many small leaves. In fact it is a single leaf. It is called a **pinnate leaf**, because it is reminiscent of a bird's feather.
wichtigste: In a pinnate leaf, leaflets sit along a central axis.
This central axis is called the rachis.
Odd-pinnate leaves have a terminal leaflet.
Ash, walnut and rowan have pinnate leaves.
A bud sits only at the base of the whole leaf.
In palmate leaves, all the leaflets come from one point.

abschnitte.text: A **pinnate leaf** consists of several **leaflets**, the pinnae. They sit left and right along a shared central axis. This axis is called the **rachis**. It continues the leaf stalk. The whole structure looks like a feather, hence the name. Leaves made of several parts are also called **compound leaves**.

A pinnate leaf can look almost like a small twig. But there is a sure clue: the **bud**. Buds form only at the base of a whole leaf, where it joins the twig. On the individual leaflets you find no buds. In autumn the whole pinnate leaf usually falls off as one unit.

If a leaf ends with a single leaflet at the tip, it is called **odd-pinnate**. The number of leaflets is then odd. Examples are **rose** and **walnut**. If the terminal leaflet is missing, it is called **even-pinnate**. In the **pea**, the uppermost pinnae are turned into **tendrils**. With them the plant holds on and climbs up supports.

The **common ash** is a native tree with long pinnate leaves. The **rowan**, also called mountain ash, also has odd-pinnate leaves. In autumn it bears bright red berries that many birds like to eat. Beech, lime and hornbeam, on the other hand, have **simple leaves** in one piece.

There is another kind of compound leaf. If all the leaflets come from one point at the tip of the stalk, the leaf is called **palmate**. It looks like a hand with spread fingers. The **horse chestnut** has such leaves. Lupins also have palmate leaves.

gewusst: A single ash leaf can be longer than a forearm.
The tendrils of the pea are actually rebuilt leaflets.

teile.einleitung: The **Fertile Crescent** is an arc-shaped area in the Near East. Here, more than 10,000 years ago, people began to grow plants and keep animals. That is why the region is regarded as one of the cradles of agriculture.
wichtigste: The term comes from the American archaeologist James Henry Breasted.
The area curves in an arc around the Syrian Desert.
In the east, the Euphrates and Tigris shape the land, Mesopotamia.
The Zagros Mountains form the eastern edge.
Usually eight founder crops of early agriculture are counted.
Sheep and goats were domesticated here very early.

abschnitte.text: The Fertile Crescent stretches from the **Levant** on the Mediterranean, across south-eastern Anatolia, to **Mesopotamia** and the Persian Gulf. It encloses the Syrian Desert in the north like a sickle. Today, countries such as Israel, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey, Iraq and parts of Iran lie there. The Arabian Peninsula with Saudi Arabia is not part of it. The term was coined by **James Henry Breasted** at the beginning of the 20th century.

In the east flow the **Euphrates** and the **Tigris**. The area between them is called Mesopotamia, which means “land between the rivers”. With their water, people later built large **irrigation systems**. Here some of the first cities arose, and cuneiform writing. In the east, the **Zagros Mountains** in present-day Iran and Iraq mark the edge of the Crescent.

Usually **eight founder crops** of early agriculture are counted. They include three cereals: **emmer**, **einkorn** and **barley**. Four are pulses: **lentil**, pea, chickpea and bitter vetch. In addition there is **flax**, a fibre plant. From these wild plants, people bred cultivated plants over many generations.

Animals were also tamed early here. **Sheep** and **goats** became domestic animals about 10,000 years ago or earlier in Anatolia and in the Zagros. Cattle and pigs soon followed. The animals provided meat, milk, wool and leather. In the foothills of the Zagros, very early traces of goat keeping were found.

The climate has **damp winters** and **dry summers**. This favours annual grasses with **large seeds** that can be stored well. People could easily gather and sow such wild grasses. The geographer **Jared Diamond** saw this as an important reason for early arable farming in this region. From here, agriculture spread to Europe, as far as Switzerland.

gewusst: Many cereals that we eat today are descended from wild grasses of the Fertile Crescent.
Agriculture reached the area of present-day Switzerland from this region only thousands of years later.
The soya bean does not come from there, but from East Asia.

teile.einleitung: The Gulf Stream is a strong, warm ocean current in the Atlantic Ocean. It flows from the Gulf of Mexico along the coast of North America towards Europe. Ocean currents such as the Gulf Stream carry warmth around the Earth and make the climate in Europe milder.
wichtigste: The Gulf Stream is a warm ocean current in the Atlantic.
It begins in the area of the Gulf of Mexico and Florida.
Its continuation towards Europe is called the North Atlantic Current.
Ocean currents carry warmth around the Earth.
Thanks to the Gulf Stream, the climate in Western Europe is milder.
The Gulf Stream is part of a worldwide system of ocean currents.

abschnitte.text: The Gulf Stream is like a huge river in the middle of the sea. It begins where warm water from the **Gulf of Mexico** flows through the Straits of Florida into the Atlantic. Then it flows north along the east coast of the USA and turns east. It carries much more water than all the rivers of the Earth together.

In the middle of the Atlantic, the Gulf Stream divides. One part flows on as the **North Atlantic Current** towards Great Britain, Ireland and Norway. There the water gives off its warmth to the air. Cooled and salty, it becomes heavy, sinks into the depths and slowly flows back south.

Thanks to the warm water, Western Europe is clearly milder than other regions at the same latitude. In Canada, which lies just as far north, the winters are much colder. The harbours on the coast of Norway mostly do not freeze over even in winter. The weather in Switzerland, too, is influenced by the warm **Atlantic** through the westerly winds.

The Gulf Stream is part of a great overturning circulation in the Atlantic, which experts call the **AMOC**. It belongs to a worldwide system of ocean currents, also called the global conveyor belt. It is driven by wind and by differences in the temperature and salt content of the water. Researchers are investigating whether this overturning is weakening because of climate change, since meltwater makes the sea less salty.

Spanish sailors noticed the strong current off Florida as early as the 16th century. The American **Benjamin Franklin** had a chart of the Gulf Stream printed around 1770. He wanted mail ships to Europe to use the current and avoid it on the way back. This way ships could save days of travel time.

begriffe.erklaerung: A constant movement of large masses of water in a particular direction.
The continuation of the Gulf Stream towards Northern Europe.
Abbreviation for the great overturning circulation in the Atlantic.
How much salt is dissolved in sea water.

gewusst: Thanks to the warm North Atlantic Current, even palm trees grow on some coasts of Ireland and south-west England.
At the surface, the Gulf Stream flows in places at up to about two metres per second, which is faster than most people walk.

teile.einleitung: If you plant the same vegetable in the same place every year, you run into problems over time. That is why plants are swapped around. This planned change is called **crop rotation**.
wichtigste: In crop rotation, the crops on an area change every year.
This way the soil is not drained of just one kind of nutrient.
Diseases and pests build up less in the soil.
A distinction is made between heavy feeders, medium feeders and light feeders.
Legumes such as beans improve the soil with nitrogen.
The three-field system in the Middle Ages was an early crop rotation.

abschnitte.text: Every plant takes certain **nutrients** from the soil. If the same thing always grows in the same place, these substances soon run short. In addition, the **disease-causing organisms** and **pests** of a plant family multiply in the soil. This is then called **soil sickness**. Changing the crops prevents this.

**Heavy feeders** such as pumpkin, cabbage and tomatoes need very many nutrients, above all nitrogen. **Medium feeders** such as carrots, lettuce or onions need less. Too much fresh manure even harms carrots and attracts the carrot fly. **Light feeders** such as beans, peas and many herbs are undemanding.

A classic vegetable crop rotation lasts **three years**. After a dose of **compost**, the heavy feeders go on the bed first. In the second year the medium feeders follow, and in the third the light feeders. Then the cycle starts again from the beginning. Many gardeners therefore divide their garden into several beds.

Beans and peas are **legumes**. **Nodule bacteria** live on their roots. These bacteria fix **nitrogen** from the air and make it usable for the plant. That is why beans hardly need any fertiliser and even leave behind better soil. It is also important that related plants should not follow directly after one another. Potatoes and tomatoes are both **nightshades** and suffer from the same late blight.

In the **Middle Ages** the **three-field system** was widespread. The arable land of a village was divided into three parts. On one grew winter cereal, on the second summer cereal. The third part lay **fallow**, so it was not planted for a year. This let the soil recover. Today the fallow is often replaced by clover or temporary grassland.

gewusst: Thanks to bacteria on their roots, beans fertilise themselves, so to speak.
Even the farmers of the Middle Ages knew that a field needs rest.
Potatoes and tomatoes are close relatives.

teile.einleitung: Clean water in lakes, rivers and in the ground is vital for people, animals and plants. **Water protection** makes sure that our waters stay clean. In Switzerland it has been regulated in the constitution and in law for decades.
wichtigste: In 1953 the electorate accepted a constitutional article on water protection.
The Water Protection Act is abbreviated GSchG.
About 80 per cent of drinking water comes from groundwater and spring water.
Residual flow must stay in the stream after water has been taken out.
A water space must be kept free along waters.
Old medicines belong back at the pharmacy.

abschnitte.text: In the past, sewage often flowed into streams and lakes untreated. This could become dangerous. In 1963, hundreds of people in the Valais holiday resort of **Zermatt** fell ill with **typhoid fever**, because sewage had got into the drinking water. Ten years earlier the people had already reacted: on 6 December **1953**, more than four fifths of those voting approved a **constitutional article** on water protection.

The constitutional article formed the basis for the first Water Protection Act. Today the law is abbreviated **GSchG**. It must not be confused with the **USG**, the Environmental Protection Act, and the **NHG**, the Federal Act on the Protection of Nature and Cultural Heritage. Thanks to **sewage treatment plants** in almost all municipalities, Swiss lakes are much cleaner again today than a few decades ago.

About **80 per cent** of Swiss drinking water comes from **groundwater and spring water**. The rest is obtained mainly from lakes. To keep the groundwater clean, there are protection zones around the catchments. There, for example, you may not store substances that could pollute the water.

When **hydroelectric power stations** take water from a stream, a minimum amount must stay in the streambed. This is called **residual flow**. This way fish and other animals can go on living there. Along streams, rivers and lakes, a strip must also be kept free, the **water space**. It serves the natural functions of the water and **flood protection**. In principle, building is not allowed there.

Old **medicines** do not belong in the toilet, but back at the **pharmacy**. In sewage treatment plants they are only partly broken down. You should also not wash the car with cleaning products over a **road drain**. Many drains lead rainwater straight into a stream, without a treatment plant. Soap, oil and dirt would then pollute the water.

gewusst: In 1953, more than four fifths of those voting said Yes to water protection.
Many road drains lead the rainwater straight into a stream.

teile.einleitung: Not every soil is the same. A **gley** is a soil that is strongly shaped by groundwater. You recognise it by grey and blue-green layers and by rust-brown spots. Gleys are found mainly in river floodplains and hollows.
wichtigste: A gley is a soil with a high groundwater table.
The word comes from Russian and means roughly “muddy earth”.
The permanently wet reduction horizon is grey to blue-green.
Rust spots form when iron oxidises with oxygen.
In a pseudogley, rainwater builds up instead of groundwater.
Many gley soils on the Plateau were made usable by drainage.

abschnitte.text: A gley is a soil whose lower part lies permanently or at times in the **groundwater**. The word comes from **Russian** and means roughly **“muddy earth”**. Gleys are typical in **river floodplains** and **hollows**, where the groundwater lies close to the surface. Soils in which **rainwater** builds up above a dense layer, on the other hand, are called **pseudogleys**. They are alternately wet and dry.

In the permanently wet part, oxygen is lacking. There, **iron** is present in divalent form and colours the soil **grey to blue-green**. This part is called the **reduction horizon** or Gr horizon, where the r stands for reduced. Above it lies the **Go horizon**, where the o stands for oxidised. There the groundwater fluctuates, and at times air gets in. The iron **oxidises** with the oxygen and forms **rust-brown spots**.

Wet gley soils are hard to plough. On the Swiss Plateau, many of them were therefore made usable by **drainage**. In this, pipes are laid in the soil that carry the water away and lower the groundwater level. This created fields. But many **wetlands**, which were important for rare plants and animals, were also lost.

gewusst: The colours of a gley reveal how high the groundwater rises.
The word gley comes from Russian.

teile.einleitung: A shallow-rooted plant is one whose roots grow flat just below the surface of the ground. This has advantages, but also dangers, for example in a storm or in a drought.
wichtigste: Shallow-rooted plants form roots that grow horizontally just below the surface.
The spruce is a typical shallow-rooted tree.
When such a tree falls over, a root plate sticks up out of the ground.
In a long drought, shallow-rooted plants suffer, because the top layer of soil dries out quickly.
On wet or rocky soils, roots often grow especially shallow.
The hurricane Lothar blew down very many spruces in December 1999.

abschnitte.text: In a **shallow-rooted plant**, the roots grow **horizontally just below the surface**. They spread far to the side, but hardly go down into the depths. Other trees such as the silver fir or the oak form a **taproot**, which grows deep down. In between there are **heart-rooted trees** such as the beech. The spruce is the best-known shallow-rooted tree in Switzerland.

How deep roots grow also depends on the **soil**. In **wet soils** there is no air in the depths, so the roots stay near the top. In **rocky soils** they simply cannot get deeper. Then other trees also form especially shallow roots. In towns, thick roots just below the surface sometimes lift **pavements** and paths.

Because shallow-rooted trees have little hold in the depths, they are easily blown over in a **storm**. The whole root ball is torn out of the ground. It then sticks up vertically in the air as a **root plate**. On 26 December **1999**, the hurricane **Lothar** blew down huge numbers of trees in Switzerland. Shallow-rooted spruces were especially badly hit.

Shallow roots can **catch rain quickly**, before it seeps away or evaporates. That is why many **cacti** have flat, widely spread roots. This way they use the rare rain in the desert. In a long **drought**, however, it is a disadvantage. The top layer of soil dries out quickly, and the roots cannot reach deep water.

gewusst: Under an overturned root plate a pit forms, in which water often collects and new living things settle.
Lothar was one of the strongest storms that Switzerland experienced in the 20th century.

teile.einleitung: Spring is the season between winter and summer, in which nature wakes up again after the cold time. The days get longer, the sun warms more strongly, and flowers and trees begin to bloom everywhere. In Switzerland, most flowers bloom for the first time in the year in spring.
wichtigste: Astronomical spring begins in the Northern Hemisphere around 20 or 21 March.
Meteorological spring lasts from 1 March to 31 May.
At the start of spring, day and night are about equally long.
Early bloomers such as snowdrops and crocuses flower very early because they store food in bulbs or tubers.
Migratory birds such as swallows and storks return from the south in spring.
Many animals wake from hibernation, and many have young.
In the mountains, spring comes later than on the Plateau.

abschnitte.text: **Astronomical spring** begins with the equinox around 20 or 21 March and ends on 21 June. At the **equinox**, day and night are about equally long all over the Earth. Weather experts keep it simpler and count the months of March, April and May as **meteorological spring**. In the Southern Hemisphere, for example in Australia, it is spring when it is autumn here.

The Earth's axis is tilted, so in spring the Northern Hemisphere leans more and more towards the sun. At midday the sun climbs higher and shines a little longer each day. As a result, the ground and the air warm up. At the end of March the clocks are also put forward to **summer time**, so that it stays light longer in the evening.

Among the first flowers are **early bloomers** such as snowdrops, crocuses, spring snowflakes and wood anemones. They bloom on the forest floor before the trees carry leaves and cast shade. They get their strength from stores in bulbs, tubers or rootstocks. After them, cherry and apple trees blossom, and the dandelion turns the meadows yellow.

Hedgehogs, marmots and dormice wake from **hibernation**. Swallows, storks and cuckoos return from Africa, and the birds sing to defend a territory and attract a partner. Frogs and toads migrate to the waters where they spawn, and on some roads volunteers help them across. Many animals now have young, because there will soon be enough food.

In the Engadine, on 1 March, children go through the villages with bells at the **Chalandamarz** to drive away the winter. In Zurich, at the **Sechseläuten** in April, the Böögg is burnt, a snowman made of cotton wool. According to the custom, the faster its head explodes, the nicer the summer will be. Easter also falls in spring and is celebrated with eggs and Easter bunnies.

In the Alps, spring comes weeks later than on the Plateau. When the cherry trees are already in blossom in Basel or Geneva, there is often still snow in the mountains. With the **snowmelt**, streams and rivers carry a lot of water, and there are avalanches of wet snow. Only in June do gentians and alpenroses bloom on the alpine pastures.

begriffe.erklaerung: The day on which day and night are about equally long.
Plants that bloom very early in the year.
Birds that fly to warmer countries in winter and return in spring.
A long, deep sleep with which some animals survive the winter.

gewusst: In Geneva, it has been recorded for over 200 years when the first leaf opens on an official horse chestnut tree.
For every 100 metres of height, spring comes roughly three to four days later.
The Sechseläuten meadow in Zurich lies right on the lake near Bellevue.

teile.einleitung: A raised bed is an elevated garden bed with walls of wood, stone or metal. It is filled in layers and therefore gets warm inside. Vegetables often grow earlier and well in it.
wichtigste: A raised bed is filled in layers: branches at the bottom, soil on top.
Warmth is produced as the plant remains rot.
A fine wire mesh at the bottom protects against voles.
You can work without bending down much.
In the first year, heavy feeders such as courgettes and cabbage do well.
A raised bed dries out faster and needs regular watering.

abschnitte.text: A classic **raised bed** is filled in **layers**. Right at the bottom lie **branches and coarse shrub cuttings**. They let air in and let water drain away. On top of them come leaves and grass cuttings, then **compost** and, right at the top, good **soil**. A fine **wire mesh** is often laid on the ground. It stops **voles** from getting in from below and eating roots.

In a freshly filled raised bed, the plant remains slowly **rot**. This produces **warmth**. That is why it is warmer in a raised bed than in a normal bed. You can often **sow and harvest earlier**. Over time the filling breaks down and **settles**. So after a few years you have to top up the soil again.

In the first year, the raised bed is very rich in **nutrients**. Hungry plants, called **heavy feeders**, make good use of this. These include **courgettes**, tomatoes and **cabbage**. In the following years the nutrients become fewer. Then plants such as lettuce, radishes or herbs are more suitable.

Because a raised bed stands free, it dries out faster through **sun and wind** than a bed in the ground. In summer it therefore needs **regular water**. A layer of **mulch**, for example made of grass cuttings, helps to keep the moisture in the soil.

A big advantage is the raised working surface. You can work **without bending down much**, which is kind to your back. This is especially important for **older people**. That is why raised beds are also popular in **schools** and care homes. Woods such as **larch** and **Douglas fir** are suitable for the walls. They contain a lot of resin and rot more slowly than other woods.

gewusst: Inside a freshly filled raised bed, it can be much warmer than in the air above it.
In Switzerland people say “Zucchetti”, in Germany usually “Zucchini”, and in Britain the vegetable is called a courgette.

teile.einleitung: **Green algae** are a large group of algae that are green like land plants. There are tiny single cells, balls made of many cells, long filaments and leaf-like forms in the sea. Land plants arose from ancestors of the green algae.
wichtigste: Like land plants, green algae have chlorophyll a and b.
They store starch as a reserve substance.
Their cell wall mostly consists of cellulose.
The conjugating green algae are regarded as the closest relatives of land plants.
Well-known green algae are Chlamydomonas, Volvox, Spirogyra and Ulva.
With the umbrella alga Acetabularia, the role of the cell nucleus was investigated.

abschnitte.text: Green algae carry out **photosynthesis** with the pigments **chlorophyll a and b**, just like trees or grass. They store **starch** in their chloroplasts and mostly have a cell wall made of **cellulose**. That is why they are closely related to land plants. Genome analyses show that the **conjugating green algae** (Zygnematophyceae) are the closest relatives of land plants.

**Chlamydomonas** is a single cell with two **flagella**, with which it swims, and a red **eyespot**, which senses light. Researchers often use it as a model organism. **Volvox** forms hollow balls of hundreds to tens of thousands of flagellate cells. The balls turn slowly through the water of a pond.

**Spirogyra** lives in ponds and forms long, slimy filaments. Its name comes from the **spirally coiled chloroplasts** in each cell. In the sea grows **Ulva**, the **sea lettuce**, with a thin, leaf-like body, the **thallus**. In some countries it is eaten. Many green algae also live in lichens or on tree bark.

The **umbrella alga Acetabularia** is a single cell, but several centimetres big. It looks like a small umbrella with a stalk. The researcher **Joachim Hämmerling** swapped parts between different species. In doing so he showed that the **cell nucleus** determines what shape the umbrella gets. This was an important sign that the hereditary information lies in the nucleus.

gewusst: Some green algae colour snow in the Alps reddish, which is called “blood snow”.
The green coating on tree trunks often consists of tiny green algae.

teile.einleitung: With a sheet of paper and a wax crayon, you can capture the pattern of tree bark. This technique is called **frottage**. It is simple, it is fun and it shows how different nature looks.
wichtigste: Frottage means rubbing a pattern through with a pencil or crayon.
The word comes from the French “frotter”, which means to rub.
For a bark rubbing, you hold paper against the trunk.
You rub over it with the broad side of a wax crayon.
Thin paper shows the pattern most clearly.
Every tree species has its own bark pattern.

abschnitte.titel: How to make a bark rubbing
abschnitte.text: You hold a **sheet of paper** firmly against the tree trunk. Then you take a **wax crayon** without its paper wrapper and lay it flat. With the broad side, you rub evenly over the paper. Where the bark sticks out, it turns dark. Where there are grooves, the paper stays light. This is how the pattern of the bark appears.

**Thin paper** fits the grooves of the bark well. That is why the pattern shows through clearly. Thick card is too stiff and shows almost nothing. Chalk, soft pencils or charcoal are also good. It helps if a second person holds the paper so that it does not slip.

Every tree species has its own **bark**. Old **oaks** have thick bark with deep grooves, and the rubbing gives strong lines. The **beech** has smooth, grey bark, and its rubbing is almost even. The birch has horizontal stripes. If you compare several rubbings, you learn to recognise trees even without leaves.

Frottage works with many things. If you put a **leaf** under the paper and rub over it, the **leaf veins** appear. Coins, patterned stones, wooden boards or grilles can also be rubbed. With different colours, colourful pictures appear. This way you can make your own nature book of rubbings.

Frottage is not only a game, but also an **art technique**. The painter **Max Ernst** made it famous in the 1920s. For example, he rubbed wooden floors and leaves and invented imaginative pictures from them. Artists still use this technique today.

gewusst: With bark rubbings you can identify trees in winter, when they have no leaves.
A long time ago, people already transferred inscriptions on stones to paper using a similar technique.

teile.einleitung: **Oats** are a cereal that grows well in cool and damp regions. From its grains, people make rolled oats, porridge and oat drink. In the past it was important mainly as horse feed.
wichtigste: Oats are a cereal from the family of true grasses.
Its grains hang on a loose panicle.
Around the grain lies a hard covering, the husk.
Oats need a lot of water while growing.
From rolled oats and milk you cook porridge.
Oat drink is also made from oats.

abschnitte.text: Like wheat and barley, oats belong to the **true grasses**. Unlike them, they have no dense ear. Their grains hang on a loose **panicle**, that is, on many fine, branched stalks. Each grain is surrounded by a hard covering, the **husk**. It is removed before eating.

Oats like a **cool, damp climate** and need a lot of **water** while growing. They cope better than wheat with poor soils. That is why they are grown a lot in countries such as Scotland, Scandinavia or Canada. There are oat fields in Switzerland too.

For **rolled oats**, the hulled grains are steamed and rolled flat. The flakes are **flat and round**. With milk you cook warm **porridge** from them. Rolled oats also go into Bircher muesli and biscuits. From oats and water, **oat drink** is also made, which many people drink as a replacement for milk.

For a long time oats were mainly feed for **horses**, which gained a lot of strength from them. Today more and more people eat them too. Oats contain many **dietary fibres**, which keep you full for a long time. They also supply protein, minerals and vitamins.

gewusst: Oats have more fat than most other cereals.
The German saying “the oats are pricking him” means that someone is frisky, like a horse that has been fed too well.

teile.einleitung: Almost everyone knows the **hook-and-loop fastener** (Velcro) on shoes, jackets or bags. It was invented by the Swiss engineer **George de Mestral**. He copied the idea from a plant that likes to cling to clothes and fur: the burdock.
wichtigste: George de Mestral was born in 1907 in Saint-Saphorin-sur-Morges in the canton of Vaud.
Around 1941, after a hunting trip, he discovered burrs in the fur of his dog.
Under the microscope he saw tiny hooks on the burrs.
In 1951 he applied for a patent for his invention in Switzerland, and it was granted in 1955.
The name “Velcro” comes from “velours” and “crochet”.
A hook-and-loop fastener consists of hooks and loops.

abschnitte.text: George de Mestral was born in 1907 in **Saint-Saphorin-sur-Morges** near Lausanne. He was an **engineer** and was already tinkering with inventions as a teenager. He became famous through a discovery that he made on a quite ordinary outing.

After a hunting trip in the Alps around 1941, he noticed the many **burrs** in the fur of his dog. The fruits of the burdock stay hanging on fur and clothes. This way their seeds are spread far by animals. De Mestral wanted to know why they stick so well. Under the **microscope** he saw many elastic **little hooks** that catch in loops of fabric and hair.

He wanted to transfer this principle to a fabric. The first strips made of **cotton** wore out quickly. Only with **nylon** did it succeed: from it, firm hooks could be formed that still stayed elastic and durable. In 1951 he applied for a **patent** for the invention in Switzerland, and it was granted in 1955. After that, industrial production began.

A hook-and-loop fastener consists of two strips. One carries small **hooks**, the other soft **loops**. If you press them together, they catch on each other. If you pull hard, they come apart again. The brand name **Velcro** is made up of the French words **velours** (velvet) and **crochet** (hook).

Anyone who copies technical solutions from plants or animals is practising **biomimetics**. This field transfers inventions of nature to technology. The hook-and-loop fastener is regarded as one of the best-known examples of it. It shows that good ideas sometimes begin with looking closely.

gewusst: The idea for the hook-and-loop fastener came from burrs in the fur of a dog.
The first attempts made of cotton did not last long, and only nylon brought success.

teile.einleitung: Medicinal plants are plants whose active substances can help against illnesses and complaints. People use them as tea, ointment, drops or tablets. Many modern medicines have their model in medicinal plants, for example aspirin in the bark of the willow.
wichtigste: Medicinal plants contain active substances that can help with complaints.
From willow bark, a remedy for fever and pain was obtained in the past.
This remedy was the model for the medicine aspirin.
German chamomile is often drunk as tea for inflammations and stomach complaints.
Arnica is applied externally for bruises and contusions.
Menthol gives peppermint its cooling taste.
Ribwort plantain is a traditional cough remedy.

abschnitte.text: Medicinal plants contain **active substances** that do something in the body, for example ease pain or inhibit inflammation. Depending on the plant, people use flowers, leaves, roots, seeds or bark. The study of treatment with plants is called **phytotherapy**. Thousands of years ago, people in all cultures already knew medicinal herbs.

Even in antiquity, people chewed **willow bark** for fever and pain. It contains the substance salicin, from which the body makes salicylic acid. Chemists made from it a better-tolerated active substance, acetylsalicylic acid. From 1899 it was sold under the name **aspirin** and is still one of the best-known medicines in the world.

**German chamomile**, with its white and yellow flowers, is used as a tea for inflammations and stomach complaints. Peppermint contains menthol, which has a cooling effect and helps with tummy ache and colds. Ribwort plantain, with its narrow leaves, grows on meadows and is used as a cough syrup. Sage helps with a sore throat, fennel with wind.

The yellow-flowering **arnica** grows on lean mountain meadows and is applied only externally as an ointment or gel, for example for bruises and contusions. Taken internally, it can be poisonous. In Switzerland, the priest Johann Künzle became very well known with his herb books. Many Swiss firms still make medicines and teas from herbs today.

Herbal remedies too can have side effects or be poisonous if you take too much of them. Some medicinal plants look very like poisonous plants, so you should collect only what you know for certain. In Switzerland, some wild plants are under **nature protection** and may not be picked. For serious complaints, you should always go to a doctor.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that has a particular effect in the body.
The treatment of illnesses with plants.
A substance from peppermint that has a cooling effect.
A greasy mass with active substances that you rub onto the skin.

gewusst: Many active substances in today's medicines were originally discovered in plants.
The name aspirin contains a reference to meadowsweet, which was then called Spiraea and also contains salicylic acid.

teile.einleitung: When there is still snow outside, the first flowers are already poking out of the ground. They are called **early bloomers**. They have a clever trick for flowering so early in the year.
wichtigste: Early bloomers flower in late winter and spring.
Many store food in a bulb or tuber.
In the woods they use the light before the trees have leaves.
Well-known early bloomers are crocus, snowdrop and spring snowflake.
In deciduous woods, liverleaf and wood anemones bloom.
Many early bloomers are protected and should not be picked.

abschnitte.text: Many early bloomers have built up a **store** in the soil. It sits in a **bulb**, a **tuber** or a thick rootstock. With it they can grow very quickly, even when it is still cool. After flowering, the leaves collect new food for the next year. In summer, often nothing more can be seen of them.

In spring, the deciduous trees are still bare. That is why a lot of **light** falls on the forest floor. Early bloomers such as the **wood anemone** and the **liverleaf** make use of this. The liverleaf blooms blue as early as March. Its leaves have three lobes like a liver. As soon as the trees carry leaves, it becomes too shady on the ground.

The **crocus** often forms purple and white carpets on meadows. It has only a very short stem. The **spring snowflake** has the month of March in its German name, “Märzenbecher”. Its white bells have green or yellow tips. The **squill** is also called “Blaustern” (blue star) in German, because its flowers look like little blue stars.

The **daffodil** is a narcissus. In the middle of its flower stands a long tube like a trumpet. The **cowslip** has several flowers on one stalk. This is reminiscent of a bunch of keys, which is why its German name is “Schlüsselblume” (key flower). Many of these plants are poisonous, for example daffodil and crocus. That is why you do not eat them.

abschnitte.titel: Tulips from all over the world
abschnitte.text: The **tulip** originally comes from Asia. Today it is famous in the **Netherlands**. There, huge colourful tulip fields bloom in spring. In Swiss gardens, too, tulips, crocuses and narcissi are popular. Their bulbs are put in the ground in **autumn** so that they flower in spring.

gewusst: Some early bloomers even grow through a thin covering of snow.
Almost 400 years ago, tulip bulbs were so sought after in the Netherlands that huge sums were paid for single bulbs.

teile.einleitung: The **rose hip** (in German, “Hagebutte”) is the red fruit of the rose. In autumn, rose hips glow in many hedges. They are full of vitamin C and can be made into tea and jam.
wichtigste: The rose hip is the fruit of the rose.
Ripe rose hips are mostly red.
They contain especially much vitamin C.
The dog rose forms many rose hips in hedges.
After the first frost they are soft and sweet.
From the seeds, children used to make itching powder.

abschnitte.text: When a rose has finished flowering, the **rose hip** forms in its place. Botanists call it an **aggregate of achenes**. The actual fruits are the many small **seeds** inside, which are tiny nutlets. The red flesh around them develops from the base of the flower. Especially many rose hips are borne by the **dog rose**, which grows wild in hedges and at the edges of woods.

Ripe rose hips are mostly **red**, some orange. Their flesh tastes **sweet and sour**. Rose hips contain especially much **vitamin C**, often even more than lemons. **After the first frost** they become soft and sweeter. Then they are also easier to process.

From rose hips you cook **jam**. For this you remove the seeds and little hairs and press the flesh through a sieve. Dried rose hips make a red, slightly sour **tea**. In Switzerland, rose hip jam, also called rose hip purée, is a popular filling for biscuits.

The seeds are surrounded by fine, **hard little hairs**. On the skin they itch strongly. Children used to make **itching powder** from them and sprinkle it down other people's collars. In winter, many rose hips still hang on the bush. Then they are important food for **birds** such as blackbirds and thrushes.

gewusst: The well-known German children's song “Ein Männlein steht im Walde” is about a rose hip.
Rose hips can stay hanging on the bush all through the winter.

teile.einleitung: A lichen is not a single living thing, but a partnership between a fungus and an alga. Together they manage to live in places where hardly anything else grows.
wichtigste: A lichen consists of a fungus and an alga.
The alga makes food using sunlight.
The fungus protects the alga from drying out and supplies water with minerals.
This living together to the benefit of both is called symbiosis.
Lichens grow on stones, walls and tree bark, even high up in the mountains.
Many different lichens indicate clean air.

abschnitte.text: A **lichen** consists of a **fungus** and an **alga**. The two live so closely together that they look like a single living thing. The **alga** makes food with the help of **sunlight**, just like green plants. The **fungus** gives it **protection from drying out** and supplies it with **water and minerals**. This living together, from which both benefit, is called **symbiosis**.

Lichens grow on **stones, walls and tree bark**. They even live on **rocks high up in the mountains**, where hardly anything else grows. When it is dry, they fall into a kind of rigid state. As soon as it rains, they become active again. Lichens mostly grow very slowly, often only a few millimetres a year.

The **yellow wall lichen** is often seen as **yellow to orange** patches on walls and branches. The **map lichen** grows on stones in the mountains. It forms yellow-green patches with black edges and looks like a colourful **map**. Other lichens are grey, form beards on branches or grow like little shrubs.

Lichens take in water and substances directly from the air. That is why many species react sensitively to air pollution. If **many different lichens** grow in a place, the **air is clean**. Researchers therefore use lichens as **indicator organisms** for air quality.

In the far north, the **reindeer lichen** grows in large carpets on the ground. In winter, **reindeer** scrape the snow away and eat it. There it is one of the most important sources of food. Similar lichens also grow in Switzerland, in mountain woods and on heaths.

gewusst: Some lichens on rocks in the mountains are hundreds of years old.
In experiments, lichens even survived the conditions in space.

teile.einleitung: The Norway spruce is the most common tree in Swiss woods. In Switzerland it is often also called “Rottanne” (red fir), although it is not a true fir at all. Houses, paper and even violins are made from its wood, and as a Christmas tree it stands in many living rooms.
wichtigste: Overall, the Norway spruce is the most common tree species in Swiss woods.
In Switzerland it is often also called “Rottanne”.
Its cones hang downwards.
The needles of the spruce feel sharp and prickly.
The spruce can grow up to 50 metres tall.
It has shallow roots and can therefore easily fall over in a storm.
Spruce wood is one of the most important building timbers in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The Norway spruce, with the scientific name Picea abies, is a **conifer** with a slender, pointed crown. Its needles are short, stiff and sharp, and they prick when you grasp a twig. The bark is reddish brown, hence the Swiss name **Rottanne**. The spruce keeps its needles in winter too. It can grow over 40 metres tall, sometimes up to 50 metres.

The cones of the spruce **hang downwards** and fall to the ground whole. With the silver fir, on the other hand, the cones stand upright on the twigs and fall apart on the tree. Most of the “fir cones” that you find in the woods are therefore really **spruce cones**. Squirrels and birds such as the common crossbill get the seeds out of the cones.

The spruce originally comes from cool regions in northern Europe and from the mountains. In Switzerland it grows naturally mainly in the Alps and in the Jura, up to a height of about 2000 metres. Because it grows quickly and gives good wood, it was also planted a lot on the Plateau. This made it the **most common tree species** in Switzerland.

The spruce is a **shallow-rooted tree**: its roots spread out like a plate just below the ground. In strong storms it therefore tips over easily. The hurricane **Lothar** blew down millions of trees in Switzerland on 26 December 1999, including a great many spruces. Heat and drought also affect it, and weakened trees are attacked by the **bark beetle**.

Spruce wood is light-coloured, light and yet sturdy. It is used to build roof frames, houses and furniture, and it is turned into **paper**. Spruce wood that has grown especially slowly in mountain forests is a sought-after **tonewood** for violins and guitars. Many people put up a spruce as a Christmas tree at Christmas.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tree with needle-shaped leaves that mostly stays green in winter too.
A tree whose roots grow only just below the surface of the ground.
A small beetle that lives under the bark and damages weakened trees.
Especially even-grained wood for building musical instruments.

gewusst: A rhyme helps with telling them apart: “The spruce pricks, the fir does not.”
The needles of the spruce are four-sided and can be rolled between your fingers, while fir needles are flat.
In the Risoud forest in the Vaud Jura, particularly fine tonewood grows, from which famous violins have been built.

teile.einleitung: **Hemlock** (in German, “Gefleckter Schierling”, or “spotted hemlock”) is one of the most poisonous plants in Central Europe. It looks harmless and can be mistaken for kitchen herbs. That is why it is important to recognise it.
wichtigste: Hemlock is very poisonous.
Its stem has reddish brown to purple spots.
The small white flowers form umbels like umbrellas.
Crushed leaves smell unpleasantly of mouse urine.
Young leaves look similar to parsley.
It often grows 1 to 2 metres tall.

abschnitte.text: The clearest feature is the **stem**. It is smooth, hollow and has **reddish brown to purple spots**. That is where the German name “Gefleckter” (spotted) comes from. The plant often grows **1 to 2 metres** tall, sometimes even taller, so taller than a child. Its leaves are finely pinnate. If you crush them, they smell unpleasantly of **mouse urine**. But it is better not to touch the plant at all.

Hemlock has many small **white flowers**. They form **umbels**, which look like opened umbrellas. It belongs to the **umbellifer family**. This family also includes carrot, parsley, dill and fennel. But other poisonous plants also belong to it. That is why caution is always needed with white-flowering umbel plants.

The young, finely pinnate leaves look similar to **parsley**. It can also be mistaken for wild chervil or meadow caraway. That is why the rule is: you only collect wild herbs if you know them quite certainly, best with an expert. If you suspect poisoning, in Switzerland you call **Tox Info Suisse** at once on the number 145.

All parts of the plant contain a strong poison, **coniine**. Even small amounts are dangerous. The poison paralyses the muscles. In antiquity, a drink made from hemlock was used as a punishment. The Greek philosopher **Socrates** was sentenced to death in 399 BC and had to drink a cup of hemlock.

Hemlock is found on **roadsides**, along hedges, on rubble heaps and on banks. It likes nutrient-rich soils. So it can also grow where many people pass by. Anyone who knows it simply leaves it standing and washes their hands after touching it.

gewusst: Hemlock is related to carrot and parsley.
In Switzerland, the emergency number 145 helps with poisonings around the clock.

teile.einleitung: The **tree of heaven** (in German, “Götterbaum”) comes from China and was brought to Europe a long time ago. Today it spreads so strongly that it pushes out native plants. In Switzerland it counts as an **invasive** species.
wichtigste: The tree of heaven comes from China.
It reproduces by seeds and by root suckers.
If you fell it, it sprouts strongly again from the stump and roots.
It gives off inhibiting substances into the soil that slow other plants.
Its fruits are winged.
In Switzerland it may no longer be planted.

abschnitte.text: The tree of heaven grows very fast and can reach over 20 metres in height. Its leaves are long and **pinnate**, similar to the staghorn sumac. If you rub them, they **smell unpleasant**. The fruits are **winged**, and the wind carries them far away. In the 18th century the tree came from **China** to Europe and was planted in parks.

In the 19th century, the tree of heaven was also planted for **silkworm breeding**. The caterpillars of a particular species of silk moth eat its leaves. People hoped to be able to make silk this way. The breeding had no great success, but the trees stayed and spread.

The tree of heaven **tolerates heat, drought and poor soils**. That is why it grows well in **cities**, on railway embankments and in cracks in walls. It reproduces by seeds and by **root suckers**. It also gives off **inhibiting substances** into the soil that slow the growth of other plants. In southern Switzerland, for example in Ticino, it already forms dense stands.

Anyone who simply **fells** a tree of heaven soon has a problem: it sprouts strongly again from the **stump and roots**. Experts therefore often first strip a ring of bark so that the tree dies slowly. Because it endangers woods and natural areas, it may no longer be planted in **Switzerland**. Communes and cantons control it in a targeted way.

gewusst: A young tree of heaven can grow over a metre in one year.
The name comes from a word from Indonesia that means “tree of heaven”.
