teile.einleitung: The tides are the regular rising and falling of the sea level on coasts. The rising is called high tide or flood, the falling low tide or ebb. Ebb and flood are caused by the pull of the moon and the sun.
wichtigste: The tides consist of ebb and flood.
Ebb and flood arise from the pull of the moon and the sun.
The moon has the greater influence of the two.
On most coasts there are two high tides and two low tides a day.
The difference between high and low water is called the tidal range.
In Swiss lakes, the tides are so small that you do not notice them.

abschnitte.text: At **high tide**, the water on the coast slowly rises until the highest level is reached, high water. After that it falls again during the **low tide** until low water. A whole cycle takes about twelve and a half hours. That is why the times of ebb and flood shift by about 50 minutes every day.

The moon pulls on the water of the Earth with its **gravity**. On the side that faces the moon, a mountain of water forms as a result. On the opposite side of the Earth, too, a mountain of water forms. The Earth turns under these two mountains, which is why there are usually two high tides a day.

The sun also pulls on the water, but its influence is about half as great as that of the moon. At new moon and full moon, the sun and moon pull in a line, and then the high tides are especially high, which is called a **spring tide**. At half moon they pull crosswise, and then the difference is smaller, which is called a **neap tide**. The word “spring” in spring tide, by the way, has nothing to do with the season.

How much the water level changes depends on the shape of the coast. In the Mediterranean, the **tidal range** is often only a few centimetres. On the North Sea it is usually two to four metres. In the Bay of Fundy in Canada, the water can rise by over 15 metres, which is as high as a five-storey house.

On flat coasts, a broad strip of sea floor dries out at low tide, the **mudflats** (in German, the “Watt”). The Wadden Sea on the North Sea has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2009. Lugworms, mussels and crabs live there, and many migratory birds find food. Anyone who walks on the mudflats needs an experienced guide, because the tide comes back quickly.

begriffe.erklaerung: The time when the sea water on the coast rises.
The time when the sea water on the coast falls.
The difference in height between high water and low water.
Sea floor that dries out at low tide.

gewusst: The monastery island of Mont-Saint-Michel in France used to be an island at high tide and could be reached on foot at low tide.
The solid rock of the Earth also rises and falls by a few decimetres because of the tides, without us feeling it.

teile.einleitung: Glacier melt means the melting of glaciers because of global warming. Since about 1850, the glaciers in the Alps and all over the world have been getting smaller and smaller. In Switzerland you can watch this retreat especially well.
wichtigste: Glacier melt is the melting of glaciers because of global warming.
The Alpine glaciers have been shrinking since about 1850.
Since the 1980s, the melting has been getting faster and faster.
In the hot years 2022 and 2023, Swiss glaciers lost especially much ice.
Melting glaciers make the sea level rise worldwide.
Without glaciers, water is lacking in rivers and reservoirs in summer.
Fewer greenhouse gases can slow the melt, but not stop it at once.

abschnitte.text: A glacier stays the same size only if as much snow is added in winter as melts in summer. Because it is getting warmer through **climate change**, much more ice melts in summer. Little snow in winter and hot summers are especially bad for glaciers. Dust and soot on the ice also make it darker, so that it takes up more of the sun's warmth.

Since the end of the **Little Ice Age** around 1850, the Alpine glaciers have lost more than half of their ice. Experts of the Swiss Glacier Monitoring Network GLAMOS measure every year how much ice disappears. In the record years 2022 and 2023, the Swiss glaciers together lost about ten per cent of their volume. Without strong climate protection, most Alpine glaciers could have disappeared by the year 2100.

The **Rhone Glacier** used to reach down into the valley near Gletsch, but today it ends far up in a meltwater lake. To protect an ice grotto from melting, part of the glacier is covered with white sheets in summer. The Pizol Glacier in the St Gallen Alps has almost completely disappeared, and in 2019 people held a kind of farewell ceremony there. At the Great Aletsch Glacier, too, the snout retreats every year.

Meltwater from glaciers fills rivers such as the Rhone, the Rhine and the Inn in summer. When the glaciers have disappeared, these rivers carry less water in hot summers. This affects **hydroelectric power stations**, agriculture and shipping. Worldwide, the melting of glaciers and ice sheets contributes to the rise in **sea level**.

When the ice disappears, mountain slopes lose their hold. Then **rockfalls** and debris flows, that is, streams of mud and rubble, can happen more often. The permafrost, the permanently frozen ground in the high mountains, also thaws. New glacier lakes can suddenly drain and flood valleys, which is why they are monitored.

begriffe.erklaerung: The long-term warming of the Earth, mainly through greenhouse gases.
A cool period from about 1300 to 1850, in which the glaciers were very large.
Ground that stays frozen all year round.
The calculation of whether a glacier has gained or lost ice in a year.

gewusst: In some places, glacier melt brings up ancient tree trunks that show that forest grew there thousands of years ago.
As the glaciers retreat, hundreds of new mountain lakes are forming in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The **daisy** is one of the best-known flowers. It grows in almost every meadow and lawn and blooms almost all year round. Children like to weave wreaths from it.
wichtigste: The daisy blooms almost all year round.
In the evening it closes its flower.
Its leaves lie flat on the ground, which is why it survives mowing.
It grows about 5 to 15 centimetres tall.
Daisies are edible.
The plant lives for several years.

abschnitte.text: What looks like a single flower is a **flower head** made of many small flowers. On the outside stand white **ray florets**, often with pink tips. In the middle sit many tiny yellow **disc florets**. That is why the daisy belongs to the **daisy family**, like the sunflower. The plant grows about **5 to 15 centimetres** tall.

abschnitte.titel: Open in the morning, closed in the evening
abschnitte.text: In the **evening** and in rain, the daisy **closes** its flower. This way it protects its pollen from wet and cold. In the morning it opens again. During the day the little head turns towards the **sun**. It blooms **almost all year round**, even in winter on mild days.

The leaves of the daisy form a **rosette** that lies **flat on the ground**. The lawnmower passes over it without catching it. Soon new flower stalks grow back. The plant is **perennial** and can also reproduce by seeds. That is why a lawn is often dotted with white.

From many daisies you can weave a **flower wreath**. The flowers and young leaves are **edible** and taste slightly nutty. You can sprinkle them over a salad as decoration, for example. It is important to take only flowers from clean meadows, where no dogs or sprays have been.

gewusst: The Latin name “Bellis perennis” means something like “lasting beauty”.
In Switzerland the daisy is often called “Gänseblüemli”.

teile.einleitung: A fen is a wet habitat that is fed by groundwater or slope water. In Switzerland, fens are rare and strictly protected.
wichtigste: A fen is also called a low moor.
It gets its water from groundwater or slope water.
Because the water brings nutrients with it, more species grow here than in a raised bog.
Many fens are mown only in autumn, as litter meadows.
Without mowing, a fen becomes overgrown with bushes and slowly grows over.
The fens of national importance cover about 0.5 per cent of the country's area.

abschnitte.titel: Water from below and from the slope
abschnitte.text: A **fen** is also called a **low moor**. It gets its water from the **groundwater** or from **slope water** that seeps out of the ground. A **raised bog**, on the other hand, gets its water only from the rain. Because the water in a fen brings **nutrients** with it, **more plant species** grow here than in a raised bog. The soil stays damp all year round.

Many fens are dominated by **sedges**. These are grass-like plants with an often **three-edged** stem. On the lake shore, **reed** often grows, a tall grass with a brown plume of flowers. Orchids, gentians, cotton grass and many other flowers join them. Dragonflies, grasshoppers and butterflies are also at home here.

Many fen meadows are used as **litter meadows**. They are mown only in **autumn**, when the plants have finished flowering. The cuttings are used as **bedding** in the stable, because they are of little use as feed. This use is important, because without mowing a fen becomes **overgrown with bushes**. Shrubs and trees spring up, and the rare bog plants disappear.

In 1987 the Swiss electorate accepted the initiative to protect bogs. Since then, bogs of special beauty and national importance have been protected. The **federal inventory** lists **about 1,400** fens of national importance (as of 2025). Together they cover only about **0.5 per cent** of the country's area. In the past there were many more bogs, and most were drained.

gewusst: The bog protection initiative was also called the “Rothenthurm initiative”, after a bog in the canton of Schwyz.
The German name “Streuwiese” (litter meadow) comes from the bedding that is obtained from it for the animals in the stable.

teile.einleitung: Wood is the hard material that the trunk, branches and roots of trees and shrubs are made of. People use it to build houses, furniture and toys, and to heat their homes.
wichtigste: Wood forms inside trees and shrubs.
Dry wood usually floats, because there is a lot of air in it.
The spruce is the most common tree in the Swiss forest and supplies a lot of building timber.
Oak wood is hard and heavy, while balsa wood is especially light.
Wood is a renewable raw material.
The carpenter builds roof frames and timber houses out of wood.

abschnitte.text: Wood is the solid part in the **trunk**, in the branches and in the roots. Every year a tree adds a new layer of wood. This is how the **annual rings** form, by which you can tell the age. Freshly felled wood still contains a lot of water. It is called **green wood** or fresh wood.

Most woods are lighter than water, because there is a lot of **air** in them. That is why dry wood usually floats. **Balsa wood** from the balsa tree is especially light, and people like to build model aeroplanes from it. **Oak wood**, by contrast, is a heavy **hardwood**. Spruce and poplar have softer wood.

In Switzerland the **spruce** is the most common tree. Its wood is widely used for building. The **carpenter** builds roof frames, staircases and whole timber houses from it. The joiner makes furniture and windows. A practical wood material is **plywood**: several thin layers of wood are glued crosswise, which makes the board stable and hardly warps.

abschnitte.titel: A raw material that grows back
abschnitte.text: Wood is regarded as a **renewable raw material**. If trees are felled and new ones are planted or allowed to grow back, there is wood again. In Switzerland, the Forest Act requires that the forest area be preserved. Animals use wood too: the **beaver** fells trees with its strong teeth and builds dams and lodges from branches.

gewusst: About a third of the area of Switzerland is covered with forest.
There are kinds of wood that are heavier than water and therefore sink, for example lignum vitae.

teile.einleitung: **Golden rice** is a genetically modified rice with yellowish grains. It is meant to help people who eat mainly rice and do not get enough vitamin A. It was developed, among others, at ETH Zurich.
wichtigste: Golden rice makes beta-carotene in its grains.
The body converts beta-carotene into vitamin A.
A lack of vitamin A can lead to night blindness.
The beta-carotene forms in the endosperm, the starchy part of the grain.
One gene of the first golden rice came from the daffodil.
In 2021 the Philippines became the first country to allow it to be grown.

abschnitte.text: In many poor countries, people eat almost only rice. Normal white rice, however, contains no **beta-carotene**, the precursor of **vitamin A**. If vitamin A is lacking, people see badly in the dusk, which is called **night blindness**. A severe deficiency also weakens the defence against disease, especially in children.

The researchers **Ingo Potrykus** of ETH Zurich and **Peter Beyer** of the University of Freiburg im Breisgau presented golden rice in the year 2000. They built in genes so that the plant makes beta-carotene in the **endosperm**, that is, in the starchy part that we eat. A gene for the enzyme **phytoene synthase** came from the **daffodil**, another from a bacterium. The beta-carotene gives the grains their golden-yellow colour.

In 2005, **Golden Rice 2** was presented. In it, the gene for phytoene synthase comes from **maize**. As a result, the rice makes clearly more beta-carotene than the first version. Even a normal portion can thus cover a large part of the need for vitamin A.

In 2018, the USA, Canada, Australia and New Zealand classed the rice as a safe food, without growing it themselves. The **Philippines** in 2021 became the first country to allow commercial cultivation. Opponents criticise the genetic engineering and call instead for a more varied diet. Supporters see the rice as a simple help against deficiency. In 2024, a court in the Philippines halted cultivation for the time being.

gewusst: The colour of golden rice comes from the same substance that makes carrots orange.
The inventors made sure that poor farmers may use the rice without licence fees.

teile.einleitung: Some plants and animals are leftovers from the ice age. When it became warmer, their relatives retreated to the north or upwards. Some stayed behind in cold special habitats. Such species are called **glacial relicts**.
wichtigste: A glacial relict is a species that has survived in isolation since the ice age.
The dwarf birch occurs in some raised bogs of the Jura.
Species that live in the Arctic and in the Alps show an arctic-alpine disjunction.
The mountain hare lives in the far north and in the Alps.
The cold phase “Younger Dryas” is named after the mountain avens.
Glacial relicts often survive in raised bogs and cold block screes.

abschnitte.text: After the glaciers retreated, the **Swiss Plateau** was at first treeless. It looked like an open **tundra** with dwarf shrubs. Only with the warming did birches, pines and later broadleaf trees move in. Many cold-loving species retreated to the north or upwards. Some stayed behind in cool places. These **glacial relicts** have survived there in isolation since the ice age.

Some species live today in the **Arctic** and in the **Alps**, but not in between. This is called **arctic-alpine disjunction**. During the ice age, these species lived in the ice-free area between the great glaciers. After that, their occurrences were separated. An example among mammals is the **mountain hare**. It lives in the far north and in the Alps.

Glacial relicts often survive in **raised bogs**. These are cool, wet and **low in nutrients**. Strongly competitive species have hardly any chance there. In some raised bogs of the **Jura**, the **dwarf birch** grows, which is otherwise widespread in the Arctic. In some **block screes**, too, cold air flows out of the hollow spaces in summer. This cool microclimate allows mountain species to survive far down.

At the end of the last ice age there was one more cold phase, the **Younger Dryas**. It is named after the **mountain avens**, whose scientific genus name is **Dryas**. Remains of this plant are common in deposits from that time. The mountain avens grows today in the Alps and in the Arctic.

gewusst: In the Jura, in some bogs, dwarf birches grow that otherwise live in the Arctic.
A whole cold phase of Earth's history is named after a small flower, the mountain avens.

teile.einleitung: The bilberry (in German, “Heidelbeere”) is a small blue berry that grows in woods and in the mountains. In German it is also called “Blaubeere”. Anyone who eats many wild bilberries has a blue tongue afterwards.
wichtigste: Heidelbeere and Blaubeere are two German names for the same fruit.
Wild bilberries are about as big as a pea.
They are dark blue to violet on the inside too.
Their pigment colours tongue, teeth and fingers blue.
They ripen around July and August.
The big blueberries from the shop originally come from North America.

abschnitte.text: The **bilberry** grows on low dwarf shrubs in woods, on heaths and in the mountains. Because of its colour, it is also called **“Blaubeere”** (“blue berry”) in German. Both names mean the same fruit. Wild bilberries are small, about **as big as a pea**, so roughly half a centimetre. In Switzerland you often find them in coniferous woods and in the Alps.

Wild bilberries contain a strong **blue pigment**. In them, not only the skin is blue, but the **flesh** too, dark blue to violet. Anyone who eats many of them has a blue tongue, blue teeth and blue fingers afterwards. Stains on clothes are also hard to get out.

The big blueberries from the shop are **cultivated blueberries**. They were bred from a species from **North America** and grow on tall shrubs. Their berries are bigger than wild bilberries, but **pale inside**. That is why they hardly colour the mouth blue.

Wild bilberries ripen in our country around **July and August**, in the mountains a little later. Because they are so small, collecting takes a lot of patience. In the past, a **berry comb** was used for it. It has many teeth with which you strip the berries from the little shrubs. In some areas the berry comb is not allowed today, because it can damage the plants.

Bilberries are also important for many animals. The **capercaillie**, a large woodland bird, likes to live in mountain woods with many bilberry shrubs. In summer it eats the berries and also the leaves. Foxes, bears, birds and mice also eat bilberries.

gewusst: The bilberry belongs to the same plant family as the alpenrose: the heath family.
The capercaillie has become rare in Switzerland and depends on woods with many bilberries.

teile.einleitung: The orange lily (in German, “Feuerlilie”, or “fire lily”) is a bright orange flower of the mountains. Its large flowers face upwards, as if they were licking like little flames into the sky.
wichtigste: The orange lily blooms bright orange.
Its flowers point upwards.
A flower has six petals with dark spots on the inside.
It grows on sunny mountain slopes.
It usually grows 20 to 90 centimetres tall.
On some orange lilies, small bulbils grow between leaf and stem.

abschnitte.text: The **orange lily** gets its name from its bright **orange** colour. Its flowers are large and wide open. Unlike many other lilies, they point **upwards**. Each flower has **six petals**. On the inside you can see **dark spots** on them.

The orange lily grows on **sunny mountain slopes**, in mountain meadows and in stony places. It likes it warm and bright. It usually grows **20 to 90 centimetres** tall. It blooms in early summer, around June and July. In Switzerland you find it mainly in the Alps.

abschnitte.titel: Bulbs underground and on the stem
abschnitte.text: Like all lilies, the orange lily has a **bulb** underground. In it, it stores nutrients for the next year. On some orange lilies, **small bulbils** also grow between leaf and stem. They fall off and can grow into new plants. This way the orange lily can reproduce even without seeds.

The orange lily has become **rare** in many areas. That is why it is **protected** in many places. You should not pick it or dig it up. It is nicest to admire it or photograph it outdoors. This way other walkers can enjoy it too.

gewusst: The orange lily belongs to the same genus as the martagon lily, which also grows in the Swiss mountains.
Its scientific name “Lilium bulbiferum” means “bulbil-bearing lily”.

teile.einleitung: In summer the cornfields turn golden yellow, and combine harvesters drive about everywhere. Now it is time for the **grain harvest**. In Switzerland it takes place mainly in July and August. In the past it was hard manual labour, but today machines do most of it.
wichtigste: The grain harvest in Switzerland takes place mainly in July and August.
Dry weather is needed for the harvest.
In the past, grain was cut with a scythe or sickle.
In threshing, the grains are separated from the stalks.
The grains are stored dry in silos.
What is left behind is straw and short stubble.

abschnitte.text: The grain harvest in Switzerland takes place mainly in **July** and **August**. By then the grains are ripe and dry. The farmer often checks whether the grain is ripe by **biting** a grain. A ripe grain is hard and can hardly be bitten through. If it is still soft, he waits. **Dry weather** is important: wet grain is hard to harvest and can go mouldy.

In the past, farmers mowed the grain by hand with the **scythe** or the **sickle**. This was very tiring, and the whole family helped. The stalks were tied together into **sheaves** and stood up in the field to dry. Later the grains were beaten out of the ears with the **flail**. This is called **threshing**.

Today the **combine harvester** does almost everything at once. It cuts the stalks, threshes the grains out and collects them in a tank. The stalks fall onto the field as **straw**. Short, hard remains of stalks stay standing in the ground, the **stubble**. Such a field is called a **stubble field**.

The grains go into large containers, the **silos**. There they stay dry and clean until they go on to the mill or as feed. The straw is pressed into bales and used as bedding in the stable. Then the field is prepared for the next sowing.

gewusst: A farmer can check with one bite whether the grain is ripe.
In the past, sheaves were stood up in the field to dry.

teile.einleitung: Pepper, cinnamon, cloves and nutmeg are in every kitchen today. In the past, these **spices** were as precious as gold. The **spice trade** linked Asia with Europe, made cities rich and shaped the history of seafaring and of the colonies.
wichtigste: The Moluccas in Indonesia were called the “Spice Islands”.
Black pepper comes from the Malabar Coast in India.
In the late Middle Ages, Venice became rich through the spice trade.
The Dutch East India Company was founded in 1602.
Saffron is obtained from the stigmas of a crocus flower.
Outside Mexico, vanilla has to be pollinated by hand.

abschnitte.text: Many spices grew only in Asia. On the **Moluccas** in Indonesia, the “Spice Islands”, **cloves** and **nutmegs** grew. Black **pepper** comes from the damp forests of the **Malabar Coast** in south-western India. **Cinnamon** is the dried inner bark of the cinnamon tree and for a long time came mainly from **Sri Lanka**, which used to be called Ceylon.

In the late Middle Ages, merchants from **Venice** bought the spices in ports such as **Alexandria** and **Beirut**. Then they sold them on all over Europe. This made Venice rich. Pepper was so expensive that traders earned great fortunes with it. A rich merchant was therefore mockingly called a **“Pfeffersack”** (pepper sack). Later, Portuguese sailors looked for the sea route to India in order to get at the spices directly.

abschnitte.titel: The fight for nutmeg and cloves
abschnitte.text: In 1602 the **Dutch East India Company**, VOC for short, was founded. It received far-reaching rights, even to wage war, and won a **monopoly** on nutmeg and cloves. The fight for the islands shaped colonial history. In the **Peace of Breda** in 1667, the Dutch kept the small nutmeg island of **Run**. In return, England kept **New Amsterdam**, which later became the world city of **New York**.

**Saffron** is obtained from the stigmas of the flower of **Crocus sativus**. Each flower yields only three strands of stigma, which are picked by hand. That is why saffron is one of the most expensive spices. In Switzerland it is grown in the Valais village of **Mund**. **Vanilla** comes from Mexico and today is grown mainly on **Madagascar**. Because its natural pollinators are missing there, each flower has to be **pollinated by hand**.

gewusst: For a small nutmeg island, the Dutch left to England what later became New York.
Each saffron flower yields only three strands, which are picked by hand.

teile.einleitung: After the long winter, many look forward to the **start of spring**. The days get longer, it gets warmer, and nature wakes up. But when exactly does spring begin?
wichtigste: By the calendar, spring usually begins on 20 or 21 March.
On this day, day and night are about equally long.
For weather experts, spring begins as early as 1 March.
In spring, the days become longer and warmer.
Swallows return from Africa.
In Zurich, the Böögg is burnt at the Sechseläuten.

abschnitte.text: By the **calendar**, spring usually begins on **20 or 21 March**. Then the sun stands exactly above the equator. From this day on, it stands a little higher at midday each day. **Weather experts**, on the other hand, work with whole months. For them, spring lasts from **1 March** to the end of May. This makes it easier to compare weather data.

At the start of spring, day and night last almost the same time, about **12 hours** each. This day is called the **equinox**. After it, the sun rises a little earlier and sets a little later each day. The **days get longer**, until the longest day in June. Plants therefore get more and more light.

Plants need **warmth** and **light** to grow. In spring the ground thaws. The roots take up water again. This sap rises with **nutrients** in the trunks up to the buds. Then leaves and flowers sprout. Early bloomers such as crocuses and snowdrops are often there even earlier.

Many migratory birds return. The **swallow** spends the winter in **Africa**. In spring it comes back, because there are then many insects again. That is why it counts as a **herald of spring**. The cuckoo and the stork also report back. Hedgehogs and marmots wake from hibernation.

In many places in Switzerland, winter is seen off with customs. In **Zurich**, the **Sechseläuten** is celebrated in April. There the **Böögg** is burnt, a snowman made of cotton wool that stands for winter. The faster its head explodes, the nicer the summer will be, so people say. In other areas there are fires and parades to drive the winter away.

gewusst: The calendar start of spring does not fall on the same day every year.
In the Southern Hemisphere, for example in Australia, autumn begins in March.

teile.einleitung: The meadow saffron (in German, “Herbstzeitlose”, or “autumn timeless”) is a pale violet flower that blooms in autumn on damp meadows. It looks like a crocus, but is very poisonous. What is special is that flowers and leaves appear at completely different times.
wichtigste: The meadow saffron flowers in September and October.
Its flowers are pale violet and recall a crocus.
In autumn it flowers without leaves.
The leaves grow only in spring, together with the seed capsule.
It is very poisonous, for cows and horses too.
It grows again every year from a corm in the soil.

abschnitte.text: The **meadow saffron** flowers in **September and October**, that is, when most flowers have already finished blooming. That is where its German name comes from. It likes to grow on **damp meadows and pastures**, in Switzerland too. Its flowers are **delicate lilac to pale violet** and stand straight out of the meadow.

The flower of the meadow saffron looks very like a **crocus**. The crocus, however, flowers in **spring**. One difference: the meadow saffron has six stamens, the crocus only three. The easiest way to recognise it is by the season. A crocus-like flower in autumn is mostly a meadow saffron.

What is special about the meadow saffron is its course through the year. In autumn you see **only the flower, without leaves**. The leaves grow only in **spring**. Together with them appears the **seed capsule**, but no flower. In the soil sits a **corm**. From it new flowers and leaves grow every year.

All parts of the meadow saffron are **strongly poisonous**. In spring, its leaves can be mistaken for edible wild herbs such as **wild garlic**. This is dangerous. **Cows and horses** can also be poisoned by the meadow saffron. Farmers therefore take care that it does not get onto pastures or into the feed. Anyone who collects wild herbs must know them for certain.

gewusst: The meadow saffron flowers in autumn, but its seeds ripen only in the following early summer.
The poison of the meadow saffron is not destroyed even when it is dried in hay.

teile.einleitung: **Garden cress** is one of the easiest plants to grow yourself. It even grows without soil, sprouts in a few days and tastes spicy and sharp. Ideal for a first plant project of your own.
wichtigste: Cress also grows on damp cotton wool or kitchen paper.
It sprouts after only two to three days.
After about a week you can harvest it.
You cut it off with scissors.
You eat the young stems with the little leaves.
The cotton wool must always stay damp.

abschnitte.text: For cress you do not need a garden. You put **damp cotton wool** or kitchen paper in a dish. On it you scatter the small **seeds** close together. It is important that the base **never dries out**. Otherwise the seedlings quickly wither. That is why you check every day whether the cotton wool is still damp.

Cress **sprouts very quickly**. After only **two to three days** you see the first small seedlings. Soon many green stems with small leaves are standing there. After about **a week to ten days**, the cress is big enough to harvest. Because it goes so fast, it is well suited to experiments at school.

You cut the cress off just above the cotton wool with **scissors**. What you eat are the tender **stems** with the small **leaves**. The roots stay in the cotton wool. Fresh cress is often sprinkled on a **slice of buttered bread**, on eggs or in a salad. It tastes spicy and slightly sharp.

Garden cress belongs to the **cabbage family** (crucifers). This family also includes mustard, radish and cabbage. Many of these plants contain **mustard oils**. These substances cause the sharp taste. Cress also contains vitamins, especially **vitamin C**.

Cress grows **all year round** in a warm home. A bright spot on the **windowsill** is ideal. This way you can harvest fresh greens even in winter. If you sow cress in soil, you can also grow it in the garden or on the balcony. With cress seeds you can even lay out letters or patterns on the cotton wool.

gewusst: With cress you can grow your own name, if you scatter the seeds in the shape of letters.
Cress is related to mustard and radish, which is why it tastes similarly sharp.

teile.einleitung: Not every soil is equally suited to arable farming. The best arable soils in Switzerland are called **crop rotation areas** (in German, “Fruchtfolgeflächen”). They are especially protected so that Switzerland can grow enough food even in crises.
wichtigste: Crop rotation areas are the best soils in Switzerland that can be ploughed.
In the Crop Rotation Areas Sectoral Plan, the Confederation sets a minimum extent.
About 438,000 hectares are required across Switzerland.
Every canton must secure its share.
The aim is food security in times of crisis.
The greatest danger is building over them, above all on the Plateau.

abschnitte.text: Crop rotation areas are soils that are especially well suited to **arable farming**. They are deep, fertile and not too steep. On them you can grow cereals, potatoes or vegetables in a **crop rotation**. That means the crops change from year to year. Such soils form over thousands of years and cannot simply be replaced.

The main aim is **food security**. Even if fewer foods can be imported in a crisis, Switzerland should be able to grow enough. That is why the Confederation lays down in the **Crop Rotation Areas Sectoral Plan** how much of such soil must be kept at a minimum. About **438,000 hectares** are required across Switzerland.

The **Confederation** divides the total area into **quotas**. Every canton gets a fixed share. The **cantons** have to designate these areas in their **structure plan** and secure them permanently. Anyone who wants to build over a crop rotation area must have good reasons. This is how the Confederation and the cantons work together in spatial planning.

Not every meadow counts as a crop rotation area. The soil must be easy to work with **machines**. That is why the **slope** may be at most 18 per cent. The climate must also be suitable so that arable farming is possible. That is why most crop rotation areas lie in lower-lying areas.

The **Plateau** has the best arable soils in Switzerland. At the same time, it is the most densely populated area. New houses, roads and industry **seal** soil there. Sealed soil is covered with concrete or asphalt and is lost for arable farming. That is why there is repeated discussion about how to build more densely inside settlements and spare good land.

gewusst: A good arable soil takes thousands of years to form.
One hectare is roughly the area of a football pitch.

teile.einleitung: Forestry workers look after the forest, fell trees and provide safety in protection forests. It is a job outdoors, in all weathers, with a lot of responsibility.
wichtigste: The apprenticeship as a forestry worker EFZ takes three years in Switzerland.
The most important tool for felling is the chainsaw.
Cut-protection trousers block the saw chain on contact.
The equipment includes a helmet with ear protection and a visor.
When felling trees, you never work completely alone.
You can continue your training at a college of higher education to become a forester HF.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, the apprenticeship as a **forestry worker EFZ** takes **three years**. EFZ stands for Federal Certificate of Proficiency (in German, Eidgenössisches Fähigkeitszeugnis). The apprentices work in a forestry business and attend vocational school. There are also inter-company courses in which they practise safe tree felling. Important qualities are a love of nature, good health and team spirit.

Forestry workers **fell trees** and prepare the wood. Their most important tool for this is the **chainsaw**. They also plant young trees and look after them. In **young forest care** they remove weak or disruptive saplings so that the best ones can grow well. They also build forest tracks, fences and protective structures against falling rocks.

Work in the forest is dangerous. That is why forestry workers wear **protective equipment**. This includes a **helmet with ear protection and a visor**. The **cut-protection trousers** contain long fibres that are pulled into the saw chain on contact and **block** it. When felling trees, forestry workers **never work completely alone**, so that someone can help at once in an accident.

After the apprenticeship you can continue your training. At a **college of higher education** you become a **forester HF**. Foresters manage forestry businesses and plan how the forest is looked after. In **Lyss** in the canton of Bern there is a **forestry training centre** where foresters are trained. A degree in forest science is also possible.

gewusst: About a third of the area of Switzerland is covered by forest.
Many forests in the mountains are protection forests, which protect villages and roads from avalanches and falling rocks.

teile.einleitung: A wet meadow is a meadow on waterlogged soil. Special plants grow here and animals live here that need a lot of moisture.
wichtigste: Wet meadows grow on wet soil, often close to the groundwater.
They are usually lightly fertilised and mown earlier than litter meadows.
Typical plants are marsh marigold, ragged robin, meadowsweet and sedges.
The lapwing breeds on the ground of wet meadows and has become rare in Switzerland.
Many wet meadows were drained with drainage pipes in the past and turned into arable land.

abschnitte.text: A **wet meadow** lies where the soil stays wet for a long time, for example on valley floors or beside streams. It is mown so that no bushes grow up. A typical wet meadow is **lightly fertilised** and **mown earlier** than a **litter meadow**. Litter meadows are not fertilised and are only cut in autumn.

Already in spring the **marsh marigold** shines with yellow flowers and glossy, roundish leaves. A little later the pink **ragged robin** blooms. Its petals are deeply cut and look dishevelled. In summer the **meadowsweet** spreads a sweetish scent along ditches. Its flower heads are creamy white.

Many **sedges** grow in wet meadows. These are grass-like plants whose stem is often **three-edged**. An old saying goes: “Sedges have edges.” Alongside them you find rushes and grasses that tolerate wet soil. These plants form the basis for many insects.

The **lapwing** is a bird with a long **crest** on its head. It breeds on the ground of wet meadows and has become rare in Switzerland. The **large marsh grasshopper** is also tied to wet meadows and carries its habitat in its name. Dragonflies, frogs and many butterflies join them.

In the past, many wet meadows were **drained**. For this, **drainage pipes** were laid in the soil, which are tubes that carry the water away. This created dry **arable land**. As a result, large parts of the former wetlands have disappeared in Switzerland. Today some areas are being made wet again in order to protect rare species.

gewusst: The marsh marigold is poisonous, and even cows usually leave it alone.
The lapwing gets its German name “Kiebitz” from its call, which sounds like “kie-witt”.

teile.einleitung: In cross-pollination, pollen travels from one plant to the flower of another plant of the same species. The wind or animals such as bees help with this.
wichtigste: In cross-pollination, the pollen comes from another plant of the same species.
The pollen is carried by wind or animals.
Many flowers prevent self-pollination by having stamens and stigma ripen at different times.
Dioecious plants such as the willow carry male and female flowers on different plants.
Most apple varieties need pollen from another variety.
Breeders often transfer pollen with a fine brush.

abschnitte.text: Flowers have **stamens**, which make **pollen**, and a **stigma**, on which pollen has to land. In **cross-pollination**, the pollen comes from **another plant of the same species**. The opposite is **self-pollination**, where the pollen comes from the same plant. Cross-pollination mixes the genes and makes plants more varied. This way they can adapt better to changes.

The pollen travels **by wind or by animals** from one plant to another. Grasses, hazel shrubs and many conifers use the wind and make huge amounts of pollen. Other plants attract **bees**, bumblebees, butterflies or flies with colours, scent and nectar. The animals carry the pollen on their bodies to the next flower.

Many flowers prevent themselves from pollinating themselves. In some, **stamens and stigma ripen at different times**. Other plants are **dioecious**. In the **willow**, flowers with stamens and flowers with carpels grow on different plants. Then cross-pollination is the only possibility.

Most **apple varieties** need **pollen from another plant** for fruit to form. That is why **different varieties** are often planted next to each other in orchards. A **cherry blossom**, too, is usually fertilised only by **pollen from another cherry**. Without bees and other pollinators there would therefore be much less fruit.

**Plant breeders** deliberately cross two plants to obtain new varieties. First they **remove the stamens** from the flower so that it cannot pollinate itself. Then they transfer the pollen of the desired partner plant to the stigma with a **fine brush**. Often they then put a little bag over the flower so that no insects bring foreign pollen.

gewusst: With some fruit trees it is enough if a suitable variety stands in the neighbouring garden.
Pollen from wind-pollinated plants can fly many kilometres.

teile.einleitung: If you bite into an unripe banana or drink strong black tea, you feel a dry, furry feeling in your mouth. **Tannins** are responsible for this. These plant substances were used in the past for tanning leather, which is where their name comes from.
wichtigste: Tannins are called that because they were used to tan animal hides into leather.
They have a tightening effect, which is called astringent.
The furry feeling in the mouth arises because they bind proteins in the saliva.
A distinction is made between hydrolysable and condensed tannins.
Oak bark is a classic source of tannins.
In the past, ink was made from oak galls and iron salts.

abschnitte.text: Tannins link the **proteins** in an animal hide. This turns the hide into durable **leather** that does not rot. In the past, the bark of **oaks** and **spruces** was mainly used for this. The craft was called **bark tanning**, because the crushed bark is called tan bark.

Tannins bind proteins in the top cell layers of skin and mucous membrane. This effect is called **tightening** or **astringent**. In the mouth, they precipitate the proteins of the saliva. The saliva then no longer lubricates well, and you feel this as dry and furry. You know this from unripe fruit, strong black tea or red wine.

Chemically, two main groups are distinguished. **Hydrolysable tannins** are compounds of **glucose** and **gallic acid**. They can be split by acid or enzymes. **Condensed tannins**, also called proanthocyanidins, on the other hand, are firmly linked chains of **catechin** building blocks. They cannot be broken down so easily.

In European folk medicine, **oak bark** is a classic remedy. It is used externally, for example for compresses or sitz baths for mild skin inflammations. Dried **blueberries** are traditionally used for mild diarrhoea, because their tannins act on the lining of the gut. Fresh blueberries are not suitable for this.

**Oak galls** are small growths on oak leaves that are caused by gall wasps. They contain very many tannins. If you mix them with **iron salts**, a dark, lasting ink forms: **iron gall ink**. Books and documents were written with it for many centuries.

gewusst: For centuries, important documents were written with ink made from oak galls.
Dried blueberries help with mild diarrhoea, but fresh ones do not.

teile.einleitung: **Rolled oats** (in German, “Haferflocken”) are rolled oat grains. They are healthy, cheap and versatile. In Switzerland they belong above all in **Bircher muesli**.
wichtigste: For rolled oats, oat grains are rolled flat.
Rolled oats are a wholegrain product, because the whole grain is used.
Coarse rolled oats are made from whole grains.
Bircher muesli is named after the Swiss doctor Bircher-Benner.
Warm oat porridge is called porridge in English.
Soaked in milk, rolled oats become soft.

abschnitte.text: First the oats are cleaned and freed of their hard **husk**. Then the grains are briefly steamed and **rolled flat** between rollers. For **coarse rolled oats**, **whole grains** are used. For delicate flakes, the grains are first cut into pieces. Because the **whole grain** is used, rolled oats count as a **wholegrain product**.

The Zurich doctor **Maximilian Bircher-Benner** invented around 1900 a dish of rolled oats, grated **apples**, nuts, lemon juice and milk. He wanted his patients to eat more raw fruit. From this came **Bircher muesli** (in German, “Birchermüesli”), which is known all over the world today. If you soak the rolled oats in milk, they become **soft** and soak it up.

If you cook rolled oats with milk or water, a warm porridge is made. In English it is called **porridge** and is especially popular in Scotland and England. From rolled oats, **butter** and **sugar** you can also bake **oat biscuits**. Rolled oats also go into bread or into home-made muesli bars.

Rolled oats contain many **dietary fibres**, which keep you full for a long time. They also supply protein, iron and vitamins. That is why they make a good breakfast before school. Traditionally, the **horse** too likes to eat oats.

gewusst: Bircher-Benner called his dish “apple diet dish”, and the word muesli came only later.
In Bircher muesli made to the original recipe, there was more apple than rolled oats.

teile.einleitung: Resin is a sticky mass that is formed mainly by conifers. The tree uses it to seal its wounds. If resin becomes millions of years old, it can turn into amber.
wichtigste: Resin is a sticky liquid from the tree.
It seals wounds in the bark.
Conifers such as spruce, pine and larch have especially much resin.
Fresh resin is sticky and becomes solid with time.
Fossilised, ancient resin is called amber.
Violin players rub their bow with rosin, which is made from resin.

abschnitte.text: **Resin** is a thick, very **sticky** mass that trees produce. Above all **conifers** such as spruce, pine and larch have a lot of resin. It flows in fine channels in the wood and in the bark. Fresh resin is pale and liquid. With time it becomes **solid** and hard in the air.

If the bark is injured, for example by a broken branch or by animals, resin comes out. It flows into the wound and **seals** it. This way it protects the tree from **fungi** and **insects** that could otherwise get in. So resin acts like a plaster.

Resin smells **spicy and fresh**. You know this scent from the coniferous forest, especially on warm summer days. It comes from aromatic substances in the resin that evaporate easily. From resin, **turpentine oil** is also obtained, which was formerly used for thinning paints.

Violin players rub the hairs of their **violin bow** with **rosin**. This is a solid resin that is obtained from tree resin. It makes the bow hairs grip. Only then do they make the strings sound properly. Players of the viola, cello and double bass also need rosin.

**Amber** is tree resin that turned hard in the ground **millions of years ago**. It is often golden yellow to orange and translucent. Sometimes you find **trapped insects** in it. Long ago they got stuck in the sticky resin. When the resin hardened, they were preserved right up to today. A lot of amber is found on the coast of the **Baltic Sea**.

gewusst: In amber, researchers have already found insects, spiders and even small feathers from prehistoric times.
Amber is so light that it floats in strongly salty water.

teile.einleitung: On walks in the mountains you see wonderful flowers. Some of them are rare and protected. These **protected plants** must not be picked, dug up or damaged, so that they do not disappear.
wichtigste: Protected plants must not be picked, dug up or damaged.
Plants are protected because they are rare.
Flowers left standing can form seeds.
Bees and butterflies find food in the flowers.
The lady's slipper orchid and many species of gentian are protected.
Instead of picking, it is best to take a photo.

abschnitte.text: Some plants now exist in only a few places. Their habitats have become smaller, and in the past many beautiful flowers were picked or dug up. So that they do not disappear, they are under **protection**. In Switzerland, the **Confederation** and the **cantons** decide which plants are protected. Anyone who picks or digs them up breaks the law.

A flower that has been picked can no longer form **seeds**. This means fewer of them grow the next year. Anyone who **digs up** a plant takes it right out of its habitat. Usually it does not survive in the garden at all. If the flowers are left standing, they can multiply and the meadow stays colourful.

**Bees** and **butterflies** are also glad of the flowers in the meadow. They collect **nectar** and **pollen** from the flowers. If flowers are picked, the insects lack them as food. At the same time, the insects carry the pollen from flower to flower, and this is how new seeds can form.

The **lady's slipper** is a rare **orchid**. Part of its flower is yellow and looks like a little shoe. The **gentian** grows in the Alps and blooms bright blue, with a bell-shaped flower. Many species of gentian are protected. The **edelweiss** is also among the well-known protected alpine flowers.

If you find a beautiful, rare flower, it is best to take a **photo**. This way you have a memory, and the flower stays standing. Other people can enjoy it too. Stay on the paths so that you do not trample plants.

gewusst: The flower of the lady's slipper looks like a little yellow shoe.
Alpine flowers that have been dug up often do not survive in the garden at all.

teile.einleitung: Flavonoids are natural colouring and protective substances in plants. They colour flowers and fruits and occur in many foods, for example in onions, soya and tea.
wichtigste: The name comes from the Latin “flavus” for yellow.
Flavonoids have a basic framework C6-C3-C6 with two aromatic rings.
Anthocyanins colour many flowers and fruits red, purple or blue.
Red cabbage juice changes colour with the pH value because of its anthocyanins.
Onion skins contain a lot of quercetin, soya beans a lot of isoflavones such as genistein.
Green tea is rich in catechins.
The enzyme chalcone synthase starts the formation of flavonoids.

abschnitte.text: The name **flavonoids** comes from the Latin word **“flavus”**, which means **yellow**. Many of these substances are yellowish in colour. Flavonoids belong to a large group of plant substances that chemists call **polyphenols**. Several thousand different flavonoids are known. Plants make them themselves, while people and animals take them in with their food.

All flavonoids have a similar **basic framework**. Chemists write it as **C6-C3-C6**. Two **aromatic rings** of six carbon atoms each are joined by a bridge of three carbon atoms. In the plant, the enzyme **chalcone synthase** starts the formation. An **enzyme** is a protein that speeds up chemical reactions.

**Anthocyanins** are flavonoids that colour many flowers and fruits **red, purple or blue**. You find them in cherries, blueberries, grapes and red cabbage. The colours attract insects and other animals. Flavonoids also protect plants from too much **UV light** from the sun.

**Red cabbage juice** can be used as an **acid-base indicator**. Its anthocyanins change their colour depending on the **pH value**. If you add lemon juice, it turns red. With soapy water or baking soda it turns blue to green. That is why red cabbage is called “blue cabbage” in some regions, depending on how it is prepared.

The flavonol **quercetin** occurs in large amounts in **onions**, especially in the skins. The **soya bean** contains many **isoflavones** such as **genistein**. **Green tea** contains especially many **catechins**. Apples, berries and cocoa also contain flavonoids. Exactly how they work in the body is still being researched.

gewusst: With onion skins you can dye Easter eggs yellow to brown, and that is also due to flavonoids.
The same group of pigments makes red cabbage purple and blueberries blue.

teile.einleitung: What we collect in the woods as a mushroom is only a small part of the whole living thing. It is the **fruiting body**. The largest part of the fungus lives hidden in the soil or in wood.
wichtigste: The fruiting body makes and spreads the spores.
The actual fungus is a fine network in the soil, the mycelium.
A typical cap mushroom consists of a cap and a stem.
Fungi have no chlorophyll and do not carry out photosynthesis.
Fungi form a kingdom of their own, beside plants and animals.
In Switzerland, most fungi grow in late summer and autumn.

abschnitte.text: A fungus consists mainly of fine threads, the **hyphae**. Together they form a network, the **mycelium**. It grows unseen in the soil, in wood or in leaf litter. When it is warm and damp enough, the mycelium forms a **fruiting body**. Its main task is to make **spores**. Wind and animals carry them on, and this is how the fungus reproduces.

A typical **cap mushroom** such as the porcini has a **stem** and on top of it a **cap**. On the underside of the cap are gills or tubes. That is where the spores form. Some mushrooms carry a ring on the stem, the **annulus**, for example the fly agaric. The death cap has a sack-like sheath at the base of the stem, the **volva**. It is an important feature of this deadly poisonous mushroom.

Not all fruiting bodies look the same. The **stinkhorn** first grows in an egg-shaped, jelly-like sheath. This structure is called a **witch's egg**. Later the stem with the stinking head shoots out of it. The **giant puffball** forms round, white balls, usually 10 to 50 centimetres across, as big as a football. Inside, countless spores ripen.

In the past, fungi were counted as plants. But fungi have no **chlorophyll**, that is, no leaf green. They cannot carry out photosynthesis. That is why they get their food from living or dead organisms. Today fungi form a **kingdom of their own**. They are even more closely related to animals than to plants.

Fungi need **warmth** and a lot of **moisture**. These conditions usually occur in **late summer and autumn**. Then many people are out in the woods. Because some mushrooms are very poisonous, in many municipalities you can have collected mushrooms checked free of charge at a **mushroom inspection point**. In some cantons there are rules about how many mushrooms you may collect.

gewusst: The invisible part of a fungus in the soil can be much bigger than all its fruiting bodies put together.
Fungi are more closely related to animals than to plants.
A single giant puffball can contain billions of spores.

teile.einleitung: The forest needs people who look after it. These are **foresters** and **forestry workers**. They make sure that the forest stays healthy, supplies wood and protects people.
wichtigste: Foresters plan which trees are felled and which are protected.
Trees that are to be felled are marked by the forester with paint.
Forestry workers do an apprenticeship and work in the forest every day.
Mixed forests usually survive storms and heat better.
In Switzerland the forest area must not get smaller.
The forest is open to everyone, even if it belongs to someone.

abschnitte.text: A **forester** is responsible for a particular area of forest. He or she plans which trees are felled and which are protected. Before felling, the forester chooses the trees and **marks** them with paint. This way the forest workers know which trees to fell. The forester also advises forest owners, that is, municipalities, cantons or private people.

In Switzerland, the specialists who work in the forest are called **forestry workers**. They do a three-year apprenticeship. They fell trees, plant young trees and look after the forest. The work is dangerous, because branches can fall down and the **chainsaw** is loud. That is why they wear a **helmet**, ear protection and **cut-protection trousers**.

Foresters make sure that different tree species grow. A **mixed forest** usually survives **storms** and **heat** better than a forest of only one species. If one tree species suffers, for example from drought or a pest, the others stay standing. Because of climate change, foresters increasingly rely on species that cope well with warmth.

In the mountains, a lot of **protection forest** grows. Trees on steep slopes hold back **avalanches** and **falling rocks**. This way they protect villages, roads and railway lines. These forests have to be looked after especially carefully. A large part of the Swiss forest is protection forest.

The Swiss **Forest Act** protects the forest strictly. The forest area must not get smaller. Simply **clearing** forest is forbidden. Anyone who gets a permit usually has to plant **replacement** forest somewhere else. In addition, every person may enter any forest, even someone else's. You must, however, show consideration for plants and animals. Wood from the forest is a **renewable raw material** for building and heating.

gewusst: About a third of the area of Switzerland is covered by forest.
As early as 1876, Switzerland passed a first law to protect mountain forests.

teile.einleitung: Hildegard of Bingen was a nun who lived in Germany almost 900 years ago. She wrote books about religion, nature and medicine, and composed music. In the Catholic Church she is honoured as a saint.
wichtigste: Hildegard lived in the Middle Ages, from 1098 to 1179.
She founded a convent near Bingen on the Rhine.
She wrote about plants, animals, stones and medicine.
She especially valued the cereal spelt.
She composed many sacred chants.
In 2012 she was officially declared a saint and named a Doctor of the Church.

abschnitte.titel: A woman in the Middle Ages
abschnitte.text: **Hildegard of Bingen** lived from **1098 to 1179**. She came to a convent as a child. Later she became an **abbess**, that is, the head of a community of nuns. She founded her own convent on the Rupertsberg near **Bingen**. The town lies on the **Rhine** in Germany, where the River Nahe flows into the Rhine.

By her own account, Hildegard had had **visions** since childhood. These were inner images and inspirations that she understood as messages from God. She wrote them down in her work **“Scivias”**. The title means “Know the Ways”. Hildegard also wrote many letters to popes, emperors and other important people of her time.

Hildegard also wrote about **nature**. In works such as the **“Physica”** she described plants, animals and stones and how they could be used for **health**. Her writings are regarded as early sources of natural history. She especially praised **spelt** as an easily digestible cereal. To this day, spelt is often linked with her. She called the life force in plants, animals and people **“viriditas”**, the **greening power**.
Hildegard was also a **composer**. She wrote numerous **sacred chants** for worship. This was very unusual for a woman in the Middle Ages. Her music is still performed today and recorded on albums.

abschnitte.titel: Saint and Doctor of the Church
abschnitte.text: Hildegard had long been honoured as a saint, but was never formally canonised. In **May 2012**, Pope Benedict XVI extended her veneration to the whole Catholic Church. In **October 2012** he named her a **Doctor of the Church**. Only a few women hold this title of honour.

gewusst: Hildegard invented her own secret language with made-up words and letters.
Hildegard lived to be over 80, which was very rare in the Middle Ages.

teile.einleitung: The buttercup family (in German, “Hahnenfussgewächse”) is a large plant family. It includes many well-known flowers from woods, meadows, gardens and mountains. Many of them are poisonous.
wichtigste: The family is named after the buttercup.
Many members of the buttercup family are poisonous.
The wood anemone flowers in March and April in deciduous woods.
The Christmas rose flowers as early as winter and is also called the snow rose.
The glacier crowfoot was found on the Finsteraarhorn at around 4270 m.
Columbine, globeflower and marsh marigold also belong to it.

abschnitte.text: The **buttercup family** is a plant family with very many species. They grow in woods, on meadows, by streams and high in the Alps. Some are popular **garden flowers**. It is typical that many species contain **poisonous substances**. You should therefore not eat them.

In March and April, the white **wood anemone** forms dense carpets in deciduous woods. It uses the light before the trees carry their leaves. After that it withdraws into its **rootstock** in the ground. The yellow **lesser celandine** also flowers early. Scharbock is an old word for **scurvy**, a disease caused by a lack of vitamin C. Before flowering, the young leaves contain a lot of vitamin C and were therefore eaten in the past.

abschnitte.titel: By streams and on mountain meadows
abschnitte.text: The **marsh marigold** flowers in spring by streams and in marshy meadows. It has yolk-yellow flowers and shiny, heart-shaped leaves. On damp mountain meadows grows the **globeflower**. Its yellow sepals bend together into a **ball**, so that only small insects can crawl in.

The **alpine pasqueflower** flowers white or sulphur-yellow on mountain meadows and has silkily hairy flowers. Its fruits carry long, **feathery tails**, which the wind spreads. The **glacier crowfoot** is one of the flowering plants that climb highest in the Alps. On the **Finsteraarhorn** in the Bernese Oberland it was found flowering at a height of around 4270 m.

abschnitte.titel: In winter and in the garden
abschnitte.text: The **Christmas rose** often flowers white as early as Christmas, hence its name. It is also called the **snow rose**. The **columbine** is a popular garden flower with nodding flowers. Each of its five petals forms a long **spur** pointing backwards. Nectar collects in it, which bumblebees reach with their long tongues.

gewusst: The glacier crowfoot tolerates frost and often has only a few weeks a year in which to grow.
The Christmas rose can even flower under a thin covering of snow.

teile.einleitung: A herbarium is a collection of pressed and dried plants. You can make one yourself to get to know plants. Large herbaria in museums and gardens are also very important for research.
wichtigste: The word comes from the Latin “herba”, which means herb or plant.
Plants are pressed and dried between absorbent paper.
For each plant there is a name, a place where it was found and a date.
You must not pick protected plants.
You take only one plant, and only if many grow there.
The herbarium of Carl von Linné is kept today in London.

abschnitte.text: A **herbarium** is a collection of **pressed and dried plants**. The word comes from Latin: **“herba”** means herb or plant. Each plant is stuck on its own sheet of paper. Such a sheet with a plant is called a **herbarium specimen**. This way you can keep and compare plants for many years.

There are important rules when collecting. **Protected plants** are rare and may not be picked. From one spot you take **only one plant**, and only if many grow there. This way enough is left for animals, insects and other people. In nature reserves you mostly may not pick anything at all.

The plant is laid flat between **absorbent paper**, for example newspaper. On top you put heavy books or use a plant press. The paper is changed regularly so that the plant does not go **mouldy**. After a few days it is dry. Then you fix it with **narrow strips of sticky tape** on the herbarium sheet. This way the plant stays clearly visible.

On the label you write the **name** of the plant, the **place where it was found** and the **date**. The name of the person who collected it is added. Without the place and the date, a specimen is almost worthless for research. For only then do we know later where and when a plant grew.

Large herbaria belong to **museums**, **universities** and **botanical gardens**. They often contain millions of specimens. Researchers compare plants from many decades there. The Botanical Gardens of the city of **Geneva** own one of the largest herbaria in the world. The herbarium of the famous researcher **Carl von Linné** was bought after his death by the Englishman James Edward Smith. Today the **Linnean Society of London** keeps it.

gewusst: Some herbarium specimens are several hundred years old and still well preserved.
With old herbarium specimens, researchers can show how the distribution of plants has changed.

teile.einleitung: **Liquid manure** (in German, “Gülle”) is a liquid fertiliser made from the dung and urine of farm animals such as cows and pigs. In Switzerland, in many dialects, it is called **Bschütti**. It supplies valuable nutrients, but can also harm the environment.
wichtigste: Liquid manure consists of the dung and urine of farm animals.
In many Swiss dialects it is called Bschütti.
It contains nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
Ammonia escapes when it is spread.
The trailing hose spreads liquid manure close to the ground.
Liquid manure in a stream can kill fish.
Life-threatening gases form in slurry pits.

abschnitte.text: In the stable, the **dung and urine** of the animals are produced every day. Together with a little water, this makes **liquid manure**. It is collected in large **slurry pits**. Liquid manure contains the three main nutrients **nitrogen**, **phosphorus** and **potassium**. That is why farmers spread it as fertiliser on meadows and fields, so the nutrients return to the cycle.

When it is spread, the gas **ammonia** escapes. You can smell it clearly. Ammonia pollutes the air and unintentionally fertilises sensitive habitats such as bogs and woods. With the **trailing hose**, the liquid manure is laid directly on the ground instead of being sprayed widely. This way far less ammonia escapes. In Switzerland, this technique has been required in many cases since 2024.

If a meadow is often given liquid manure, **fast-growing grasses** and dandelions grow especially well. They **push out** many meadow flowers that need nutrient-poor soils. If liquid manure gets into a **stream**, it takes oxygen from the water and contains poisonous substances. Then **fish can die**. That is why liquid manure must **not** be spread on **frozen** or **snow-covered** ground: it cannot soak in and is washed into waters.

In a slurry pit, **poisonous gases** such as **hydrogen sulphide** form. They are heavier than air and collect at the bottom of the pit. Anyone who climbs down can quickly lose consciousness. That is why **entering** a slurry pit is **life-threatening** and allowed only with protective equipment. You must also be careful when the liquid manure is stirred up.

gewusst: A dairy cow produces many litres of liquid manure per day.
From liquid manure, energy can also be obtained in a biogas plant.

teile.einleitung: A glacier is a huge mass of ice that moves slowly down the valley. Glaciers form where more snow falls than melts in summer. In Switzerland there are many glaciers, and the biggest is the Great Aletsch Glacier in the Valais.
wichtigste: A glacier is a huge mass of ice.
Glaciers form from snow that turns to ice over many years.
The ice flows slowly downhill because of its weight.
The Great Aletsch Glacier is the longest glacier in the Alps.
Glaciers have shaped valleys and lakes in Switzerland.
Glaciers store large amounts of fresh water.

abschnitte.text: High in the mountains, snow stays on the ground in summer too. Year after year new layers are added and press the lower ones together. The snow first becomes granular **firn** and after many years solid glacier ice. When the mass of ice becomes thick and heavy enough, it begins to flow.

At the top lies the **accumulation zone**, where more snow falls than melts. At the bottom lies the ablation zone, where the ice melts in summer. The lower end is called the **glacier snout** (in German, the “tongue”), and a glacier stream often flows out there. Glaciers usually move only a few dozen to a few hundred metres a year, and deep crevasses form as they do.

Glaciers grind rocks smooth and push stones and rubble ahead of them. These ridges of debris are called **moraines**. In the ice ages, glaciers covered almost the whole Swiss Plateau. They gouged valleys into a U shape and formed basins for lakes such as Lake Zurich or Lake Geneva.

In Switzerland there are still about 1,400 glaciers. The **Great Aletsch Glacier** in the Valais, at about 20 kilometres, is the longest glacier in the Alps and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Also well known are the Rhone Glacier, the Gorner Glacier near Zermatt and the Morteratsch Glacier in the Engadine. All Swiss glaciers are getting smaller because of the warming.

Glaciers are huge water stores. In summer they supply meltwater for rivers such as the Rhone and the Rhine. This water is used for drinking water, agriculture and hydroelectric power stations. Worldwide, about ten per cent of the land area is covered with ice, mainly in Antarctica and Greenland.

begriffe.erklaerung: Old, granular snow that slowly turns into glacier ice.
The lower end of a glacier.
A deep crack in the ice that forms because of the movement.
A ridge of stones and debris that a glacier has deposited.

gewusst: Glacier ice often looks blue, because the dense ice swallows the red light and throws back the blue.
Air bubbles trapped in glacier ice tell researchers how the air was made up thousands of years ago.

teile.einleitung: In mosses and ferns there are two quite different generations that take turns. This interplay is called **alternation of generations**. It explains why a moss or a fern can look quite different over the course of its life.
wichtigste: In alternation of generations, two different generations follow one another.
The sporophyte makes spores.
The gametophyte makes the reproductive cells.
In mosses, the green little plant is the gametophyte.
In ferns, the large plant with fronds is the sporophyte.
Wilhelm Hofmeister described alternation of generations in 1851.

abschnitte.text: From a **spore** grows a generation that makes **reproductive cells**. It is called the **gametophyte**, because in technical language reproductive cells are called **gametes**. From the joined reproductive cells grows a second generation that makes spores again. It is called the **sporophyte**. The word is made up of “spore” and the Greek word for plant. This way the two always alternate.

The two generations also differ in their **chromosomes**. When spores are formed, the set of chromosomes is halved. Cells with a single set are called **haploid**. The gametophyte is haploid. Cells with a double set are called **diploid**, like the sporophyte.

In **mosses**, the green **little moss plant** that you see in the woods is the **gametophyte**. On it grows a thin stalk with a **spore capsule**. This is the sporophyte. It is not independent, because it is supplied with **nutrients** by the green moss plant. When the capsule is ripe, it scatters the spores.

In **ferns**, it is the other way round. The large, conspicuous plant with **fronds** is the **sporophyte**. On the underside of the fronds it makes spores. From a spore grows a tiny, heart-shaped **prothallus**. This is the gametophyte. On it, a young fern plant with fronds then develops, which later makes spores itself.

The German botanist **Wilhelm Hofmeister** showed in **1851** that in mosses, ferns and even in seed plants, two generations alternate. This discovery was a **milestone of botany**. It showed that all these plant groups are related to each other. In seed plants, however, the gametophyte is so small that you can only see it under the microscope.

gewusst: The prothallus of a fern is often only a few millimetres across and looks quite different from a fern.
The brown dots under a fern frond are clusters containing countless spores.

teile.einleitung: Sometimes in the early morning small drops of water hang on the edges of leaves, although it has not rained. Often this is not dew, but **guttation**: the plant itself gives off water in drops.
wichtigste: Guttation is the giving off of liquid water in drops.
The water comes out through special openings, the hydathodes.
Guttation occurs mainly at night and in the early morning when the air is damp and the soil wet.
In lady's mantle, silvery drops on the leaf edge are typical.
Dried drops leave white crusts.
In the case of dressed maize, the drops can be dangerous for bees.

abschnitte.text: Plants constantly take up water with their roots. During the day a lot of it evaporates through the leaves. At night, however, the air is often damp, and little evaporates. The roots still keep pushing water upwards, which is called **root pressure**. The surplus water then comes out through **hydathodes**, small water openings at leaf tips and leaf edges.

Guttation is best seen **at night and in the early morning**, when the air is damp and the soil wet. On meadows, many grasses show small drops at their tips. Famous is **lady's mantle**: it carries silvery drops like pearls on its toothed leaf edge. **Dew**, on the other hand, covers the whole leaf evenly. Guttation drops sit specifically at tips and edges.

If you prune **vines** in spring, sap comes out of the cuts. It is called **bleeding sap** and is likewise driven upwards by root pressure. Winegrowers say that the vine is “weeping”. Birches too make a lot of such sap in spring.

Guttation drops are not pure water. They contain dissolved **salts** and organic substances. When they dry up, **white crusts** often remain on the leaf. In **maize** from dressed seed, the drops can contain **insecticides** from the seed dressing. Bees that drink such drops can be poisoned by them.

gewusst: The name comes from the Latin word “gutta” for drop.
Houseplants and strawberries also sometimes show guttation.

teile.einleitung: The **greater burdock** (in German, “Grosse Klette”) is a strong plant with purple flowers and hooked fruit heads. Anyone who brushes past it quickly has the burrs hanging on clothes or hair.
wichtigste: The fruit heads of the burdock carry tiny hooks.
The flowers are purple.
The burdock often grows at wayside edges.
It usually lives for two years.
In Japan, its root is eaten as a vegetable.
The burdock inspired the Swiss inventor of Velcro.

abschnitte.text: The greater burdock can grow over a metre tall and has very large leaves. It belongs to the **daisy family**, like the sunflower and the thistle. Its round flower heads carry **purple** flowers. All around sit bracts with small **hooks** at the tip. The burdock is **biennial**: in the first year it forms leaves, in the second it flowers and then dies.

The hooked fruit heads stay stuck in the fur of animals or on clothes. This way animals carry the seeds far away before they fall off somewhere. In our country the burdock often grows at **wayside edges**, on rubble sites and on banks. Many animals and people pass by there.

The Swiss engineer **Georges de Mestral** noticed, after a walk with his dog, how firmly the burrs stuck in its fur. Under the microscope he saw the fine hooks. From this he developed the **hook-and-loop fastener** with little hooks on one side and loops on the other. Today you find it on shoes, jackets and bags. When technology learns from nature in this way, it is called **biomimetics**.

abschnitte.titel: Burdock as food and a saying
abschnitte.text: In **Japan**, people eat the long **root** of the burdock as a vegetable, which is called gobo there. In Europe the root was formerly used as a medicinal plant. The German saying to hang on to someone “like a burr” means that someone does not leave your side.

gewusst: The name Velcro for the hook-and-loop fastener is made up of French words for velvet and hook.
A single burdock can produce a great many seeds.

teile.einleitung: An altitude gradient describes how temperature, air pressure, radiation and other conditions change as you climb higher in the mountains. In the Alps, you can therefore experience quite different climate zones within a few kilometres.
wichtigste: On average, the temperature falls by about 0.6 °C for every 100 m of height.
With height, the growing season becomes shorter.
The subalpine zone is characterised by conifer forest up to the tree line.
Air pressure halves roughly every 5,500 m.
UV radiation increases with height.
In a temperature inversion, it is colder on the valley floor than on the slope.

abschnitte.text: When air rises, it **expands** and **cools**. On average the temperature falls by about **0.6 °C** per 100 m. A worked example: at 400 m you measure 14 °C. Up to 2,500 m is a difference of 2,100 m, so 21 times 0.6 °C equals 12.6 °C. Up there, you can therefore expect about **1.4 °C**.

Higher up, snow lies longer and autumn begins earlier. The **growing season**, in which plants can grow and flower, therefore becomes **shorter**. This shapes the plant world. In the **subalpine zone** of the Swiss Alps, mainly **spruces**, **larches** and **Swiss stone pines** grow. This conifer forest reaches up to the **tree line**.

With height, **air pressure** falls. It halves roughly every **5,500 m**, where only about 500 hPa remain. The share of **CO2** in the air stays almost the same, but its **partial pressure** falls along with the total pressure. This makes photosynthesis slightly harder. At the same time, **UV radiation** increases, because the layer of air above is thinner. On top of that comes reflection from snow.

abschnitte.titel: A lake of cold air in the valley
abschnitte.text: Sometimes it is the other way round. Cold, heavy air flows into the **valleys** at night and collects on the valley floor. Warmer air lies above it. The temperature then, unusually, **rises** with height. This is called a **temperature inversion**. In the Swiss Central Plateau, an inversion in winter often forms a blanket of fog, while it is sunny in the mountains.

Altitude gradients are very useful for research. A few hundred metres of height correspond to large **temperature differences**. On the plain, you would have to travel hundreds of kilometres for that. This makes it possible to compare, in a small area, how plants and animals react to warmth and cold. Researchers observe, for example, how plant species move to higher altitudes with **global warming**.

gewusst: On the summit of Mount Everest, air pressure is only about a third of the pressure at sea level.
At great heights, water boils at less than 100 °C, because the air pressure is lower.

teile.einleitung: Many animal and plant species are becoming rarer and rarer. They are called **endangered species**. With laws, agreements and protected areas, people try to save them from extinction.
wichtigste: The Red List shows how seriously a species is endangered.
The CITES agreement of 1973 regulates trade in endangered species.
The CITES secretariat has its seat in Geneva.
The greatest danger is the loss of habitat.
Poaching threatens elephants and rhinoceroses.
In Switzerland, for example, the tree frog and the capercaillie are endangered.

abschnitte.text: The **Red List** shows how seriously a species is threatened. There is a worldwide list by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) and lists for individual countries, including Switzerland. The categories range from “not threatened” through “endangered” to “extinct”. If animals live only in zoos or enclosures, the species counts as **extinct in the wild**. For a long time one example was the **Przewalski's horse**, which was later released back into the wild.

In 1973 the **CITES** agreement was signed in Washington. Its full name is the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora. It bans or restricts trade in thousands of animal and plant species. Its **secretariat** is in **Geneva**. Anyone who brings protected corals, shells or ivory home from holiday can get into trouble at customs.

The greatest danger is the **loss of habitat**. **Orangutans** live in trees on Borneo and Sumatra. If rainforests are cleared for plantations, they lose food and shelter.
