Another danger is **poaching**. Elephants are hunted for their **ivory**, rhinoceroses for their **horn**. Both are sold illegally at high prices.

In Switzerland, too, there are endangered species. The **tree frog** needs warm, fish-free ponds, and many such waters have disappeared. The **capercaillie** lives in light mountain woods. Disturbance by winter sports costs it a lot of energy in winter. The **lady's slipper orchid** is one of the largest native orchids, with a yellow, shoe-shaped flower. It is protected and must not be picked or dug up.

Protection can help. **Mountain gorillas** now live only in a few mountain forests of the Virunga volcanoes and nearby, in Rwanda, Uganda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Thanks to strict protection, their numbers are slowly rising again. In Switzerland the **bearded vulture** was reintroduced after it had been wiped out. The ibex, too, had once disappeared and today lives in the Alps again.

gewusst: The ibex had been wiped out in Switzerland and was reintroduced at the start of the 20th century.
The agreement to protect endangered species is administered from Geneva.

teile.einleitung: Trees hold themselves firmly in the soil with their roots. Depending on the species, the roots grow in very different ways. In a heart root system, several strong roots grow downwards at a slant in all directions.
wichtigste: With trees, people mainly distinguish between heart root, taproot and shallow root systems.
The heart root system is a mixture of a taproot and a shallow root system.
Seen from the side, the roots form a heart-shaped to half-round shape.
There is no single, dominant main root.
Beech, lime and larch are typical trees with heart root systems.
Trees with heart root systems usually stand up well to storms.

abschnitte.text: With trees and shrubs, people mainly distinguish three root forms. **Shallow-rooted** trees spread their roots close beneath the surface, like the spruce. **Taprooted** trees push one strong main root straight down into the depths, like the oak or the silver fir. The **heart root system** lies in between. This classification is important in **forestry**, for example.

In a **heart root system**, several strong roots grow **slanting downwards and sideways**. Seen from outside, this gives a **heart-shaped** to **half-round** form. The roots reach deeper than in shallow-rooted trees, but not as deep as in taprooted trees. There is no single, all-powerful **main root**. Several roots of similar strength share the work.

One well-known example is the **beech**, one of the most common trees in Swiss forests. Its roots grow slantwise in all directions to a medium depth. The **lime** also has a heart root system. Among the conifers, the **larch** belongs here. The spruce, by contrast, roots shallowly, while the silver fir and the Scots pine form taproots.

Because the roots of a heart-rooted tree reach **in all directions**, the tree is held evenly in the soil. That is why trees with heart roots are usually **quite storm-resistant**. Shallow-rooted trees such as the spruce can be blown over more easily in a strong storm. How firmly a tree stands also depends on the soil, though. On wet or shallow soil, many trees root less deeply.

gewusst: When a shallow-rooted tree falls over, you often see a flat root plate, but with heart-rooted trees the root ball is much deeper.
The root shape of a tree can change depending on the soil.

teile.einleitung: Frogspawn is the eggs of frogs. In spring you find it in ponds and pools, and soon tadpoles hatch from it.
wichtigste: Frogspawn is the eggs of frogs.
It consists of black dots in clear jelly.
The common frog lays its spawn in large clumps.
A female common frog can lay more than a thousand eggs at once.
Tadpoles hatch from the spawn.
In Switzerland, frogs and toads are protected, and you must not take spawn away.

abschnitte.text: **Frogspawn** is the **eggs of frogs**. Each egg is a small **black dot**. Around it lies a **clear jelly** that looks like wobbly pudding. The jelly swells up in the water and protects the eggs. It keeps them moist and makes things harder for predators.

In Switzerland you find frogspawn mainly in **spring**. Frogs like best to lay it in **still waters** such as ponds, pools and small lakes. There the water is calm and warms up faster. The **common frog** lays its spawn in **large clumps**. A female can lay **more than a thousand eggs** at once. Toads, on the other hand, lay their eggs in long strings.

After a few days to weeks, **tadpoles** hatch from the eggs. They live in the water, breathe with gills and have a paddle-like tail. In time they grow legs, and the tail disappears. This change is called **metamorphosis**. In the end, small frogs leave the water. Only a few of the many eggs become adult frogs, because many animals eat spawn and tadpoles.

In Switzerland, **frogs and toads are protected**. That is why you must **not take frogspawn home from a pond**. You can, however, look at it carefully from the bank. Many amphibians have become rare because pools and wetlands have disappeared. A natural garden pond without fish can help them.

In spring, many toads and frogs migrate to their **spawning pond**. On the way they often have to cross roads. That is why helpers put up small **fences** beside roads. The animals fall into buckets and are carried safely across the road. This way they are not **run over**.

gewusst: Many toads return every year to the same pond in which they themselves once hatched.
On some roads in Switzerland, thousands of amphibians are carried across the road every spring.

teile.einleitung: Bread, pasta, muesli and polenta have something in common: they are made from **cereals**. Cereals are grasses whose grains we eat. They are among the most important foods in the world.
wichtigste: Wheat, barley, rye, oats and maize are cereals.
Cereals grow in an arable field.
In Switzerland, wheat is grown the most.
Polenta is cooked from maize and is popular in Ticino.
A new plant grows from the embryo in the grain.
After threshing, straw is what is left of the stalks.

abschnitte.text: Cereals are **grasses** that people grow for their grains. They include **wheat**, **barley**, **rye**, **oats** and **maize**. Potatoes, carrots and peas, on the other hand, are not cereals. From the grains, **flour** is made for bread, flakes for muesli, or semolina. Wheat is the cereal that is grown the most in Switzerland. It is mainly made into bread.

A field in which cereals grow is called an **arable field**. It is ploughed and then planted. On a **pasture**, by contrast, animals eat grass. For a grain to **sprout**, it needs **water** and warmth in the soil. Then root and stalk grow. The new plant is in the **embryo**, a small part of the grain.

When the cereal is ripe, it is harvested. In **threshing**, the grains are loosened from the ears. In the past you needed a **flail** for this: you hit the ears on the ground with it until the grains fell out. Today the combine harvester does this. The dry stalks without grains are called **straw**. Farmers use it, for example, as bedding in the stable.

Many dishes are made from cereals. **Polenta** is a porridge made of **maize semolina** and is especially popular in Ticino. From oats, rolled oats are made, from barley soup or malt. Durum wheat is needed for pasta. So cereals are in almost every meal.

gewusst: All kinds of cereal are really grasses.
In the past, the grains were beaten out of the ears by hand with a flail.

teile.einleitung: **Silverweed** (in German, “Gänsefingerkraut”, or “goose cinquefoil”) is a low plant with yellow flowers and silvery leaves. It likes to grow where the soil is trampled hard, for example on pastures and beside paths. It has long been used as a medicinal plant.
wichtigste: The underside of the leaf of silverweed is silvery and hairy.
The leaves are pinnate and have many toothed leaflets.
The flowers are yellow.
It belongs to the rose family.
It spreads with long, creeping runners.
Because of its tannins, it is used as a tea for mild diarrhoea.

abschnitte.text: The leaves of silverweed are **pinnate**: on one stalk sit many small, **toothed leaflets**. Their underside is densely **silvery and hairy**, and sometimes the upper side shines too. The plant stays flat and grows only a few centimetres tall. The **yellow** flowers have five round petals.

Silverweed belongs to the **rose family**, like the strawberry and the apple. Like the strawberry, it forms long, **creeping runners**. On these, new little plants grow that take root themselves. This way it soon covers whole areas. It copes well when animals or people tread on it.

In the past, many villages kept geese on shared pastures. This herb especially liked to grow there, which is how the **goose** got into its German name. The second part comes from the cinquefoils, a genus to which it belongs. Even today you find it on pastures, at the edges of paths and on banks, in Switzerland too.

Silverweed is traditionally used for **cramping tummy aches**. For this, you drink a tea made from the dried herb. It contains **tannins**, which can help with mild **diarrhoea**. If the symptoms are severe or last long, though, you should always go to the doctor.

gewusst: The roots of silverweed used to be eaten in times of need.
The silvery little hairs on the leaves protect the plant from strong sun and drying out.

teile.einleitung: In the middle of winter, trees can die of thirst even though snow lies everywhere. This danger is called **winter desiccation** (in German, “Frosttrocknis” or “Winterdürre”). It mainly affects evergreen plants and trees at the tree line in the Alps.
wichtigste: Winter desiccation is drying out when the ground is frozen.
From frozen ground, the roots cannot take up water.
The needles and leaves lose water all the same through evaporation.
Sunny days in late winter are the most dangerous.
Twigs under the snow cover are well protected.
Damage can be recognised in spring by reddish brown needles.

abschnitte.text: Plants constantly give off some water through their leaves and needles. Normally the roots replace it with new water from the soil. But if the ground is frozen, this does not work. The **water balance** becomes negative: the plant loses more water than it takes up. If this goes on for long, needles and shoots dry out.

In **late winter** the sun already shines strongly, but the ground is still frozen deep down. The sun's rays warm the needles well above the air temperature. Warm needles evaporate more water. The tree cannot replace this water. That is why clear, sunny days in February and March are especially dangerous.

At the **tree line** in the mountains, the summer is short. Young needles there often do not have enough time to finish forming their protective layer of wax. This layer is called the **cuticle**. If it is immature, more water is lost in winter. The Innsbruck plant physiologist **Walter Tranquillini** studied these connections thoroughly at the alpine tree line. Winter desiccation is regarded as one reason why trees do not grow up to any height.

Under the **snow cover** it is dark, damp and evenly cool. There the needles hardly evaporate any water. That is why the lower twigs of young trees often stay healthy. The parts that stick out of the snow, on the other hand, are exposed to wind and sun. In spring their dried-out needles turn **reddish brown** and fall off later.

**Evergreen garden plants** such as cherry laurel, box or rhododendron can also suffer from winter desiccation. They keep their leaves and evaporate water in winter too. It helps to **water on frost-free days**. Shade netting or fleece protects against strong winter sun. A layer of mulch prevents the soil from freezing too quickly and too deeply.

gewusst: Trees can die of thirst in winter in the middle of the snow.
In winter, the sun's rays can make needles much warmer than the air around them.
On young trees you can often see a clear line: green below, where the snow lay, and brown above.

teile.einleitung: A spruce forest is a wood in which mainly spruces grow. In the Swiss mountains, spruce forests are naturally common, while on the Plateau many were planted.
wichtigste: Spruces can grow up to about 50 metres tall.
They carry needles in winter too, so it is often dark on the ground.
The needle litter makes the soil more acidic over time.
In many mountain spruce forests, bilberries grow in the undergrowth.
The common crossbill uses its beak to get seeds out of the cones.
In warm areas of the Plateau, spruces suffer from heat and drought.

abschnitte.text: The **spruce** is the most common tree in Switzerland. It can grow **up to about 50 metres** tall and has a straight trunk. Its needles are short and sharp. Because spruces carry **needles in winter too**, it is rather dark on the ground of a dense spruce forest all year round. Their cones hang downwards and fall off as a whole.

In the mountains, spruce forests are naturally widespread. There, spruces cope well with cold and a lot of snow. Their needle litter breaks down only slowly and makes the **soil more acidic**. That is why in many acidic subalpine spruce forests the **bilberry** shapes the undergrowth. Mosses, ferns and cowberries join it.

The **common crossbill** has beak tips that **cross over**. With them it can prise apart the scales of the cones and get the seeds out. Squirrels also like to eat spruce seeds. Wood ants, woodpeckers and the capercaillie also live in the spruce forest. The **bark beetle** can attack weakened spruces and make many trees die.

Spruce wood is light and is widely used for building. Especially sought-after is the wood of **slow-growing mountain spruces**. It has very fine, even annual rings. From it, **soundboards** are made for violins, guitars and pianos. Such wood is called **tonewood**.

On the Plateau, many **spruce monocultures** were planted in the past. These are woods in which, over a large area, almost only spruces of the same age stand. They are vulnerable to storms and bark beetles. In low, warm areas, spruces also suffer from **heat and drought**. That is why mixed woods with broadleaf trees are increasingly planted there today.

gewusst: You can tell spruces and firs apart by their cones: spruce cones hang, fir cones stand upright.
Many “fir trees” at Christmas are really spruces.

teile.einleitung: In many Swiss communes, the **green waste collection** (in German, “Grünabfuhr”) picks up garden and kitchen waste. From this **green waste**, compost, fertiliser and even energy are later made.
wichtigste: The green waste collection picks up garden and kitchen waste.
Vegetable and fruit waste is called “Rüstabfälle” (kitchen trimmings) in Switzerland.
Grass cuttings belong in the green bin, cat litter does not.
The green waste goes to a composting or fermentation plant.
Biogas is produced in fermentation plants.
In autumn there is especially much green waste because of the leaves.

abschnitte.titel: What the green waste collection does
abschnitte.text: Many communes provide a **green bin** or collect the green waste regularly. For this, people often pay a fee or a sticker on the bin. What is collected is **garden waste** such as grass cuttings, leaves and branches, as well as **kitchen trimmings**, that is, peelings and scraps of vegetables and fruit. What exactly is allowed is decided by each commune itself.

abschnitte.titel: What does not belong in it
abschnitte.text: Green waste must not contain **cat litter**, plastic bags, glass bottles or stones. Ashes, vacuum cleaner bags and nappies are also wrong. Such **foreign matter** later contaminates the compost. Plastic in particular breaks into tiny pieces that reach fields as **microplastic**. That is why some communes check the bins.

The green waste is taken to a **composting plant**. There, tiny living things break it down with air into **compost**, that is, nutrient-rich soil. Other plants **ferment** it without air. This produces **biogas**, from which electricity, heat or fuel is obtained. The rest, the **digestate**, serves as fertiliser for fields and gardens.

Green waste is not rubbish, but a raw material. If it is collected separately, its nutrients return to the soil and it **becomes soil again**. In a waste incineration plant this would not be possible. In **autumn**, when the leaves fall, and in spring during garden clearing, there is especially much green waste. If you have a garden, you can also compost yourself.

gewusst: In some cities, biogas made from green waste powers buses or refuse lorries.
Compost made from green waste is often sold as soil at the garden centre.

teile.einleitung: The hazelnut is the fruit of the hazel shrub. It is a true nut with a hard shell. People eat it raw, roasted or in sweets such as nougat.
wichtigste: The shell of the hazelnut is very hard, and you open it with a nutcracker.
Young hazelnuts sit in a green, leaf-like husk.
The hazel shrub flowers towards the end of winter.
Nougat is made from roasted hazelnuts.
Turkey harvests more than half of all the hazelnuts in the world.
Squirrels and dormice like to eat hazelnuts.

abschnitte.text: The hazelnut grows on the **hazel shrub**. It flowers **towards the end of winter**, often in February, when there are no leaves yet. Its male flowers hang on the shrub like little yellow sausages. They are called **catkins**. From the tiny female flowers, the nuts grow by autumn.

A young hazelnut sits in a **green husk** that looks like slashed leaves. When the nut is ripe, the shell turns brown and the nut falls out of the husk. The **shell** is very hard. It is best opened with a **nutcracker**. Inside lies the edible kernel.

Hazelnuts can be eaten raw or **roasted**. Roasted, they taste even stronger. For **nougat**, roasted hazelnuts are ground finely and mixed with sugar, often with chocolate too. Hazelnuts are also found in chocolate, baked goods, muesli and spreads. In our country they are especially popular in Christmas baking.

**Turkey** harvests far more than half of all the hazelnuts in the world. There they grow on the coast of the **Black Sea**. Many hazelnuts are also grown in Italy. In Switzerland the hazel grows wild at the edges of woods and in hedges. In autumn you can collect nuts yourself.

In autumn, **squirrels** bury nuts in many places as a **store for the winter**. The **dormouse** is a small sleeper with a bushy tail that is named after the hazel shrub. From empty shells you can tell who has been eating: **mice** gnaw a **round hole** in the shell. Squirrels, on the other hand, usually split the nut into **two halves**.

gewusst: The dormouse often sleeps through more than half a year in hibernation.
From nuts that squirrels forget, new hazel shrubs can grow.

teile.einleitung: The silver birch (in German, “Hänge-Birke”, or “hanging birch”) is a tree with white bark and fine, hanging twigs. It grows fast and is one of the first trees to sprout on open ground.
wichtigste: Young birches have white bark.
Old birches are black and cracked at the bottom of the trunk.
The thin twigs hang down, hence the German name.
The leaves are roughly triangular and finely toothed.
The flowers are called catkins.
Birches are pioneer trees, and their seeds fly on the wind.

abschnitte.text: The **silver birch** is recognised at once by its **white bark**. In old trees, the bark at the bottom of the trunk gets **dark, deep cracks** and turns black. Higher up it stays white. The fine, thin **twigs hang** downwards. They move even in a little wind. That is where the German name “hanging birch” comes from.

The leaf of the silver birch is roughly **triangular** to diamond-shaped. The edge is finely **toothed**. In spring the birch flowers with long, hanging flower clusters. These are called **catkins**. The birch is pollinated by the **wind** and gives off a great deal of **pollen** into the air as it does so.

Many people react to birch pollen with an **allergy**. They get **hay fever**, have to sneeze and have itchy eyes. In Switzerland, birch pollen mostly flies in **March and April**. The pollen flight is announced in pollen reports. This way people with allergies can prepare.

Birch seeds are **tiny** and have small **wings**. The wind carries them far away. This way they reach open, empty areas such as gravel pits, fallow land or burnt woodland. There the birch grows as one of the first. It is therefore called a **pioneer tree**. It needs a lot of light and grows fast.

gewusst: The white colour of birch bark comes from a substance called betulin.
Birch bark burns well even when damp and was used in the past for lighting fires.

teile.einleitung: The **cucumber** is a popular vegetable that we often eat raw in salad. It consists for the most part of water and is therefore especially refreshing.
wichtigste: The cucumber has a green skin.
Its flowers are yellow.
It belongs to the gourd family.
It originally comes from India.
Small cucumbers pickled in vinegar are called gherkins.
In Switzerland, cucumbers often grow in greenhouses.

abschnitte.text: The cucumber is an annual plant with long shoots. With small **tendrils** it holds on and climbs upwards. It has large, rough leaves and **yellow flowers**. Botanically it belongs to the **gourd family**, so it is related to pumpkin, courgette and melon. The cucumber is actually a fruit, but in the kitchen we call it a vegetable.

The cucumber originally comes from **India**, where it was already grown thousands of years ago. Later it came to Europe by way of the Near East. It needs a lot of **warmth** and water. In Switzerland, cucumbers therefore often grow in a **greenhouse**. In summer they also thrive in the garden in a sunny spot.

The **skin** is green, the flesh pale and juicy. In the middle lie **many small seeds**, which you can eat as well. A cucumber consists of around 95 per cent **water**. That is why it has few calories and quenches thirst.

For **cucumber salad**, you mostly cut the cucumber into **thin slices**. You also eat it raw as a snack, on bread or in Greek tzatziki. Small cucumbers are pickled in vinegar, and are then called **gherkins** (in German, “Cornichons”) or pickled cucumbers. In Switzerland they go well with raclette.

gewusst: Cucumbers are harvested when they are not yet quite ripe, and ripe cucumbers turn yellow.
In the Middle Ages, cucumbers were common in monastery gardens in Europe.

teile.einleitung: A semi-dry grassland is a lean, dry meadow with very many different plants. In Switzerland you find such meadows mainly on limestone, for example in the Jura. They are among the most species-rich habitats of Central Europe.
wichtigste: Semi-dry grasslands are somewhat better supplied with water than true dry grasslands.
They often grow on limestone soil, for example in the Jura.
Most arose through centuries of mowing or grazing without fertiliser.
Typical plants are meadow sage, Carthusian pink and carline thistle.
They are especially valuable for butterflies.
Heavy fertilising makes the diversity of species shrink.

abschnitte.text: A **semi-dry grassland** is a meadow on dry, nutrient-poor soil. Compared with a true **dry grassland**, it is somewhat better supplied with water. So it dries out less strongly, and the plant cover is denser and more closed. Such meadows are also called **lean meadows**, because the soil has few nutrients.

In Switzerland you find many semi-dry grasslands on **limestone rock**, for example in the **Jura**. Limestone lets rainwater seep away quickly. Often the layer of soil above the rock is only thin. On such shallow soils, especially species-rich meadows develop. There are also semi-dry grasslands on sunny slopes in the Alpine valleys.

Most semi-dry grasslands are **cultural landscapes**. In the past, people cleared woods and then **mowed or grazed** the areas for centuries without fertilising. Without this care, bushes and trees would grow there again in time. That is why many of these meadows are now deliberately looked after and protected.

**Meadow sage** flowers blue-violet and loves warm, limy meadows. Bumblebees like to visit its flowers. The **Carthusian pink** has pink flowers that stand densely in a little head. The **carline thistle** lies almost flat on the ground. Its silvery bracts close in damp air, which is why it counts as a **weather indicator**. Many orchids also grow on semi-dry grasslands.

Because so many different flowering plants grow there, **butterflies** find nectar and food plants for their caterpillars here. Grasshoppers, wild bees and beetles also like to live on these meadows. If a semi-dry grassland is heavily **fertilised**, however, a few fast plants grow especially well. They push out the many small species, and **species diversity falls**.

gewusst: Semi-dry grasslands are among the most species-rich meadows of Central Europe: many dozens of plant species grow there on a small area.
The carline thistle closes its bracts in wet weather like an umbrella.

teile.einleitung: Fire blight is a dangerous disease of fruit trees such as apple and pear. It is caused by a bacterium and can kill whole trees.
wichtigste: Fire blight is caused by the bacterium Erwinia amylovora.
It mainly affects pome fruit plants such as apple, pear and quince.
The disease originally comes from North America.
Affected parts of the plant look as if they had been burnt.
Young shoot tips curl into a hook shape.
Bees and other insects carry the pathogen from flower to flower.
Warm, damp weather during flowering greatly raises the risk.

abschnitte.text: **Fire blight** is caused by the bacterium **Erwinia amylovora**. It mainly attacks **pome fruit plants** such as **apple, pear and quince**. Ornamental plants such as hawthorn or cotoneaster can also fall ill. The disease originally comes from **North America**. From there it reached Europe and later Switzerland too.

Fire blight gets its name because affected flowers, leaves and shoots turn **brown to black**. They look as if they had been scorched with fire. A typical sign is that the **shoot tips curl into a hook shape**, like a shepherd's crook. Sometimes a sticky slime oozes out, containing many bacteria.

During flowering, **bees and other insects** carry the bacteria from flower to flower. Rain, wind and tools can also spread them. **Warm and damp weather** during the flowering period is particularly dangerous. Then the bacteria multiply very quickly. Through the flowers they enter the twigs and travel on into the tree.

Fruit growers use an **infection forecast model**. It uses **weather data** to calculate on which days the risk is high. This way they can take protective measures at the right time. Affected branches are cut off well into the healthy wood and disposed of safely. Tools are cleaned afterwards so that the disease is not carried on.

In Switzerland, the large **standard fruit trees** are particularly at risk. They shape many landscapes and are valuable for birds and insects. In years of severe fire blight, many trees had to be felled. That is why people are looking for varieties that are less susceptible.

gewusst: Fire blight was the first plant disease for which it was proved that a bacterium causes it.
A heavily affected tree can die within a single season.

teile.einleitung: Plants know where up and down are. This ability to react to **gravity** and to grow accordingly is called **gravitropism**. Roots grow downwards, shoots upwards.
wichtigste: Gravitropism is growth towards or against gravity.
Main roots grow downwards, they are positively gravitropic.
Shoots grow upwards, they are negatively gravitropic.
In the root cap, amyloplasts serve as gravity sensors.
The plant hormone auxin controls the bending.
Lateral roots grow at a slant, which is called plagiogravitropic.

abschnitte.text: If you put a seedling into the soil the wrong way round, the root still bends downwards and the shoot upwards. If an organ grows towards the centre of the Earth, it is called **positively gravitropic**, like the main root. The shoot is **negatively gravitropic**. **Lateral roots** grow at a slanting angle, and are **plagiogravitropic**. This way they spread well through the soil.

In the **root cap**, the protective cap at the root tip, lies an area called the **columella**. There sit special cells, the **statocytes**. They contain heavy, starch-filled grains, the **amyloplasts**. These always sink to the lower side of the cell. This is how the plant senses in which direction gravity pulls.

If a root lies horizontally, the hormone **auxin** collects on its underside. In the root, auxin inhibits the stretching of cells. So the upper side grows faster and the root bends downwards. In the shoot it is the other way round: there auxin promotes stretching. That is why a bent-over **cereal stalk** straightens up again after a few days, because the underside of its nodes grows more strongly.

In 1806 the Englishman **Thomas Andrew Knight** fixed seedlings on a quickly spinning wheel. The roots grew outwards, that is, in the direction of the **centrifugal force**. This showed that they react to centrifugal force as to gravity. With a **clinostat**, a slowly rotating device, the one-sided effect of gravity is cancelled out. Plant growth in weightlessness has also been studied in space.

gewusst: The word comes from the Latin “gravis” for heavy and the Greek “tropos” for turning.
A cereal field that lies flat on the ground after a thunderstorm can partly straighten up again.

teile.einleitung: Wood energy is energy that is released when wood is burned. In Switzerland, many houses, school buildings and whole neighbourhoods are heated with wood from their own forests.
wichtigste: Wood can be burned as logs, wood chips or pellets.
Wood from sustainable forestry is regarded as almost CO2-neutral.
Firewood has to be well dried.
A stere is one cubic metre of stacked firewood with gaps in between.
Badly run wood-burning stoves produce a lot of fine dust.
A wood heating system can supply many houses through a district heating network.

abschnitte.text: The best known is **log wood**, that is, split pieces of wood for stoves and fireplaces. Stacked firewood is measured in **stere**: one stere is a cube with sides of one metre, filled with logs. Because there is air between them, it contains less wood than a solid cubic metre. For large heating systems, branches, treetops and leftover wood are chopped into **wood chips**. Many municipalities use them to heat school buildings.

As a tree grows, it takes **CO2** from the air. When it is burned, about the same amount is released again. If as much grows back in the forest as is used, the balance stays almost even. That is why wood from **sustainable forestry** is regarded as almost **CO2-neutral**. For transport and processing, however, some energy is needed too.

Firewood should be well **dried** before it is burned. In wet wood, the water first has to evaporate, which costs energy. Wet wood also smokes more and leaves more soot. Poor burning produces a lot of **fine dust**, tiny particles that can get deep into the lungs. Lighting the fire properly and using dry, untreated wood reduce the emissions.

A **tiled stove** stores the warmth of the fire in its thick walls of stone and ceramic. These go on giving it off for hours after the fire has long gone out. In many places today there are **district heating networks**. In a heating plant, heat is produced with wood and delivered through insulated pipes as hot water to many houses. The individual houses then do not need a stove of their own.

gewusst: After hydropower, wood is one of the most important renewable energy sources in Switzerland.
Wood pellets are small sticks of pressed sawdust that hold together without glue.

teile.einleitung: Plants cannot walk around to find a partner, and yet they reproduce in a surprising number of ways. Some form flowers, seeds and fruits, while others simply send runners or tubers into the soil. In the reproduction of plants, a distinction is made between sexual and asexual reproduction.
wichtigste: In sexual reproduction, the genetic material of two parent plants mixes.
In asexual reproduction, an exact copy of the mother plant is produced.
In flowering plants, pollination brings pollen to the stigma of a flower.
After fertilisation, the fruit develops from the ovary, and the seed inside it.
Seeds are spread by wind, water or animals, for example maple fruits fly as helicopter seeds.
The strawberry reproduces asexually by runners.
Ferns and mosses reproduce not with seeds, but with spores.

abschnitte.text: The flower is the reproductive organ of seed plants. In the stamens, the **pollen** is made, a fine powder containing the male reproductive cells. In **pollination**, the pollen reaches the stigma, usually with the help of insects such as bees, bumblebees and butterflies, or by the wind. Grasses, hazel shrubs and birches let the wind carry their pollen, which people with hay fever notice.

On the stigma, a fine pollen tube grows from the pollen grain down to the ovule. There the male and female reproductive cells fuse, and this is **fertilisation**. Afterwards the ovule develops into the seed, and the **ovary** becomes the fruit. With the cherry you can see this well: the white flower in April becomes a red cherry with a stone in summer.

So that young plants do not grow in the shade of the mother plant, seeds are spread. The dandelion has little parachutes, and the fruits of the maple spin through the air as **helicopter seeds**. Birds eat berries and pass the seeds out again in another place. The **burdock** has little hooks that catch on the fur of animals, and the coconut can float across the sea.

Many plants can also reproduce without flowers. The strawberry forms long **runners**, on which new little plants take root. Potatoes grow from tubers, and tulips and onions from bulbs. Gardeners often cut off **cuttings**, that is, pieces of twig that form new roots in soil or water.

Ferns, mosses and horsetails form no seeds, but tiny **spores**. In the fern, they sit in small clusters on the underside of the leaf. Spores are so light that the wind can carry them far. For their fertilisation, these plants need water, which is why they like to grow in damp places.

The Swiss engineer **George de Mestral** wondered about the burrs in his dog's fur after a walk. Under the microscope he saw the many small hooks of the fruits. Following this model, he developed **Velcro**, which today holds shut shoes, jackets and bags. When technology takes ideas from nature, it is called biomimetics.

begriffe.erklaerung: Pollen travels from the stamens to the stigma of a flower.
A male and a female reproductive cell fuse with each other.
The lower part of the pistil, from which the fruit develops.
A long shoot on which a new plant grows.
A piece of plant cut off that forms new roots.

gewusst: A single dandelion plant can produce several thousand seeds.
Many bananas in the shop no longer have seeds that can sprout and are only reproduced asexually.
Some seeds stay able to sprout for decades and wait in the soil for good conditions.

teile.einleitung: Frost is when it gets so cold that water freezes, that is, below 0 degrees Celsius. You can see it especially well when water on the ground, on grass and on car windows turns to ice. In Switzerland there is frost almost everywhere in winter, and in the mountains even in summer.
wichtigste: Frost means that the temperature falls below 0 degrees Celsius and water freezes.
Ground frost occurs when it is colder than 0 degrees close to the ground, even if the air higher up is still warmer.
On clear nights without clouds, it gets cold especially quickly.
Frozen water vapour forms hoar frost, rime and frost flowers.
Late frost in spring can destroy blossom and young plants.
Freezing water expands and can even split rocks.
In high parts of the Alps there is permafrost, which is permanently frozen ground.

abschnitte.text: We speak of **frost** when the temperature falls below 0 degrees Celsius. At this temperature, water freezes into ice. A day on which it gets below 0 degrees at some point is called a frost day. If it stays below zero all day, it is called an **ice day**.

On clear, windless nights, the ground gives off a lot of heat into space, because no clouds hold it back. The cold, heavy air collects on the ground and in hollows. That is why there is often **ground frost**, while two metres higher it is still above 0 degrees. Cold air from the north or east can also bring frost.

When water vapour from the air freezes directly on cold surfaces, **hoar frost** forms, a white coating on grass and cars. In fog and cold, long needles of ice form on trees, called **rime**. On cold window panes, ice crystals sometimes grow in patterns that look like fern leaves, the frost flowers. If rain freezes on the ground, there is dangerous black ice.

Many plants here are adapted to frost: trees drop their leaves, and flowers spend the winter as bulbs in the ground. Dangerous, however, is **late frost** in spring, when fruit trees are already in blossom. That is why many people in Switzerland wait to plant sensitive vegetables until after the **Ice Saints** in mid-May. Fruit growers sometimes spray their trees with water on frosty nights, because heat is released when water freezes, and the layer of ice protects the blossom.

Water expands by about a tenth when it freezes. If it gets into cracks in rock and freezes, it can burst stones apart, which is called **frost shattering**. This is how large scree slopes form on mountainsides. In the Alps, the ground above about 2500 metres is often permanently frozen, which is the **permafrost** that holds rocks and slopes together.

In frost, municipalities spread salt or grit on roads and pavements so that nobody slips. Water pipes outdoors have to be drained, or they can burst. Our skin can be damaged in severe cold, which is called **frostbite**. Warm gloves, a hat and good shoes protect against it.

begriffe.erklaerung: Frost directly above the ground, while the air higher up can be warmer.
White ice crystals that form from water vapour on cold surfaces.
Days in mid-May, after which frost is usually over.
Ground that stays frozen all year round.

gewusst: The lowest temperature officially measured in Switzerland was minus 41.8 degrees Celsius, recorded in 1987 in La Brévine in the Neuchâtel Jura.
Because ice is lighter than water, lakes freeze from the top and fish can survive underneath.
A frozen drop of water in a crack in the rock can push with great force and so split stones.

teile.einleitung: Plants control their growth with their own messenger substances, the plant hormones. An important group of them are the **gibberellins**. They make stems grow longer, help seeds to sprout and are used deliberately in agriculture.
wichtigste: Gibberellins were discovered through the rice disease “bakanae” in Japan.
Affected rice plants grow excessively long.
Chemically, gibberellins are diterpenes with 20 carbon atoms.
They trigger the breakdown of growth-inhibiting DELLA proteins.
In a sprouting barley grain, they stimulate the formation of alpha-amylase.
Short-stalked wheat varieties respond less to gibberellins.

abschnitte.text: In Japan, the fungus **Gibberella fujikuroi** attacked rice plants. The disease was called **“bakanae”**, which means roughly “foolish seedling”. The affected plants grew **excessively long**, fell over and gave little yield. Japanese researchers isolated the active substance from the fungus and named it **gibberellin** after the fungus. Later it turned out that plants themselves also make such substances.

Chemically, gibberellins belong to the **diterpenes**. Their basic framework consists of **20 carbon atoms** and is built from isoprene units. In the cell they work by a trick: **DELLA proteins** put the brakes on growth. When gibberellin binds to its **receptor**, the DELLA proteins are broken down, and the brake is released. The plant can grow.

In a sprouting **barley grain**, the embryo sends gibberellins into the **aleurone layer**. This then makes the enzyme **alpha-amylase**. It breaks down the starch in the endosperm into sugar, which feeds the embryo. In **rosette plants** such as lettuce, gibberellins cause the sections between the leaves to stretch greatly. The plant **bolts** and forms a long flower stem.

Many wheat varieties of the **Green Revolution** have short stalks. The reason is the so-called **Rht genes**: they change proteins of the gibberellin signalling pathway, so that the stalks respond less to the hormone. Short stalks do not bend over so easily under heavy ears. **Growth retardants** such as **chlormequat** work in a similar way. They inhibit enzymes of gibberellin formation, and the stalks stay shorter and sturdier.

In fruit and wine growing, gibberellins are also used deliberately. Seedless **table grapes** are often sprayed with **gibberellic acid**. This promotes the growth of the berries and loosens up the bunch. This produces bigger fruits that sell better.

gewusst: Gibberellins were discovered through a fungal disease that made rice plants grow too long.
The short stalks of modern wheat varieties are due to a lower sensitivity to gibberellins.

teile.einleitung: Foxgloves are tall plants with bell-shaped flowers. They are very poisonous, but they also supply important active substances for heart medicines.
wichtigste: Foxgloves contain cardiac glycosides, which act on the heart.
The medicine digoxin is obtained from the woolly foxglove.
In 1785 the English doctor William Withering described the healing effect in detail.
Foxgloves are now counted among the plantain family.
The common foxglove likes to grow in woodland clearings with acidic soil.
In Switzerland the large yellow foxglove and the small yellow foxglove grow wild, and both bloom yellow.
The healing dose and the poisonous dose lie very close together.

abschnitte.text: **Foxgloves** carry many tube-shaped flowers on a tall stem. You can put a finger into them like into a thimble for sewing. The scientific name is **Digitalis**, from the Latin word for finger. In the past, foxgloves were counted among the figwort family. Today they are placed in the **plantain family**.

In nature, the **common foxglove** especially likes to grow in **woodland clearings with acidic soil**. It often appears where trees have been felled. In gardens it is a popular ornamental plant. In Switzerland the **large yellow foxglove** and the **small yellow foxglove** grow wild. Both have **yellow** flowers.

All parts of foxgloves are **highly poisonous**. Even a few leaves can be dangerous for a person. Before flowering, the leaves are sometimes mistaken for the harmless **comfrey**. That is why you must never prepare foxglove as a tea yourself. The **healing dose and the poisonous dose** lie very close together. If you suspect poisoning, in Switzerland you call the emergency number 145 of Tox Info Suisse at once.

The active substances of foxgloves are called **cardiac glycosides**. In the right amount, they strengthen the force of the heart and slow the heartbeat. The English doctor **William Withering** described the healing effect in detail in **1785**. The medicine **digoxin** is still obtained from the **woolly foxglove** today. It is only prescribed by doctors and carefully dosed.

gewusst: Withering had heard of a herbal recipe and then spent years investigating how foxglove works.
Digoxin is still obtained from the plant today, because making it in a laboratory is very costly.

teile.einleitung: Not all deer look the same, and not all apple trees bear the same apples. The reason is **genetic diversity**: the living things of a species differ in their genetic material. These differences are very important for the survival of a species.
wichtigste: Genetic diversity means differences in the genetic material within a species.
A species with high genetic diversity can adapt better to change.
Clones, that is, genetically identical plants, are especially prone to disease.
Very small animal populations lose diversity, and inbreeding occurs.
Wildlife bridges and corridors connect separated populations.
In the seed vault on Svalbard, seeds are stored as a reserve for the whole world.

abschnitte.text: Every living thing carries in its cells the **genetic material**, a kind of blueprint. Within a species, this blueprint is not the same in all of them. That is why there are bigger and smaller roe deer, lighter and darker foxes. These differences are called **genetic diversity**. Alongside the diversity of species and of habitats, it is a part of **biodiversity**.

The environment is constantly changing: new diseases appear, the climate gets warmer or drier. If the genetic material of a species is varied, there are often some animals or plants that cope with the new situation. They survive and pass on their characteristics. This way the species can **adapt**. If diversity is lacking, a single disease can strike very many living things at once.

Most bananas in the shops belong to the **Cavendish** variety. It is reproduced from offshoots, so the plants are **clones**. A fungal disease can therefore threaten whole plantations. A sad example from history is the **Great Famine in Ireland**: from 1845, potato blight destroyed large parts of the harvest there. Because the same varieties grew almost everywhere, the disease spread unchecked.

abschnitte.titel: When only a few animals are left
abschnitte.text: If a population consists of only a few animals, they are often closely related. This is called **inbreeding**. Genetic diversity falls, and hereditary diseases or epidemics have a stronger effect. A well-known example is the **cheetah**: cheetahs are genetically very similar to one another, probably because of a sharp decline in their numbers in the past.

Roads, settlements and railway lines cut up habitats. **Wildlife bridges** and **wildlife corridors** help animals to move between separated areas. This way populations mix again. In Switzerland, too, there are such wildlife crossings over motorways. For crop plants there are seed banks. Since 2008, the **Svalbard Global Seed Vault** on Svalbard has stored seed from all over the world in the permafrost.

gewusst: The seed vault on Svalbard serves as a safety copy for seed banks all over the world.
The bananas that we buy in the shop are almost all genetically nearly the same.

teile.einleitung: In the Alps it is getting warmer. Many plants react to this by slowly advancing to higher altitudes. This is called the uphill migration of plants.
wichtigste: For every 100 metres of height, the air gets about 0.6 °C cooler on average.
When it gets warmer, many plants only find suitable conditions further up.
Even 1 °C of warming shifts the warm zones by around 170 metres of height.
On many European summits, more plant species grow today than in the past.
High-alpine specialists cannot move out of the way any further at the summit.
The tree line rises only slowly, because trees grow slowly and need soil.

abschnitte.titel: Colder with every metre of height
abschnitte.text: Anyone who climbs a mountain notices that it gets cooler. On average, the air temperature falls by about **0.6 °C** per 100 metres of height. That is why there are different **altitudinal zones** in the mountains, from deciduous forest in the valley through conifer forest to the alpine grassland and the rock. Each plant species grows where warmth, snow and soil suit it.

If the temperature rises by 1 °C, the same warmth now lies further up. You work out 1 divided by 0.6 times 100 metres. That gives around **167 metres**, so about 170 metres. That is how far a plant would have to move uphill to be as warm as before. Plants cannot walk: they “move” because their seeds sprout further up and new plants grow there.

For many years, researchers have been counting the plants on European **mountain summits**. Repeated counts show that on many summits, species from lower altitudes have arrived. The stronger the warming, the faster the number of species increases. On Swiss summits, too, plants were already counted in the 19th century, so a good comparison is possible today.

For **high-alpine plants** this is not good news. They are adapted to cold and short summers. Above the summit there is no more room to move out of the way. In addition, they face competition from plants that move up from below and grow faster. Some specialists could therefore become rarer.

Above the closed mountain forest lies the **struggle zone**. There, only single, often stunted trees stand, fighting against cold, wind and snow. When it gets warmer, trees and shrubs advance upwards. But this happens slowly: young trees need decades at great height, and on rock and scree there is often no soil. Grazing and avalanches also hold the forest back. Where the forest does advance, the **alpine grasslands** become smaller.

gewusst: A difference of 1 °C corresponds in the mountains to about 170 metres of height.
Plants do not move as a whole, but through their seeds, which sprout further up.

teile.einleitung: If you look at a tree stump, you see light and dark rings. Each annual ring consists of two parts: the light **earlywood** and the darker **latewood**. They reveal a lot about the life of the tree.
wichtigste: An annual ring consists of the earlywood and latewood of one year.
Earlywood has wide, thin-walled cells and carries a lot of water.
Latewood has narrow, thick-walled cells and gives strength.
Latewood looks darker because it is denser.
A lot of latewood makes wood heavier and stronger.
In winter growth rests, and the cambium is inactive.

abschnitte.text: Under the bark lies a thin growth layer, the **cambium**. It forms new wood every year. In spring, the tree needs a lot of water for the new leaves. So it forms **wide, thin-walled cells**. A lot of water can flow upwards through them. This wood is called **earlywood** and is usually light.

In the second half of the growing season, from **summer** to late summer, this changes. Now **narrow cells with thick walls** form. This **latewood** contains more cell wall material per volume. That is why it looks **darker** and denser. It makes the trunk stable. In winter the cambium rests.

An **annual ring** includes the earlywood and the latewood of one growing season. Between the dark latewood and the light earlywood of the next year there is a sharp boundary. This is how you can count the rings and work out the **age** of a tree. In the **tropics** there are often no pronounced seasons. There, many trees show hardly any clear annual rings.

The more latewood there is, the higher the **density** and **strength**. In the **oak**, the pore-rich earlywood zone almost always stays the same width. A wide ring therefore consists mainly of additional dense latewood. In oaks, wide rings usually mean stronger wood. In the **spruce**, on the other hand, narrow, even rings count as a mark of quality.

Spruces from **mountain areas** grow slowly. Their annual rings are narrow and very even. Such wood is suitable as **tonewood** for the tops of violins, guitars and pianos. In the Swiss mountain forests, too, tonewood is in demand. Scientists can even read earlier climate conditions from annual rings, which is called **dendrochronology**.

gewusst: With annual rings you can work out the age of wood in old houses to the exact year.
A dry summer often leaves a particularly narrow annual ring.

teile.einleitung: The **ginkgo** is a very special tree. Its leaves look like small fans, and it already existed in the time of the dinosaurs. That is why it is called a “living fossil”. Today it grows in many parks and towns, in Switzerland too.
wichtigste: The ginkgo leaf has the shape of a fan, often with a notch in the middle.
The scientific name Ginkgo biloba means two-lobed.
The ginkgo comes from China.
It was already growing in the time of the dinosaurs.
It is neither an ordinary broadleaf tree nor a conifer.
In autumn its leaves turn golden yellow.

abschnitte.text: The ginkgo leaf is broad and tapers towards the stalk. It looks like an open **fan**. Many leaves have a **notch** in the middle and are thus divided into **two** parts. That is why the tree is scientifically called **Ginkgo biloba**, which means two-lobed. In autumn the leaves glow **golden yellow**. Often they then all fall off within a few days.

Fossilised ginkgo leaves are many millions of years old. Ginkgo trees were already growing in the time of the **dinosaurs**. That is why the ginkgo is called a **“living fossil”**. It is neither an ordinary broadleaf tree nor a conifer. It is the **last living species** of a very old plant group.

The ginkgo comes from **China**. In the wild it now grows in only a few places there. Today it stands all over the world in parks and along streets. Ginkgos are very **robust**: exhaust fumes, heat and pests bother them little. That is why they are often planted in towns.

There are male and female ginkgo trees. Only the female ones bear **seeds**. Their fleshy covering smells very unpleasant in autumn, a little like **rancid butter**. That is why mostly male trees are planted in towns. In China and Japan, the **seed kernels** are roasted and eaten in small amounts. Raw or in large amounts they are not good for you.

gewusst: Ginkgo trees already existed when dinosaurs lived.
The seeds of female ginkgos smell of rancid butter in autumn.

teile.einleitung: The hornbeam (in German, “Hainbuche”) is a common tree in Swiss woods and gardens. Despite its German name, it is not a true beech. It is known for its very hard wood and as a hedge plant.
wichtigste: The hornbeam belongs to the birch family, not to the beeches.
It is also called white beech or hedge beech in German.
Its trunk is fluted and looks as if it had muscles.
The leaf has a finely, doubly toothed edge.
Its wood is among the hardest woods of our forests.
It tolerates cutting well and is a popular hedge.

abschnitte.text: The **hornbeam** is called a beech in German (“Hainbuche”), but is not closely related to the copper beech. It belongs to the **birch family** and is thus a relative of the birch and the hazel. Because its wood is very pale, it is also called **white beech** (“Weissbuche”). Another old name is **hedge beech** (“Hagebuche”). A “Hag” is an old word for a hedge.

The trunk of the hornbeam is not round. It has **ridges and grooves** that run lengthways along the trunk. That is why it looks as if it had strong muscles. The bark is smooth and grey. This also makes the hornbeam easy to recognise in winter.

The leaf of the hornbeam has a **finely and doubly toothed edge**. The leaf surface looks as if folded, because the veins are deeply impressed. The fruits are small **nutlets**. Each hangs on a **three-lobed wing**. In the wind the fruits spin and fly a little way from the tree.

The wood of the hornbeam is among the **hardest woods** in our forests. In the past it was used to make parts that had to withstand a lot, for example **cogwheels** in mills, tool handles and chopping blocks. As firewood, too, it is very highly valued.

The hornbeam tolerates **cutting** very well. It sprouts again and again afterwards and becomes dense. That is why it is a popular **hedge plant** in gardens in Switzerland. Many clipped hedges keep their **dry brown leaves** all winter. Only in spring, when new leaves grow, do they fall off. This way the hedge stays opaque in winter too.

gewusst: Hornbeam wood is so hard that cogwheels for mills were once made from it.
A hornbeam hedge can keep its brown leaves until spring.

teile.einleitung: Poisonous plants are plants that contain substances that can harm people or animals. Some are only slightly poisonous, others dangerous to life even in small amounts. The most poisonous plant in Europe is regarded as the blue monkshood, which also grows in the Swiss Alps.
wichtigste: Poisonous plants contain substances that can harm people and animals.
The blue monkshood is regarded as the most poisonous plant in Europe.
Edible wild garlic is often mistaken for the poisonous lily of the valley.
In the yew, only the red aril is not poisonous.
In case of poisoning, in Switzerland you dial 145.
Paracelsus taught that the dose alone decides whether something is poisonous.
Plants make poison mainly as protection against animals that want to eat them.

abschnitte.text: Plants cannot run away when an animal wants to eat them. Many therefore protect themselves with **poisonous substances** in leaves, berries, roots or seeds. Some of these substances taste bitter and so warn the animals. Often it is not the whole plant that is equally poisonous, but mainly certain parts.

The **blue monkshood**, with its helmet-shaped, blue-violet flowers, grows in damp mountain meadows and is regarded as the most poisonous plant in Europe. Also very poisonous are deadly nightshade with its black berries, foxglove, meadow saffron and laburnum. In the **yew**, needles and seeds are poisonous. Only the red aril around the seed is not poisonous, but the seed inside it is.

In spring, many people collect **wild garlic** in the woods. Its leaves look very similar to those of the poisonous lily of the valley and meadow saffron. You recognise wild garlic by its strong smell of garlic when you rub a leaf. Anyone who is not quite sure should never eat a plant.

The physician **Paracelsus** was born around 1493 near Einsiedeln. He put forward the idea that the dose alone decides whether a thing is a poison. In fact, some plant poisons are used as medicines in tiny, precisely measured amounts. From foxglove, for example, a heart medicine was obtained.

abschnitte.titel: What to do in case of poisoning?
abschnitte.text: If someone may have eaten a poisonous plant, in Switzerland you call the number **145** at once. Tox Info Suisse answers there, the advice centre for poisonings, which can be reached around the clock. You should if possible be able to say which plant it was and how much of it was eaten. If the person is unconscious or short of breath, you dial the emergency number 144.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that can harm the body even in small amounts.
The amount of a substance that you take in.
The red, fleshy covering around the seed of the yew.
The Swiss advice centre for poisonings, telephone 145.

gewusst: The poison of the blue monkshood can even be taken up through the skin, which is why you should not pick the plant.
Birds eat the red yew berries without harm, because they pass the poisonous seeds out again undigested.

teile.einleitung: The **Norway spruce** is the most common tree in Switzerland. In Switzerland it is also called the **Rottanne**. It supplies a lot of wood, but it also has its weaknesses.
wichtigste: The spruce is a conifer with a pointed, cone-shaped crown.
Its needles sit all around the twig.
The cones hang and fall off as a whole.
Naturally, the spruce grows mainly in the mountains.
It has shallow roots and is easily blown over in a storm.
The bark beetle can harm many spruces.

abschnitte.text: Young spruces have a narrow, **pointed crown** that looks like a **cone**. The needles stand singly **all around the whole twig**. This makes it look like a bottle brush. The bark is reddish brown, hence the Swiss name **Rottanne**. Spruces often grow 30 to 50 metres tall.

The **cones** of the spruce are elongated and about **10 to 15 centimetres** long, as long as a hand. They **hang** downwards. When ripe, they are brown. The spruce lets its cones fall as a whole. That is why there are often many cones lying under it. With the silver fir, on the other hand, the cones fall apart on the tree.

Naturally, the spruce grows mainly in **mountain forest**. It tolerates cold and a lot of snow. On the **Plateau** it was often planted by people, because it grows quickly. There, however, it is often too warm and too dry for it. Because of **climate change**, it is expected to become rarer in low-lying areas.

The roots of the spruce spread out **flat like a plate** under the ground. That is why the **storm** can blow it over more easily. Another enemy is the **bark beetle**. It bores tunnels under the bark. Weakened spruces can die of it. If the bark is injured, the spruce seals the wound with sticky **resin**. This way it protects itself against fungi and insects.

**Spruce wood** is light, pale and grows back quickly. It is used for **roof beams**, boards and furniture. **Paper** is also often made from spruce wood. Slowly grown mountain spruces even supply **tonewood** for violins. Many Christmas trees in Switzerland are also spruces.

gewusst: Although it is called Rottanne (red fir) in Switzerland, the spruce is not a fir.
A piece of spruce wood in a violin can come from a mountain tree centuries old.

teile.einleitung: The **style** (in German, “Griffel”) is a part of the flower. It connects the stigma, on which the pollen lands, with the ovary. Without it, the pollen could not reach the ovules.
wichtigste: The style connects the stigma with the ovary.
Ovary, style and stigma together form the pistil.
The pollen tube grows down through the style.
An apple blossom has five styles.
In clematis, the styles form feathery tails on the fruits.

abschnitte.text: In the middle of many flowers stands the **pistil**. It consists of three parts: at the bottom the **ovary** with the ovules, above it the **style** and at the top the **stigma**. The stigma is often sticky or hairy so that pollen sticks well. The style is mostly a thin stalk. Some flowers have several styles, the **apple blossom** for example five.

If a pollen grain lands on a suitable stigma, it germinates. It forms a fine **pollen tube**, which grows down through the style to the ovary. The tube brings the male reproductive cells to the **ovule**. There **fertilisation** takes place, and a seed can form. The ovary becomes the fruit.

In the **primrose** there are two flower forms: flowers with a long style and flowers with a short style. The stamens sit at the other height in each case. This way a bumblebee mostly carries the pollen from one flower form to the other. This promotes **cross-pollination**, that is, pollination between different plants. Charles Darwin had already studied this.

In some plants the style stays on after flowering. **Clematis**, a climbing plant in Swiss hedges and woods, forms long, feathery tails from it. With them the wind carries the fruits away. The **cranesbill** gets its name from its long, beak-shaped fruit, which develops from the style.

gewusst: The silvery hairy fruit clusters of clematis look like little beards in winter.
In the cranesbill, the ripe fruit can fling the seeds a little way.

teile.einleitung: A **green manure** (in German, “Gründüngung”) is plants that you do not harvest, but sow in order to improve the soil. They protect empty beds, loosen the soil and supply nutrients.
wichtigste: Green manure is plants meant to improve the soil.
Phacelia has blue flowers and is also called “bee friend”.
Clover and lupins fix nitrogen from the air with nodule bacteria.
Green manure protects empty beds from being washed away by rain.
The plant remains become humus.
You cut the green manure before it forms seeds.

abschnitte.text: After the harvest, a bed is often left empty. If you then sow plants such as **phacelia**, **mustard**, **clover** or **lupins**, the soil stays covered. Their roots **loosen** the soil and hold it together. Before the plants form **seeds**, you cut them and leave them lying as **mulch** or work them in lightly. This way they do not self-seed all over the garden.

Clover, lupins and vetches belong to the **legumes**. In small nodules on their roots live **nodule bacteria**. These bacteria can fix **nitrogen** from the air and give it to the plants. When the plants rot later, the nitrogen stays in the soil. The next crop is thus fertilised naturally.

Bare soil is exposed to wind and rain in winter. Heavy rain can **wash away** the fertile soil, which is called **erosion**. A green manure prevents this and holds on to nutrients that would otherwise be washed out. From the dead plant remains, **humus** forms, the dark, fertile part of the soil. Earthworms and other soil animals find food in it.

The blue-flowering **phacelia** is also called **bee friend**, because bees and bumblebees love it. It is not related to any vegetable and therefore fits almost everywhere. **Mustard**, on the other hand, should not be sown before **cabbage**. Both belong to the **brassicas** and share the same diseases and pests. In Swiss agriculture too, intermediate crops are often grown.

gewusst: Phacelia originally comes from North America.
Lupin roots can reach very deep into the soil and break up compacted earth.

teile.einleitung: Green beans, kidney beans and dried beans have something in common: they all come from the **common bean**. This plant originally comes from America and is now a popular vegetable.
wichtigste: Raw beans are poisonous, so you must always cook them.
The runner bean climbs up long poles.
The bush bean grows low and needs no support.
The kidney bean is a red variety of the common bean.
Yellow beans are called wax beans.
“Dörrbohnen” are dried beans, for example for the Berner Platte.

abschnitte.text: The **common bean** comes from **Central and South America**. There, people grew it thousands of years ago. After the discovery of America, it came to Europe. It belongs to the **legumes**, like the pea and the lentil. Bacteria live on its roots that fix nitrogen from the air. That is why it needs little fertiliser.

The **runner bean** grows several metres tall. That is why you put long poles in the ground. It has no tendrils. Its whole **stem winds** in circles around the pole. The **bush bean**, on the other hand, stays low and grows as a small bush. It needs no climbing aid and is ready to harvest sooner.

Raw beans contain a **poisonous substance**, **phasin**. Even a few raw beans can cause tummy ache and nausea. When **cooked**, the poison is destroyed. That is why you never eat beans raw, not even from the garden. This applies to green beans as well as to dried bean seeds.

With **green beans** you eat the young, tender **pod** together with the small seeds. **Wax beans** are yellow, and their colour is reminiscent of wax. With other varieties you eat only the ripe, dried seeds. The **kidney bean** is red and has the shape of a kidney, because “kidney” is the English word for the organ. It is often found in chilli con carne.

In the past there was hardly any fresh vegetable in winter. That is why green beans were **dried** in summer. These **dried beans** (“Dörrbohnen”) keep for a long time. Before cooking, you soak them in water. To this day they are part of the **Berner Platte**, a traditional dish with various kinds of meat. In other cantons, too, dried beans are popular.

gewusst: The runner bean always winds in the same direction around its pole.
Beans improve garden soil, because bacteria on their roots collect nitrogen.

teile.einleitung: The **Great Famine** struck Ireland between 1845 and about 1849. A plant disease destroyed the potatoes, the most important food of the poor population. Around a million people died.
wichtigste: The famine lasted from 1845 to about 1849.
In Irish it is called “An Gorta Mór”.
Potato blight destroyed the potato harvests.
Around a million people died.
More than a million emigrated, mainly to North America.
Ireland then belonged to the United Kingdom.

abschnitte.text: In the 19th century, many Irish people lived as poor smallholders and farm labourers. Their food consisted almost only of **potatoes**. In the fields, almost everywhere the same variety grew. It was **propagated vegetatively**, that is, grown from tubers, and all the plants were therefore equally susceptible. This made the fields very vulnerable.

In 1845, **potato blight** appeared in Ireland. A pathogen made leaves and tubers rot within a short time. It had come from America to Europe and also hit other countries, even Switzerland. In Ireland, however, the harvests failed almost completely for several years in a row. Because there was no other food, a famine broke out.

Ireland was then part of the **United Kingdom**. The government in London helped only hesitantly and too little. While people starved, grain, cattle and other goods continued to be **exported** from Ireland. Many families also lost their land because they could not pay the rent. These events strained the relationship between Ireland and Great Britain for a long time.

Around **a million people** died of hunger and disease. More than a million **emigrated**, mainly to the USA and Canada. Through death and emigration, the population of Ireland fell by about **20 to 25 per cent**. Even afterwards, many more moved away. In Ireland today, memorials and museums recall the famine.

gewusst: Many Americans have ancestors who emigrated from Ireland at that time.
To this day, Ireland has fewer inhabitants than before the famine.

teile.einleitung: Millet is a cereal with tiny, round grains. It also grows where it is hot and dry. In the past, millet porridge was an important food in Switzerland, and today millet is a staple food in many countries of Africa.
wichtigste: Millet grains are small, round and mostly pale yellow.
Millet contains no gluten.
In many countries of Africa and Asia it is an important food.
Before the potato arrived, people in Switzerland often ate millet porridge.
Millet is cooked in water, much like rice.
Spray millet is a popular food for budgies.

abschnitte.text: **Millet** is a **cereal**, like wheat, barley or rice. Its grains, however, are tiny, **round** and mostly **pale yellow**. They are much smaller than wheat grains. Millet is one of the oldest crops grown by humans. The word millet refers to various grass species with small grains.

Millet also grows where it is **hot and dry**. It needs less water than many other cereals. That is why it is an especially important food in **many countries of Africa** and in parts of **Asia**. There it is eaten as porridge, as flatbread or in soups.

Before the **potato** came to Europe, **millet porridge** was an important dish in Switzerland too. Millet is easy to cook and fills you up. The fairy tale **“The Sweet Porridge”** by the Brothers Grimm is also well known. In it, a magic pot cooks so much millet porridge that the whole town fills up with it.

Millet is **cooked** in **water**, much like rice. Afterwards it is soft and fluffy. It goes well with vegetables or as a sweet porridge. You can also buy **millet flakes** and add them to muesli. Millet contains **no gluten**. Gluten is a protein found in wheat, spelt or barley that some people cannot tolerate. For them, millet is a good choice.

Many pets like millet too. **Spray millet** is a popular food for **budgies** and other cage birds. The grains are still attached to the long spikes. The birds peck off the small grains one by one and are kept busy for a long time.

gewusst: Millet was already grown many thousands of years ago and is one of the oldest cereals in the world.
The year 2023 was declared the International Year of Millets by the United Nations.

teile.einleitung: Hail is small, solid grains of ice that can fall from the sky during a thunderstorm. Usually they are the size of peas, but sometimes as big as tennis balls. Hail can cause great damage to fields, cars and houses in a short time.
wichtigste: Hail consists of solid grains of ice that fall during thunderstorms.
Hailstones form in tall thunderclouds.
Strong updrafts carry the grains upwards several times.
Only from a diameter of about five millimetres do we speak of hail.
In Switzerland it hails mainly in summer.
Hail can severely damage harvests, cars and roofs.

abschnitte.text: Hail forms in a tall **thundercloud**, in which it is ice-cold at the top. Strong updrafts tear water droplets upwards, where they freeze into small grains of ice. More droplets freeze onto these grains, so that they grow layer by layer. Only when they are too heavy do they fall to the ground as **hailstones**.

If you cut open a large hailstone, you often see layers like those of an onion. Clear and milky layers show how the grain was whirled up and down in the cloud. Small, soft grains under five millimetres are called **graupel**. Most hailstones are a few centimetres across, and very rarely they can reach over ten centimetres.

In Switzerland it hails mainly between May and September, often after hot, muggy days. Especially affected are the Plateau, the Napf region, the Jura and Ticino. MeteoSwiss uses radar to make maps of where it has hailed, and warns of violent thunderstorms. Since 1880 there has been **hail insurance** in Switzerland for farming families.

A heavy hailstorm can destroy a whole harvest in a few minutes. Hailstones leave dents in cars and smash roof tiles, windows and blinds. For people and animals outdoors, large grains can be dangerous. Hail damage costs many millions of francs in Switzerland every year.

Many fruit growers stretch **hail nets** over their apple and cherry trees. Vineyards, too, are partly protected with nets. When there is a hail warning, you should put the car in a garage and pull up blinds so that they are not damaged. If you are outside, quickly look for shelter in a building.

begriffe.erklaerung: A single grain of ice from a hail shower.
Small, soft grains of ice, smaller than hail.
Air that flows strongly upwards.
A net that protects fruit trees and vines from hail.

gewusst: Hail falls almost only in summer, although it is made of ice, because only then are there such powerful thunderstorms with strong updrafts.
Large hailstones can be faster than 100 kilometres per hour on impact.

teile.einleitung: In timber felling, trees in the forest are cut down and the wood is brought out. This is dangerous work that needs a lot of knowledge and good planning so that people and the forest stay protected.
wichtigste: The felling notch determines the direction in which a tree falls.
The hinge wood acts like a hinge when the tree is felled.
In Switzerland, timber has traditionally been felled mainly in winter.
On steep ground, trunks are often brought out with a cable crane.
A harvester fells, strips and saws up trees.
Machines drive only on skid trails.

abschnitte.text: First the forest worker saws the **felling notch**, a wedge-shaped cut on the side on which the tree is to fall. Then the **felling cut** follows from the opposite side. Between them a narrow strip of wood is left standing, the **hinge wood**. It acts like a **hinge** and steers the trunk in the desired direction. After that the tree is **limbed**, that is, the branches are sawn off the trunk.

In Switzerland, timber has traditionally been felled mainly in **winter**. Then the sap in the tree is resting, and the birds are not nesting. In addition, frozen ground is firmer. The machines press it down less and damage it less. Logging is dangerous work, which is why forest workers wear helmets, ear protection and cut-resistant trousers.

On flat ground, a **harvester** often does the work. With a single gripping head, it fells trees, strips their branches and saws them into pieces. To spare the forest floor, machines may drive only on firm tracks. These are called **skid trails**. The rest of the ground stays loose and healthy that way.

abschnitte.titel: Cable crane and solid cubic metres
abschnitte.text: In the Alps and the Pre-Alps, the terrain is often very steep. There, the trunks are brought out with a **cable crane**. It pulls them along a carrying cable across the slope to a road. The quantity of timber harvested is measured in **solid cubic metres**. One solid cubic metre corresponds to one cubic metre of solid wood without air gaps.

gewusst: In the Swiss mountains, trunks used to be brought down into the valley by wooden chutes or on rivers.
In Switzerland, only as much timber may be felled as will keep the forest in existence.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland, farmers are not allowed to grow genetically modified plants in order to sell them. This is regulated by the **GMO moratorium** (in German, “Gentech-Moratorium”). A moratorium is a postponement, that is, a ban for a limited time. It goes back to a popular vote in 2005.
wichtigste: On 27 November 2005, the electorate accepted the GM-free initiative.
The initiative won about 56 per cent Yes votes and carried every canton.
The moratorium bans the commercial growing of genetically modified plants.
Originally it applied for five years, and Parliament extended it several times.
In 2025 the National Council and the Council of States extended it to the end of 2030.
Research with a permit is allowed, including field trials.

abschnitte.text: On 27 November 2005, the Swiss people voted on the popular initiative “for food from GM-free agriculture”. It was accepted with about **56 per cent** Yes votes, and in **all cantons**. That was a surprise at the time. The initiative demanded a moratorium of **five years**. In this time, no genetically modified plants and animals were to be put on the market for agriculture.

abschnitte.titel: What is forbidden and what is not
abschnitte.text: What is forbidden is the **commercial growing** of genetically modified plants, **GMOs** for short. So farmers may not grow and sell such plants. **Research** and **medicine** are not affected by the moratorium. Field trials are also possible with a permit. The research institute **Agroscope** runs a protected trial area for this in Zurich-Reckenholz.

The handling of GMOs in animals, plants and the environment is regulated by the **Gene Technology Act** (GTG) of 2003. The moratorium is included in it as a transitional provision. After the first five years, Parliament extended the ban several times. It would have expired at the end of 2025. In 2025 the **National Council and the Council of States** extended it by another five years, **to the end of 2030**.

Meanwhile there are new methods such as **genome editing**. With it you can change the genetic material very precisely. For such new breeding technologies, Parliament demanded a **risk-based regulation**. The Federal Council proposed a separate law for it. Supporters hope for sturdier plants, while opponents worry about nature and freedom of choice. The discussion is politically contested.

gewusst: The GM-free initiative was accepted in all cantons in 2005.
A moratorium that was meant to last five years applies, after several extensions, until the end of 2030.

teile.einleitung: In shady woods, large green ferns often grow in a circle. Very often it is the **male fern** (in German, “Gewöhnlicher Wurmfarn”, or “common worm fern”). It is one of the most common ferns in Swiss woods. It gets its odd German name from an old remedy.
wichtigste: The male fern is one of the most common ferns in Swiss woods.
It likes shady, damp soils.
Its fronds stand in a circle like a funnel.
The fronds often grow over a metre long.
In the past, remedies from the rootstock were given against tapeworms.
The male fern is poisonous.

abschnitte.text: The male fern grows very often in the **woods**. It likes **shady** and **damp soils**. Ferns have no flowers. Their large leaves are called **fronds**. In the male fern they often grow half a metre to over a metre long. That is why it is a stately fern.
