All the fronds grow from a shared **rootstock** in the ground. They stand in a circle and together form a **funnel**. In spring the young fronds are still curled up like a snail and slowly unroll. In autumn and winter most fronds turn **brown** and die. The rootstock survives in the ground, and new fronds grow from it in spring.

Ferns form no seeds, but tiny **spores**. They form on the underside of the fronds in small **clusters of spores**. In the male fern, each cluster is covered by a small, **kidney-shaped** membrane. This is how you can tell it from other ferns. The fern reproduces with the spores.

In the past, remedies made from the rootstock were given against **tapeworms** in the gut. That is where the fern gets its German name (“Wurmfarn”, or “worm fern”). The male fern does, however, contain **poisonous substances**. That is why you must not eat it or nibble at it. Today it is no longer used as a remedy.

gewusst: The male fern gets its German name from an old remedy against tapeworms.
Young fern fronds are curled up in spring like a snail shell.

teile.einleitung: The honey fungus (in German, “Hallimasch”) is a mushroom that grows in dense clusters on wood. It can make trees ill and forms huge networks of fungal threads in the soil. Some of them are among the biggest living things on Earth.
wichtigste: The honey fungus grows in clusters on tree stumps and trees.
It is honey-yellow to brown.
Raw it is poisonous, and only when well heated does it become tolerable.
It can attack living trees and cause them to die.
A giant honey fungus was found in the Swiss National Park.
It appears mainly in autumn.

abschnitte.text: The **honey fungus** grows in dense **clusters** on tree stumps, on roots and on trees. Often dozens of mushrooms stand close together. Its caps are **honey-yellow to brown**. In English it is therefore called “honey fungus”. You find it mainly in **autumn**, often then in large numbers.

The honey fungus does not live only on dead wood. It can also **attack living trees**. In doing so its threads grow under the bark and into the roots. The trees become ill and can **die**. For foresters and gardeners, the honey fungus is therefore a feared fungus.

The real fungus is not the cap, but a network of fine threads in the soil and in the wood. This network is called the **mycelium**. In the honey fungus it can become huge. In the **Swiss National Park** in Graubünden, researchers found a honey fungus whose network is **several hundred metres** across. In the **USA**, a honey fungus even spreads through many square kilometres of forest floor. It counts as one of the **biggest living things** on Earth.

Wood in which the mycelium of the honey fungus grows can **glow faintly** in the dark. It is called **foxfire**. The light is produced by a chemical process in the fungus. In the past, people who saw the glow at night in the woods told spooky stories about it.

**Raw honey fungus is poisonous.** It becomes tolerable only through good, long heating. Even then, not everyone can tolerate it. You should collect and eat mushrooms only if you know them for certain. In Switzerland, you can have collected mushrooms checked at a **mushroom inspection**.

gewusst: The giant honey fungus in the USA is probably several thousand years old.
The faint glow of honey fungus wood can be seen only in complete darkness.

teile.einleitung: Grasshoppers are insects that can jump far with their long back legs. In summer you can hear them chirping in many meadows. In Switzerland there are around a hundred different species.
wichtigste: Grasshoppers jump with their long, strong back legs.
They chirp by rubbing parts of their body together.
Many are green or brown and well camouflaged in the grass.
The great green bush-cricket has its ears on its front legs.
Small grasshoppers are often called “Grashüpfer”.
Birds such as the stork like to eat grasshoppers.

abschnitte.text: **Grasshoppers** have long, strong **back legs**. With them they can jump much further than their own body length. Many species can also fly. Small grasshoppers that hop through the grass are often called **“Grashüpfer”** in German. Many grasshoppers are **green or brown**. This helps them blend in with grass and soil, so they are **camouflaged** from enemies.

Grasshoppers make music by **rubbing parts of their body together**. Some rub a leg against a wing, while others rub two wings together. This produces the typical **chirping**. Each species has its own song. You hear them most in **summer**, on warm days. By then the grasshoppers are adult and active.

The **great green bush-cricket** is a large, green grasshopper. It has **antennae** that are longer than its whole body. With them it feels and smells. What is astonishing is where its **ears** are: on its **front legs**. In other grasshoppers, such as the field grasshoppers, the hearing organs are on the side of the abdomen instead.

Grasshoppers are an important food for many animals. The **stork** looks for food in meadows. It eats frogs, mice, worms and also grasshoppers. Other birds, lizards and spiders eat them too. Grasshoppers themselves mostly eat plants, and some species also eat small insects.

In Switzerland, most grasshoppers live in **species-rich meadows**. If meadows are mown often or heavily fertilised, they find less habitat. In Africa and Asia there are **migratory locusts**. They can form huge swarms and strip whole fields bare.

gewusst: A swarm of desert locusts can consist of many millions of animals.
You can recognise many grasshopper species by their song, without seeing them.

teile.einleitung: The **Haber-Bosch process** is a chemical method with which **ammonia** is made from nitrogen from the air and hydrogen. From ammonia, artificial fertiliser is made. The process changed world food supply fundamentally.
wichtigste: The process makes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen.
It takes place at several hundred °C and around 100 to 300 bar.
For 2 molecules of ammonia, 3 molecules of hydrogen are needed.
In 1913, BASF put the first large plant into operation in Oppau.
About half of humankind is fed with the help of artificial fertiliser nitrogen.
Ammonia synthesis uses around 1 to 2 per cent of the world's energy.

abschnitte.text: The chemist **Fritz Haber** found out how ammonia can be made in the laboratory from nitrogen and hydrogen. **Carl Bosch** of the company **BASF** turned it into a process for large factories. In 1913 the first industrial-scale plant went into operation in **Oppau**. Both later received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

The reaction is: **N2 + 3 H2 gives 2 NH3**. So for 2 molecules of ammonia, 3 molecules of hydrogen and 1 molecule of nitrogen are needed. On the product side there are fewer gas particles than on the starting side. That is why a **high pressure** favours the formation of ammonia. The process works at **several hundred °C**, around **100 to 300 bar** and with a **catalyst** made of iron.

Plants need **nitrogen** to grow, but cannot take it directly from the air. From ammonia, **artificial fertiliser** is made. As a result, harvests rose sharply worldwide. Experts estimate that today about **half of humankind** is fed with the help of artificial fertiliser nitrogen. At the same time, the process uses a lot of energy, around **1 to 2 per cent** of world consumption.

In the **First World War**, Fritz Haber led the development and use of **poison gas** for the German army. This burdens his reputation to this day. Ammonia was also a raw material for explosives. The process shows that an invention can bring great benefit and great harm. Today, research is also being done into how the hydrogen could be obtained in a more climate-friendly way.

gewusst: Air consists of about 78 per cent nitrogen.
A large part of the nitrogen in our bodies comes from artificial fertiliser made by this process.

teile.einleitung: In autumn, many leaves turn yellow, orange, red or brown. Whole woods and vineyards then glow in colour. The autumn colours have to do with the pigments in the leaves.
wichtigste: The yellow pigments are already in the leaf in summer, and the green hides them.
In autumn the tree breaks down the green, and yellow and orange come to light.
Sunny days and cool nights make the colours especially bright.
Birches turn golden yellow, beeches copper brown.
The larch is a conifer whose needles turn golden yellow.
Maple and Virginia creeper turn bright red.

abschnitte.text: In summer the leaves are green. This is due to the green pigment **chlorophyll**, with which the plant makes food from sunlight. In the leaf there are also **yellow and orange pigments**. In summer they are **hidden** by the green. In autumn the tree breaks down the chlorophyll and takes valuable substances back into branches and trunk. Then yellow and orange come to light.

Some plants make the **red pigment** anew only in autumn. Especially much of it is made on **sunny days and cool nights**. Then the woods glow especially strongly. Famous for its red autumn foliage is the **maple**. A red maple leaf is on the **flag of Canada**. There, whole maple woods turn red in autumn.

The **birch** turns bright **golden yellow**. Its white bark and the yellow foliage are easy to recognise. The leaves of the **beech** first turn yellow and then orange to **copper brown**. A beech wood then glows warmly. On house walls climbs the **Virginia creeper**, whose leaves turn deep red and then fall.

Most conifers stay green in winter. The **larch** is an exception. In autumn its needles turn **golden yellow** and then fall off. In the **Engadine** and in many other Alpine valleys of Switzerland, whole mountain slopes then glow golden. Many people go walking in the mountains in October specially for this.

The **grapevines** also change colour after the grape harvest. In **Lavaux** on **Lake Geneva**, the steep vineyards then glow yellow and red. Lavaux is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In other wine-growing regions of Switzerland too, for example in the Valais or in Ticino, the vines are colourful in autumn.

gewusst: The yellow pigments of autumn leaves are related to the pigment of carrots.
The larch is the only native conifer in Switzerland that loses its needles in winter.

teile.einleitung: A fairy ring is a circle of mushrooms growing in a meadow or in a wood. In the past, people thought that witches or fairies had danced there. Today we know that an underground network of fungal threads is behind it.
wichtigste: A fairy ring is a circle of mushrooms.
It forms because the fungal network grows outwards in all directions.
It is especially easy to see on meadows and lawns.
The grass in the ring is often darker green or brown.
In German it is called a “Hexenring”, which means “witches’ ring”.
Some fairy rings are several hundred years old.

abschnitte.text: Sometimes mushrooms stand in a meadow in an almost perfect **circle**. This is called a **fairy ring**. It is especially noticeable on **meadows and lawns**. But there are fairy rings in woods too. They can be small or many metres across.

The actual fungus lives underground. It is made of fine threads, called the **mycelium**. The mycelium grows from one point **evenly in all directions**. In the middle it has used up the food in the soil and dies off. Only at the **outer edge** is it active. There the mushrooms grow out of the ground. In this way the circle gets a little bigger every year.

The fungus changes the **soil**. That is why the grass in the ring often looks different. Sometimes it is **darker green** than the grass next to it, because the fungus releases nutrients. In other places it turns **brown**, because the dense mycelium lets water through badly. That is why you can sometimes see a fairy ring even when no mushrooms are growing.

In the past, people could not explain the circles. In old **legends** it was said that **witches** had danced there at night. That is why in German it is called a “Hexenring”, or witches’ ring. Another name is **fairy ring**, because there were also stories about fairies dancing in a circle. Today we know that the growth of the fungus is behind it.

Because the ring grows a little every year, some fairy rings can become very **large**. They have been growing for **centuries**. Their mycelium is then **several hundred years old**. It is not only one species of fungus that forms fairy rings. One well known for it is the fairy ring champignon, a small mushroom on lawns and pastures.

gewusst: Some fairy rings are so big that you can only really see them from the air.
A fairy ring gets a little bigger every year, like a ripple on water slowly spreading out.

teile.einleitung: The moisture content of wood tells you how much water is in a piece of wood. It is very important for joiners, carpenters and everyone who builds with wood, because wood changes its shape with the water.
wichtigste: Wood moisture content is measured relative to the mass of oven-dry wood.
Very wet wood can therefore have over 100 per cent moisture content.
To measure it, samples are dried at around 103 degrees Celsius.
The fibre saturation point is at about 28 to 30 per cent.
Wood shrinks most in the tangential direction and hardly at all along the grain.
From around 20 per cent moisture content, the risk of fungal attack rises.

abschnitte.text: Wood moisture content is the **mass of water** divided by the mass of the **oven-dry** wood, times 100 per cent. An example: a sample weighs 150 g wet and 120 g oven-dry. So the water weighs 30 g, and 30 divided by 120 gives **25 per cent**. Because you divide by the dry mass, very wet wood can reach more than 100 per cent. A board with 10 kg of dry mass and 80 per cent moisture content contains 8 kg of water.

abschnitte.titel: Measuring in the oven and on site
abschnitte.text: The most accurate is the **oven-drying method**. The sample is weighed and dried in a drying oven at **103 degrees Celsius**, plus or minus 2 degrees, until its weight no longer changes. On a building site it is quicker with an **electrical resistance meter**. Two electrodes are driven into the wood. Damp wood conducts electricity better, and the device converts the resistance into moisture content.

In wood there is water in the **cell cavities** and water in the **cell walls**. At the **fibre saturation point**, about 28 to 30 per cent, the cell walls are full of water but the cavities are empty. Above it, only free water evaporates, without the wood changing shape. Below it, the wood gives off water from the cell walls and starts to **shrink**, that is, to get smaller.

Wood does not shrink equally in all directions. **Tangentially**, that is, in the direction of the annual rings, it shrinks about twice as much as **radially**. Along the **grain** it shrinks only minimally, usually less than 0.3 per cent. When wood takes up water again, it **swells**. That is why boards can warp or crack if they are used in building when too wet.

Wood adjusts its moisture to the climate of the room. This is called **equilibrium moisture content**. In heated living rooms it is usually about **8 to 10 per cent**. Wood-destroying **fungi** need a permanent moisture content of more than about **20 per cent**. Dry, well-ventilated wood is therefore well protected against rot.

gewusst: A wooden floor can get narrow gaps in winter, which close again in the damper summer.
Freshly felled wood can contain more water than wood substance.

teile.einleitung: Every crop plant descends from wild plants that were first grown somewhere in the world. The region in which a crop plant has its greatest genetic diversity is called its **centre of diversity** (in German, “Genzentrum”). Such areas are very valuable for the future of our food.
wichtigste: A centre of diversity is the region with the greatest genetic diversity of a crop plant.
The Russian researcher Nikolai Vavilov described the centres of diversity.
Arabica coffee comes from the highlands of Ethiopia.
The soya bean comes from north-eastern China, the apple from the Tian Shan.
The loss of genetic diversity in crop plants is called genetic erosion.
The Swiss foundation ProSpecieRara preserves old varieties and breeds.

abschnitte.titel: What is a centre of diversity?
abschnitte.text: The Russian plant researcher **Nikolai Vavilov** found that the diversity of a crop plant is greatest where it has been grown the longest. These regions are called **centres of diversity**. They are therefore often also regarded as the **areas of origin** of plants. There, many old landraces and wild relatives grow side by side.

**Arabica coffee** comes from the mountain forests of Ethiopia, where wild coffee plants still grow today. The **soya bean** became a crop in north-eastern China. The chickpea comes from the Near East, the potato and the sunflower from America. The cultivated apple has its most important wild ancestor, **Malus sieversii**, in the forests of the **Tian Shan mountains** in Central Asia, for example in Kazakhstan.

Modern varieties bring high yields, but they often lack important characteristics. In the centres of diversity, breeders find **wild relatives** and old varieties that are, for example, resistant to certain diseases. They can bring these characteristics into new varieties by crossing. This way centres of diversity help to breed plants for a changed climate.

When a few high-performance varieties push out the old landraces, genes are lost for ever. This process is called **genetic erosion**. That is why seeds are kept in seed banks. The **Svalbard Global Seed Vault** lies in a mountain near Longyearbyen on **Svalbard** (Norway), in the permafrost. It keeps safety copies of seed banks from all over the world.

In Switzerland, the foundation **ProSpecieRara** works for rare crop plants and breeds of farm animals. It passes seed and animals on to nurseries, farms and hobby gardeners. This way old varieties are not only stored, but continue to be grown and used. Anyone who plants an old variety of tomato or bean in their own garden helps too.

gewusst: The ancestor of our apples still grows wild today in the forests of Kazakhstan.
Wild coffee still grows today in the mountain forests of Ethiopia.

teile.einleitung: The **common ash** is a large, light-coloured broadleaf tree. You recognise it easily by its black buds and pinnate leaves. Unfortunately it is now seriously threatened by a fungal disease.
wichtigste: The ash has conspicuous black buds.
Its leaves are pinnate and consist of many leaflets.
It likes to grow beside streams and on damp soil.
It gets its leaves late, often only in May.
Ash wood is tough and suitable for tool handles.
Ash dieback threatens many ash trees in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The ash can grow up to about **40 metres** tall. In winter you recognise it by its conspicuous **black buds**. Its leaves are **pinnate**. They consist of several leaflets on a shared stalk. The ash opens its leaves **late**, often only in **May**, when other broadleaf trees are already green.

The fruits of the ash have an elongated **wing**. They often hang in **bunches** on the tree, sometimes all winter long. When they fall, they spin and glide a little way. This way the wind carries them away from the tree. Where they land, new ash trees can sprout.

The ash likes **damp, nutrient-rich soils**. You often find it along **streams** and rivers and in floodplain woods. But it also grows in drier places. In Switzerland it is one of the most common broadleaf trees. It grows mainly on the Plateau and in the Pre-Alps.

**Ash wood** is hard and elastic. It bends without breaking. That is why **handles** for hammers, axes and shovels are made from it. In the past, skis, sledges and gymnastic equipment were also made from ash wood. To this day it is used for furniture and parquet flooring.

For some years now, many ash trees have suffered from **ash dieback**. This disease is caused by a **fungus** that was brought in from East Asia. It attacks leaves and shoots, and the crown becomes thinner and thinner. Many ash trees fall ill and die. Some trees are, however, resistant. Researchers hope to use them to raise healthy ash trees.

gewusst: In the old Norse sagas, the world tree Yggdrasil is a giant ash.
The fruits of the ash spin like little propellers as they fall.

teile.einleitung: Almost every child knows the **stinging nettle** (in German, “Grosse Brennnessel”), because anyone who touches it feels a burning. Even so, it is a very useful plant, for butterflies and for people too.
wichtigste: The nettle has stinging hairs on its leaves and stem.
After touching it, small, itchy weals appear.
The burning goes away again after a while.
Caterpillars of butterflies such as the peacock butterfly eat nettles.
You can make tea from the leaves.
The dead-nettle looks similar, but does not sting.

abschnitte.text: Leaves and stem carry many fine **stinging hairs**. Each hair is like a tiny syringe with a tip that breaks off easily. If you touch it, the tip penetrates the skin and gives off irritating substances. Small, itchy **weals** appear on the skin. This is unpleasant, but mostly harmless and passes after a while. **Cool water** eases the burning.

For many **butterflies**, the nettle is vital. The caterpillars of the **peacock butterfly**, the small tortoiseshell and the red admiral eat mainly its leaves. A clump of nettles in the garden therefore helps butterflies. The stinging hairs even protect the caterpillars from some animals that want to eat them.

The nettle often grows at **wayside edges**, along **fences**, in gardens and at the edge of the woods. It likes soils with a lot of nitrogen, for example near stables or compost heaps. It grows to over a metre in height and often forms dense stands. Anyone who plays there is best protected by **long trousers**.

From young leaves you can brew **tea**, and they can also be prepared like spinach. When cooked or dried, the stinging hairs lose their effect. In the past, cloth was even made from the fibres of the stems. The **dead-nettle** looks similar, but does not sting. It is not even closely related, and has pretty white or purple flowers.

gewusst: The stinging hairs contain tiny amounts of silica, which is why their tips are as hard as glass.
Gardeners make a liquid manure from nettles, which serves as fertiliser.

teile.einleitung: The Great Red Spot is a giant storm, centuries old, on the planet Jupiter. It is so big that the Earth would fit inside it. With a telescope you can see it as a reddish spot in Jupiter's cloud cover.
wichtigste: The Great Red Spot is a giant storm on Jupiter.
The storm has been observed for almost 200 years.
It is bigger than the whole Earth.
The winds at its edge reach several hundred kilometres per hour.
The spot has become smaller in recent decades.
Space probes such as Juno have studied it from close up.

abschnitte.text: The Great Red Spot is a **cyclone** that is constantly turning anticlockwise. It lies in the southern hemisphere of Jupiter. One full turn takes about six days. Experts call such a vortex a **high-pressure area** or anticyclone.

In the 19th century the spot was more than twice as wide as the Earth. Today it is only a little wider than the Earth, but still huge. It is becoming rounder and smaller with time. Why it is shrinking is not yet entirely clear.

As early as the 17th century, astronomers described a spot on Jupiter, and perhaps it was this storm already. The present Great Red Spot has been reliably observed since about 1830. This makes it the biggest and oldest known storm in the **Solar System**. On Earth, even a strong hurricane lasts only a few weeks.

The exact cause of the red colour is not yet known for sure. Researchers suspect that sunlight changes chemical substances in the upper clouds and colours them reddish. The colour can vary from strong red-orange to pale salmon pink. The storm reaches higher into the **atmosphere** than the clouds around it.

The space probes **Voyager 1** and Voyager 2 photographed the spot from close up in 1979. Since 2016 the probe Juno has been orbiting Jupiter, and in 2017 it measured the storm precisely. It found out that the storm reaches several hundred kilometres deep into the atmosphere. The Hubble Space Telescope also observes the spot regularly.

begriffe.erklaerung: A storm in which the air turns in a circle.
A vortex around an area of high air pressure.
An unmanned spacecraft that explores planets.
The layer of gas around a planet.

gewusst: Jupiter has other storms too, one of them a smaller reddish vortex nicknamed Red Junior.
Because Jupiter has no solid surface, the storm is not slowed by mountains or land, which could explain why it lasts so long.

teile.einleitung: With its red cap and white spots, the fly agaric is one of the best-known mushrooms. As pretty as it looks, it is poisonous and must not be eaten.
wichtigste: The fly agaric is poisonous and must not be eaten.
It has a red cap with white spots.
The gills and the stem are white.
It often grows under birches and spruces.
After heavy rain, the white spots can be washed off.
Its German name “Fliegenpilz” (fly mushroom) comes from the fact that people used it to catch flies in the past.

abschnitte.text: The **fly agaric** has a bright **red cap** with **white spots**. The spots are remains of a covering that surrounded the young mushroom. After **heavy rain** they can be **washed off**, and then the cap is completely red. Under the cap there are white **gills**, which are thin little blades. The **stem** is also **white** and has a ring like a little skirt.

The fly agaric often grows **under birches and spruces**. It lives closely together with the roots of these trees. The underground network of fungal threads helps the tree to take up water and minerals. In return, the fungus gets sugar from the tree. You find it mainly in late summer and autumn.

The fly agaric is **poisonous**. Anyone who eats it can get tummy ache, vomiting, confusion and strong drowsiness. That is why you must **not eat it**. In Switzerland, anyone who collects mushrooms has them checked at a **mushroom inspection point**. If you suspect poisoning, call the emergency number 145 of Tox Info Suisse at once.

In the past, people put pieces of the mushroom in a bowl of milk or sugar water. The **flies** drank from it and were stunned. This is how people used the mushroom to **catch flies**. That is where the fly agaric gets its name. Today it is mainly known as a good luck symbol.

gewusst: In many countries the fly agaric is regarded as a good luck symbol, for example on New Year cards.
The cap of a large fly agaric can grow over 15 centimetres wide.

teile.einleitung: The hart’s-tongue is a special fern. Unlike most ferns, it has no feathery fronds but long, smooth leaves. It likes to grow in shady, damp places on limestone.
wichtigste: The leaves of the hart’s-tongue are undivided and tongue-shaped.
It is named after the tongue of the hart, a male deer.
It grows in damp, shady gorges, on rocks and on old walls.
It likes limy soil, for example in the Jura.
Its leaves stay green in winter too.
The clusters of spores look like slanting brown stripes.

abschnitte.text: Most ferns have **feathery fronds** made up of many small leaflets. The **hart’s-tongue** is different. Its leaves are **undivided** and shaped like a **tongue**. They are smooth and **glossy green**. They usually grow **10 to 60 centimetres** long, and rarely even a metre.

The long leaves are reminiscent of the **tongue of a hart**, a male deer. That is how the fern got its name. The leaves grow out of the ground in a tuft. They often droop a little. Because they are glossy, you can see them well even in a dark wood.

The hart’s-tongue needs **shade** and **moisture**. It can be found in **ravine woods**, on damp rocks and on old walls. It especially likes to grow on **limestone**. That is why in Switzerland it can be found in the **Jura**, for example. The hart’s-tongue is **wintergreen**: its leaves stay green in winter too.

Ferns do not produce flowers or seeds. They reproduce with tiny **spores**. On the hart’s-tongue, long, **rust-brown stripes** sit on the **underside** of the leaves. They lie slanting side by side like dashes. The spores are formed inside them. When they are ripe, the wind carries them away.

gewusst: The hart’s-tongue is one of the few native ferns with completely undivided leaves.
Because it looks so special, the hart’s-tongue is also often planted in shady gardens.

teile.einleitung: During the ice ages, a large part of Europe was covered with ice. Plants and animals had to move to warmer areas. Such a retreat area is called a **glacial refugium**. From there, many species returned after the ice age.
wichtigste: A glacial refugium is a retreat area during the ice age.
Many broadleaf trees survived on the Iberian Peninsula, in Italy and in the Balkans.
The last glaciation of the Alps reached its peak about 20,000 years ago.
The last cold period in the Alpine region is called the Würm glaciation.
Nunataks are ice-free peaks that stuck out of the ice.
Refugia can be recognised today by high genetic diversity.

abschnitte.text: The last cold period in the Alpine region is called, in the classical division, the **Würm glaciation**. The cold periods are named after rivers in the Alpine foreland. About **20,000 years ago** the glaciation reached its peak. The glaciers then reached far out onto the **Plateau**. After that they melted back quickly.

Many broadleaf trees of Central Europe could not survive in the cold north. They survived on the southern European peninsulas: on the **Iberian Peninsula**, in **Italy** and in the **Balkans**. There the climate was mild enough for forests. After the ice age, **beech**, **oak** and other trees returned from there and settled the areas that had become free.

In the Alps, too, there were places of retreat. **Nunataks** are ice-free peaks that stuck out of the ice like islands of rock. Some alpine plants may have survived the ice age there. At the edge of the Alps, areas also stayed ice-free, for example in the **Southern Alps** such as the Bergamasque Alps. There, species survived that later did not spread far. That is why these areas are rich in **endemic plants**, which occur only there.

How do researchers know this? In bogs and lakes, **pollen** is preserved layer by layer. From it you can tell when which tree species returned to an area. The **genetic material** also helps: in refugia, populations lived for a very long time and accumulated many genetic variants. Former refugia can therefore be recognised by a **high genetic diversity**.

gewusst: About 20,000 years ago the Alpine glaciers reached far onto the Plateau.
Tiny grains of pollen in bogs reveal when the trees came back after the ice age.

teile.einleitung: The bogbean (in German, “Fieberklee”, or “fever clover”) is a plant of bogs and shallow waters. Its leaves are reminiscent of clover, but it is not related to meadow clover.
wichtigste: The leaves of the bogbean have three parts, like clover.
It belongs to a different family from meadow clover.
Its white flowers are fringed on the inside.
It grows in shallow water and in wet bogs.
The leaves taste very bitter.
Today it is mainly used to stimulate digestion.

abschnitte.titel: A clover that is not a clover
abschnitte.text: The **bogbean** has **three-part leaves** like clover. That is where the second part of its German name comes from. Even so, it is **not** related to meadow clover. Meadow clover belongs to the pea family. The bogbean forms a family of its own, the **bogbean family**.

In Switzerland the bogbean mostly blooms in **May and June**. The flowers sit in a cluster on an upright stem. They are **white**, often tinged with pink on the outside. The special feature is the **fringes** on the inside of the petals. This makes the flowers look as if they were covered with fine little hairs.

The bogbean likes to grow **in shallow water** and in **wet bog**. You find it on the banks of ponds, in ditches and in fens. Its stems creep through the mud and form dense stands. Because many bogs have disappeared, it has become rarer.

The leaves of the bogbean taste **very bitter**. In the past the plant was used against **fever**, which is where its German name comes from. In today's **herbal medicine**, the leaves are mainly used to **stimulate digestion**, for example when someone has no appetite. The bitter substances stimulate the stomach. Medicinal plants should only be used on the advice of experts, though.

gewusst: In the past the bogbean was used instead of hops for brewing beer, because of its bitterness.
Another German name for the bogbean is “Bitterklee” (bitter clover).

teile.einleitung: When a glacier melts and gets shorter, bare land of debris and rock is left in front of it. This area is called the **glacier foreland**. Here you can watch how plants and animals conquer new land.
wichtigste: A glacier foreland is the area that a retreating glacier releases.
Since about 1850, the Alpine glaciers have retreated markedly.
Glaciers leave behind ridges of debris, the moraines.
The colonisation of bare rock is called primary succession.
The fresh soil almost completely lacks humus.
Glacier streams are milky and cloudy because of rock flour.

abschnitte.titel: New land in front of the ice
abschnitte.text: Around **1850** the so-called **Little Ice Age** ended. At that time the Alpine glaciers were very large. Since then they have shrunk greatly and released large **forelands**. A glacier carries stones and sand. At its edge and at its front, it deposits the debris as **moraines**. These ridges still show today how far the ice once reached.

In a glacier foreland there is at first no real soil. **Humus**, which only forms when dead plants and animals are broken down, is almost completely lacking. Living things have to begin on bare rock. This development from raw soil to plant communities is called **primary succession**. First come pioneer plants, lichens and mosses, later grasses, shrubs and trees.

What lies far from the ice became free long ago. There, plants had plenty of time to form soil and spread. That is why you find the most and the largest plants **far away from the edge of the glacier**. For researchers this is exciting: areas that have been ice-free for different lengths of time lie next to each other. This way they can watch how **life conquers new land**, over many decades.
The water of glacier streams is often **milky and cloudy**. The glacier grinds rock into fine **rock flour**. This colours the meltwater. It is therefore called **glacier milk**.

At the **Morteratsch Glacier** in the Upper Engadine in Graubünden, there is a glacier trail. Signs along the path show where the glacier snout ended in earlier years. When walking, you can see directly in the landscape how far the glacier has retreated.

gewusst: The further away from the glacier, the older the land is and the more grows on it.
At the Morteratsch Glacier, signs show where the ice used to end.

teile.einleitung: Hardwood forests (in German, “Hartlaubwälder”, or “hard-leaf forests”) grow in regions with hot, dry summers and mild, rainy winters. The best-known example is the forest around the Mediterranean. Typical are trees with hard, leathery, evergreen leaves.
wichtigste: Hard, leathery leaves protect against water loss in the dry summer.
Most of the rain falls in winter.
The holm oak is a typical tree of the Mediterranean hardwood forest.
The olive tree is the typical crop plant of these regions.
After clearing, maquis and garrigue develop.
In the Köppen climate system, this climate is called Cs.

abschnitte.text: Hardwood regions have a **Mediterranean climate**. In summer they lie under a lasting high-pressure area. That is why it is hot and hardly rains. In **winter**, low-pressure areas bring most of the **rain**. In the **Köppen** climate classification, this climate is called **Cs**: C stands for warm temperate, s for dry summer.

The plants in the hardwood forest have **hard, leathery leaves**. A thick layer of wax, the **cuticle**, and firm tissue reduce evaporation. This way the leaves lose little water in the dry summer. Most hardwood plants are **evergreen** and keep their leaves all year.

A typical tree is the **holm oak**. It has small, leathery, evergreen leaves. In the past it formed large forests around the Mediterranean. The most important crop plant is the **olive tree**. It too is a hardwood plant and tolerates dry summers well. Where olive trees can be grown, there is roughly a Mediterranean climate.

Through clearing, fires and grazing, the hardwood forest was pushed back in many places. In its place grew the **maquis**, a dense, tall scrub. Where the soil was damaged even more, the **garrigue** arose. This is a low, patchy shrub heath with fragrant herbs such as **thyme** and **rosemary**.

Hardwood regions exist not only by the Mediterranean. A similar climate is found in **California**, in parts of **Chile**, in the south-west of **Australia** and in the **Cape region of South Africa**. There grows the **fynbos**, a shrub vegetation with an incredible number of plant species. It counts as one of the most species-rich plant regions in the world.

gewusst: Many kitchen herbs such as thyme, rosemary and lavender come from the hardwood regions by the Mediterranean.
The Cape region with the fynbos counts as a floral kingdom of its own, the smallest in the world.

teile.einleitung: A timber high-rise is a very tall building whose structure is made largely of wood. New fire safety rules and modern timber construction technology have made such buildings possible in Switzerland too.
wichtigste: In Switzerland, a building with a total height of more than 30 metres counts as a high-rise.
Since the VKF fire safety regulations of 2015, wood has also been allowed in high-rises.
Thick timber beams form a protective layer of char in a fire.
Many timber high-rises have a core made of reinforced concrete.
In 2019, the Mjøstårnet in Norway was the tallest timber building in the world.
In Zug, the timber high-rise “Pi”, about 80 metres tall, is being built.

abschnitte.text: The Swiss fire safety regulations come from the **Association of Cantonal Fire Insurers**, or **VKF** for short. They classify buildings with a total height of more than **30 metres** as high-rises. Particularly strict rules apply to high-rises. With the **2015 fire safety regulations**, wood was permitted in all building categories if the requirements are met. This gave a boost to timber high-rises in Switzerland.

A thick timber beam burns from the outside inwards, and quite evenly. This produces a **layer of charcoal** that insulates the core. The inner part stays cool and keeps carrying the load. An example: if a beam burns away about 0.7 mm per minute on each side, after 60 minutes that is around **42 mm**. Experts allow for this **char depth** when designing.

Many timber high-rises have a **core made of reinforced concrete**. The stairwell and the lift shaft are inside it. The core makes the building stiff against **wind** and **earthquakes**. At the same time, it is a safe **escape route**. Because wood and concrete are combined, this is called **hybrid construction**.

The **Mjøstårnet** in Brumunddal on Lake Mjøsa in **Norway** is 85.4 metres tall. When it opened in 2019, it was the tallest timber building in the world. In Switzerland, the project **“Pi”** with 27 storeys and about 80 metres in height is being built in **Zug**. In **Winterthur**, another timber high-rise, “Rocket”, is planned.

As trees grow, they take up **CO2**. The carbon stays stored in the built-in wood for as long as the building stands. The production of **cement** for concrete, by contrast, causes large CO2 emissions. That is why timber buildings are regarded as better for the climate. Wooden parts can also be prefabricated in a factory and quickly assembled on site.

gewusst: A thick timber beam can stay load-bearing in a fire for longer than an unprotected steel girder, which goes soft in the heat.
The Swiss fire safety regulations apply in all cantons.

teile.einleitung: **Glucose** is one of the most important substances of life. In everyday speech it is called **grape sugar** (in German, “Traubenzucker”). Plants make it during photosynthesis, and for almost all living things it is an important source of energy.
wichtigste: Glucose is called grape sugar in everyday speech.
As a simple sugar, it is one of the carbohydrates.
Plants make glucose during photosynthesis.
Cellulose consists of long chains of glucose building blocks.
Household sugar consists of glucose and fructose.
The hormone insulin lowers the glucose level in the blood in humans.

abschnitte.text: Glucose was first obtained from **grapes**. That is where the German name **Traubenzucker** (“grape sugar”) comes from. Glucose is a **simple sugar**. Sugars and the substances built from them belong to the group of substances called **carbohydrates**. Grape sugar tastes sweet and gets into the blood especially quickly.

Plants make glucose during **photosynthesis**. In doing so they use sunlight, water and carbon dioxide from the air. For the plant, glucose serves as an **energy source** for its life processes. It is also a **building material**: the plant builds other substances from it, for example starch, cellulose, fats and proteins.

**Cellulose** consists of long chains of glucose building blocks. It makes the cell walls of plants stable and is the main component of **wood** and **paper**. **Starch** is also built from glucose. Ordinary household sugar is called **sucrose**. It consists of one building block each of **glucose** and **fructose** and is obtained from sugar beet or sugar cane. In Switzerland, mainly sugar beet is processed.

In the laboratory, glucose can be detected with the **Fehling test**. A blue solution is heated together with glucose. If glucose is present, a **brick-red precipitate** forms. This way you can see the sugar, even though it is dissolved invisibly in the water.

Humans also need glucose as energy. It is carried to all cells with the blood. The body keeps the amount in the blood, the **blood sugar level**, as steady as possible. The hormone **insulin** helps with this. It is made in the **pancreas** and makes sure that the body's cells take up glucose from the blood. This way the glucose level falls again.

gewusst: Wood and paper consist largely of glucose building blocks strung together.
In the Fehling test, glucose turns a blue solution brick-red.

teile.einleitung: The Release Ordinance (in German, the Freisetzungsverordnung) is a Swiss legal text that regulates how organisms must be handled in the environment. It is meant to protect people, animals and nature from dangers, for example from invasive plants.
wichtigste: The abbreviation of the Release Ordinance is FrSV.
It regulates the handling of organisms in the environment.
The Federal Council issued the ordinance that applies today in 2008.
It is based mainly on the Environmental Protection Act.
For plants in Annex 2.1, only controlling them is allowed.
The cantons are mainly responsible for enforcing the bans.

abschnitte.text: The **Release Ordinance**, **FrSV** for short, is an ordinance of the Confederation. The **Federal Council** issued the version that applies today in **2008**. It is based mainly on the **Environmental Protection Act**. An ordinance lays down exactly how a law is put into practice. The FrSV regulates the **handling of organisms in the environment**, that is, plants, animals, fungi and microorganisms.

An important part of the FrSV concerns **invasive alien plants**. These are plants from other parts of the world that spread strongly here and push out native species. They are often called **neophytes**. For plants listed in **Annex 2.1**, handling is forbidden. **Only controlling them** is allowed. So you may neither plant them nor sell them or give them away.

With a revision, the rules were tightened. Since September 2024, further invasive plants may no longer be sold. These include, for example, the **cherry laurel** and the **butterfly bush**. The **Chinese windmill palm** may also no longer be sold, because it has gone wild in the woods of **southern Switzerland**. Now **customs** also checks imported plants.

The Confederation makes the rules, but the **cantons** are mainly responsible for **enforcing** the bans. They check garden centres, for example, and organise the control of the plants. Many municipalities help and inform the public. Private individuals can also help, by removing invasive plants in their own garden and disposing of them properly.

gewusst: Remains of invasive plants do not belong on the compost heap, but mostly in the household waste, so that they do not spread further.
The FrSV also regulates the handling of genetically modified organisms in the environment.

teile.einleitung: Grasses are plants with narrow, long leaves and round stalks. They include not only the grasses of the meadow, but also important food plants such as wheat, rice and maize. Even the giant bamboo is a grass.
wichtigste: Grasses have long, narrow leaves and hollow stalks with nodes.
Wheat, rice, maize, barley and oats are grasses.
Bamboo is a very tall grass plant.
Popcorn is made from the kernels of maize.
Dried grass is called hay and serves as animal feed in winter.
Grasses are pollinated by the wind.
Their pollen causes hay fever in many people.

abschnitte.text: The **true grass** family includes around 12,000 species worldwide. Typical is the round, mostly hollow **stalk**, which is strengthened by nodes. The leaves are long and narrow and have parallel veins. The flowers are inconspicuous and sit in ears or panicles.

Grasses grow on all continents, even in Antarctica. They form huge grasslands such as the steppes of Asia, the prairies of North America and the savannas of Africa. In Switzerland they shape meadows, pastures and alpine pastures. Many grasses grow back quickly after being grazed or mown, because their growth zone lies at the bottom of the plant.

The most important food plants of humankind are grasses that we call **cereals**. They include wheat, rice, maize, barley, rye and oats. From their grains, people make flour, bread, pasta, flakes and polenta. From the kernels of maize you can also make popcorn. They burst open when heated, because the water inside turns to steam.

Cows, sheep, goats and horses eat mainly grass. In Switzerland, meadows and pastures are therefore the basis for milk and cheese. Dried grass is called **hay** and is stored in barns for the winter. Grass that ferments in airtight bales is called silage.

**Bamboo** is a grass that in some species grows over 20 metres tall. Some species of bamboo are among the fastest-growing plants in the world and add almost a metre in a single day. In Asia, scaffolding, furniture and houses are built from bamboo. Sugar cane, from which sugar is obtained, is also a grass.

begriffe.erklaerung: The round, mostly hollow stem of a grass.
Grasses whose grains people use as food.
Dried grass as winter feed for animals.
An allergy to pollen, for example from grasses.

gewusst: Rice, wheat and maize together supply about half of all the calories that people eat worldwide.
Some species of bamboo flower only every few decades, but then often all the plants of a species at the same time.

teile.einleitung: **Lords-and-ladies** (also called cuckoo pint, in German “Gefleckter Aronstab”) is a special woodland plant. Its flower is a clever insect trap, and in summer it bears bright red berries. But be careful: the whole plant is poisonous.
wichtigste: Lords-and-ladies grows in damp, shady deciduous woods.
Its leaves are arrow-shaped and often spotted dark.
The flower sits in a large, cone-shaped bract.
The flower holds small midges prisoner for a short time.
The ripe berries are bright red and sit densely on a spike.
The plant is poisonous and burns in the mouth.

abschnitte.text: Lords-and-ladies grows in **damp, shady deciduous woods**. In spring its large leaves appear. They have the shape of an **arrowhead** and often carry **dark spots**. That is where the German name “Gefleckter” (spotted) comes from. The plant spends the winter as a tuber in the ground.

The flower is unusual. A large, greenish **bract** surrounds it like a **cone**. Inside stands a brown or purple **spadix**. At the very bottom of the bract lies a small chamber with the actual flowers. The spadix can warm up and gives off a smell that attracts small midges.

The midges land on the smooth bract and **slide** into the chamber. Above the chamber sit **little hairs** that block the exit. This way the insects stay trapped until the next morning. While there, they pollinate the flowers and are covered with new pollen. Then the little hairs wither, and the midges may leave again. This kind is called a **pitfall-trap flower**.

After flowering, the bract withers. In summer, many **berries** stay standing close together on an upright **spike**. It looks like a small corn cob. At first the berries are green, and when ripe they become **bright red**. They look tempting, but are **poisonous**. Red berries on a spike in the woods are therefore left alone.

Young lords-and-ladies leaves often grow among **wild garlic**. Both like damp deciduous woods. Anyone who collects wild garlic must check every leaf carefully. Wild garlic smells clearly of garlic when rubbed, while lords-and-ladies does not. If you bite into a piece of lords-and-ladies, it **burns** badly in your mouth and throat. This comes from **sharp substances** in the plant.

gewusst: The flower spike of lords-and-ladies can warm up well above the surrounding temperature.
The trapped midges are not eaten, but released again after a night.

teile.einleitung: Hans Carl von Carlowitz was a Saxon official who lived over 300 years ago. He is regarded as one of the fathers of the term “sustainability”. In his book on forestry, he warned of a shortage of wood.
wichtigste: Carlowitz was born in 1645 and died in 1714.
He was chief mining commissioner in Freiberg in present-day Saxony.
In 1713 his book “Sylvicultura oeconomica” appeared in Leipzig.
He warned of a timber shortage.
He called for a “sustained” use of the forest.
His principle: fell only as much wood as grows back.

abschnitte.text: **Hans Carl von Carlowitz** lived from 1645 to 1714, that is, in the time of the **Baroque**. He was **chief mining commissioner** and headed the mining administration in **Freiberg**. The town lies in the Ore Mountains in what is now the German state of **Saxony**. His duties included the mines and the smelting works, in which ore was processed into metal.

abschnitte.titel: The fear of a timber shortage
abschnitte.text: Mines and smelting works needed huge amounts of **wood** at that time. Wood was used for building, for supports in the tunnels and above all as fuel. The towns also used a great deal of it. Many forests had already been heavily cut down. Carlowitz feared a **timber shortage**: soon there would not be enough wood any more.

In **1713**, his book **“Sylvicultura oeconomica”** appeared in Leipzig. It is regarded as one of the first books on forestry. In it, Carlowitz called for a “continuous, steady and **sustained** use” of the forest. From this word, the term **sustainability** later developed.

Carlowitz demanded a balance: you should **fell only as much wood as grows back**. Areas that had been cut down should be **sown and planted** with trees again. He also recommended using wood more sparingly with **better stoves**. These thoughts are still the core of the principle of sustainability today.

Today people speak of sustainability not only in connection with forests, but also with energy, food or the economy. What is always meant is that we live in such a way that later generations still have enough. In Switzerland, the Forest Act requires that the forest be used in such a way that it is preserved.

gewusst: The word “sustainability”, which appears everywhere today, goes back to a book on forestry from 1713.
Carlowitz died only a year after his famous book appeared.

teile.einleitung: Hardly any flowering plant grows as high as the **glacier crowfoot**. You find it in the rubble near glaciers, sometimes at over 4000 metres. Its flowers change colour over time from white to red.
wichtigste: Fresh flowers of the glacier crowfoot are white.
Older flowers turn pink to dark red.
On the Finsteraarhorn it was found at about 4275 metres.
It grows in rubble and on moraines near glaciers.
Like all buttercups, it is poisonous.
It is related to the yellow meadow buttercup.

abschnitte.text: The glacier crowfoot blooms **white** at first. With time the flowers turn **pink** and in the end **dark red**. That is why you often see flowers of different colours side by side in one spot. It is closely related to the **meadow buttercup**, the yellow “butter flower” of our meadows. Both belong to the same genus.

On the **Finsteraarhorn**, the glacier crowfoot was found at about **4275 metres**. So it grows higher than almost all other flowering plants. It thrives on damp **rubble** and bare rock, mostly on rock low in lime. It often stands on **moraines**. These are ridges of stones and debris that a glacier pushes ahead of it and leaves lying.

Sometimes the glacier crowfoot grows very close to the ice, even under **overhanging ice**. There it is protected from the wind. The ice acts like a small **greenhouse**. This way the plant can use the short summer at great height.

All species of buttercup are **poisonous**, the glacier crowfoot too. That is why you must not eat it. It is best simply to admire it and leave it standing. This way it can go on flowering in its barren place.

gewusst: On the Finsteraarhorn, the glacier crowfoot blooms at about 4275 metres.
In one spot, white, pink and red flowers of the same plant can stand side by side.

teile.einleitung: Wood anatomy studies how wood is built on the inside. Under the microscope, it turns out that wood is made of many different cells that carry water, support the tree and store substances.
wichtigste: The cambium forms wood (xylem) inwards and inner bark (phloem) outwards.
Softwood consists of around 90 per cent tracheids.
Hardwood has vessels, which show up as pores in cross-section.
Wood rays run through the trunk from the inside to the outside.
The cell wall is made of cellulose, hemicelluloses and lignin.
Pits connect neighbouring cells.

abschnitte.text: Between the wood and the bark lies a thin ring of cells that can divide, the **cambium**. It is a growth tissue. Inwards it forms new wood, the **xylem**. Outwards it forms **inner bark**, the **phloem**, in which sugary sap is carried. This is how the trunk gets thicker every year.

Softwood consists of around **90 per cent** **tracheids**. These are long, narrow cells that carry water and at the same time give strength. Neighbouring cells are connected by **pits**, thin spots in the cell wall. In softwood these are mostly **bordered pits** with a movable closing plate. Spruce, larch, pine and Douglas fir have **resin canals**, but the silver fir normally does not.

Hardwood also has **vessels**, also called **tracheae**. These are wide tubes that show up as **pores** in cross-section. In **ring-porous** woods such as oak and ash, the large vessels lie in a ring in the earlywood. Beech, maple and birch are **diffuse-porous**. Sometimes **tyloses** grow out of neighbouring cells into the vessels and block them. That is why the wood of white oak is dense enough for barrels.

To examine wood, it is cut in three directions. The **cross-section** or **end-grain cut** lies at right angles to the axis of the trunk and shows the annual rings as circles. The **radial cut** and the **tangential cut** run lengthways. In the cross-section you can also see the **wood rays**, formerly called medullary rays. They consist mainly of parenchyma cells and carry and store substances across the axis of the trunk.

abschnitte.titel: What the cell wall is made of
abschnitte.text: The cell walls of wood are made of three main substances. Around 40 to 50 per cent is **cellulose**, long fibres of sugar. In addition there are **hemicelluloses** and **lignin**. Lignin makes the wall woody and able to resist pressure. Together these substances form a natural **fibre composite**, similar to reinforced concrete made of steel and concrete.

gewusst: Because the silver fir has no resin canals, its wood is resin-free and is valued for saunas, for example.
From the arrangement of the pores in the cross-section, experts can identify many kinds of wood.

teile.einleitung: The **death cap** (in German, “Grüner Knollenblätterpilz”) is one of the most poisonous mushrooms in Europe. Even a single mushroom can be deadly for a person. Anyone who collects mushrooms must know it.
wichtigste: The death cap can be deadly.
Its poison destroys mainly the liver.
Cooking does not make the poison harmless.
It has a greenish cap, white gills and a bulb at the base of the stalk.
Poisoning is often noticed only after many hours.
In an emergency you can reach Tox Info Suisse on the number 145.

abschnitte.text: The cap is **greenish**, sometimes yellowish or olive-green. Under the cap sit **white gills**, the thin little plates. A pale ring hangs on the stalk. At the very bottom, the stalk sits in a **bulb** with a membranous sheath. This bulb is often hidden in the ground. The mushroom grows in summer and autumn in deciduous woods, especially under oaks and beeches.

The mushroom contains **amatoxins**. These poisons destroy mainly the **liver**. **Cooking**, frying or drying does **not** make them harmless. The treacherous thing is that you often get stomach pains, vomiting and diarrhoea only **after many hours**. After that, some people seem to feel better, while the liver goes on being damaged. Without quick treatment in hospital, the poisoning can end fatally.

abschnitte.titel: What to do in an emergency
abschnitte.text: If you suspect mushroom poisoning, you call **Tox Info Suisse** at once on the number **145**, or in case of severe symptoms the ambulance on 144. You do not wait until it gets worse. You take **leftovers of the mushrooms eaten** with you to the **hospital**, including trimmings. This way experts can tell which mushroom was eaten.

In Switzerland, anyone who collects mushrooms has them checked by an **official mushroom inspection**. Many communes offer this service free of charge. Young death caps can be mistaken for edible mushrooms such as button mushrooms. Children should never collect or taste mushrooms without adults. The rule is: only eat what has been identified with complete certainty.

gewusst: A large share of fatal mushroom poisonings in Europe goes back to death caps.
Unlike the death cap, button mushrooms have pink to brown gills.

teile.einleitung: Red flowers on balconies and at windows are simply part of many Swiss villages. Usually they are **geraniums**. Strictly speaking, these balcony flowers are called **pelargoniums**, but in everyday speech almost everyone says geranium.
wichtigste: The popular balcony flower is actually called a pelargonium.
Most balcony geraniums come from southern Africa.
Geraniums love sun and cannot tolerate frost.
Too much standing water makes their roots rot.
In Switzerland you see red geraniums especially often.
Their wild relatives, the cranesbills, grow in our meadows.

abschnitte.text: What we call a **geranium** in the balcony box is actually a **pelargonium**. The two names are often mixed up, because the plants are closely related. They belong to the same plant family, the **cranesbill family**. Their fruits look like a long bird's beak, which is where this name comes from.

Most balcony geraniums originally come from the **south of Africa**. It is warm and sunny there. That is why geraniums here also like a **sunny spot**. In the sun they bloom most beautifully. Their wild relatives, the **cranesbills**, on the other hand, also grow in Switzerland, in meadows and at the edge of woods.

Geraniums need **water** regularly. But if the water stays standing in the pot, their roots rot. A pot with a hole in the bottom is therefore good. Geraniums cannot tolerate **frost** at all, and they die of the cold. That is why you bring them into the house in autumn and put them in a bright, cool place. In spring, when there is no more danger of frost, they go back outside.

Geraniums come in **red**, pink, white and purple. In Switzerland you see **red geraniums** especially often on farmhouses and chalets. A special group is the **scented geraniums**. When you rub their leaves, they smell of lemon or rose, for example.

gewusst: Scented geraniums smell of lemon or rose when you rub their leaves.
The name cranesbill comes from the long, beak-shaped fruits.

teile.einleitung: Plants need water to live and grow. If it does not rain enough or the plant stands in a pot, we have to **water** it. It matters when, how and how much you water.
wichtigste: You water with a watering can directly onto the soil near the roots.
In summer it is best to water early in the morning.
In the midday heat, a lot of water evaporates.
If the soil is dry, the plant needs water.
Too much water makes the roots rot.
In winter, houseplants usually need less water.

abschnitte.text: For watering you usually need a **watering can**. With it you bring the water exactly where the plant needs it. At the front you can fit a **rose**. This is an attachment with many small holes. It spreads the water in fine streams, so delicate plants are not washed away.

In summer it is best to water the garden **early in the morning**. Then it is still cool, and the water can seep into the soil. In the **midday heat**, on the other hand, a lot of water **evaporates** before it reaches the roots. You do not water the leaves, but **the soil** near the roots. This is because the plant takes up water with its roots.

Whether a potted plant needs water, you notice with the **finger test**: stick a finger into the soil. If it feels **dry**, it is time to water. Too much water also does harm, though. If the soil stands in water all the time, the roots get no air and can **rot**. In **winter**, most houseplants grow more slowly and need water less often.

**Rainwater** is good for watering. You can collect it in a barrel, and it costs nothing. Rainwater is **soft**, so it contains little lime, and is good for many plants. This also saves drinking water.

gewusst: With the finger test you quickly notice whether a potted plant needs water.
Rainwater is soft and contains little lime, which is why many plants like it.

teile.einleitung: Garden soil looks unremarkable, but it is full of life. It gives plants support, water and nutrients. Anyone who looks after it well harvests beautiful flowers and plenty of vegetables.
wichtigste: In a handful of soil live countless tiny living things.
Good garden soil is loose and crumbly.
Between the crumbs there is air and water.
Compost makes the soil more fertile.
Many earthworms indicate a healthy soil.
You should not walk about on freshly loosened beds.

abschnitte.text: In a handful of healthy soil live **billions** of tiny living things. Most are **bacteria** and **fungi**, which you can only see under the microscope. In addition there are woodlice, springtails, centipedes and worms. They break down dead leaves and plant remains. From this **humus** forms, the dark, nutrient-rich part of the soil.

**Earthworms** eat soil and plant remains. Their droppings are a valuable fertiliser. With their tunnels they **loosen** the soil. This lets air and water get deeper in. Earthworms live in large numbers only where the soil is loose, damp and nourishing. Many worms are therefore a sign of **healthy soil**.

Good garden soil falls apart into small **crumbs**. You can easily crumble it with your fingers. Between the crumbs there are many small hollow spaces. In them are **air** and **water** for roots and soil animals. If you tread on a bed, the soil is pressed down. Then air, water and roots get through less well. That is why narrow paths are laid between the beds.

With a **digging fork** or a spade, you loosen the soil. This makes it easier for roots to grow. To make the soil more fertile, you mix **compost** in. It brings humus and nutrients. If it has not rained for a long time, the soil becomes dry and hard. Then you **water** the beds, best in the morning or in the evening.

Sometimes there are small heaps of soil in the garden. These are **molehills**. The **mole** digs long tunnels under the ground and eats worms and insect larvae. It pushes the loose soil upwards. Moles show that there is a lot of life in the soil. In Switzerland it is forbidden to kill moles, except in special cases with a permit.

gewusst: In a handful of good soil there live more living things than there are people on Earth.
It can take a hundred years or more for a layer of just one centimetre of soil to form anew.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Federal Institute for Forest, Snow and Landscape Research, WSL for short, studies the nature of Switzerland. It deals with forests, natural hazards, snow and avalanches.
wichtigste: The WSL has its headquarters in Birmensdorf in the canton of Zurich.
It belongs to the ETH Domain.
The WSL includes the Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research SLF in Davos.
The SLF publishes the avalanche bulletin.
The WSL was founded in 1885 as the “Central Institute for Forestry Experiments” (“Centralanstalt für das forstliche Versuchswesen”).
Together with the FOEN it carries out the National Forest Inventory.

abschnitte.text: The **WSL** is the **Swiss Federal Institute for Forest, Snow and Landscape Research**. Its **headquarters** are in **Birmensdorf** in the canton of Zurich. It also has other sites in different parts of the country. The WSL belongs to the **ETH Domain**, together with ETH Zurich, EPFL in Lausanne and other research institutes.

The WSL was founded in **1885**. At that time it was called the **“Central Institute for Forestry Experiments”** (in German, “Centralanstalt für das forstliche Versuchswesen”). In the 19th century many forests in Switzerland were overused, and there were floods. Research was meant to help look after the forests better. Later, topics such as landscape, natural hazards and biodiversity were added.

The WSL includes the **Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research SLF** in **Davos**. It studies snow, ice, permafrost and avalanches. In winter the SLF publishes the **avalanche bulletin**. It shows how great the avalanche danger is in the different regions. Many people in the mountains, for example ski tourers, rely on it.

Together with the **Federal Office for the Environment FOEN**, the WSL carries out the **National Forest Inventory**. In it, the Swiss forest is regularly studied on many sample plots. This shows how much wood is growing and how healthy the forest is. In the programme **LWF**, the **Long-term Forest Ecosystem Research**, the WSL observes selected forests closely over many years.

The WSL uses **dendrochronology**. In it, the **annual rings** of trees are studied. Wide rings show good growing years, narrow rings often cold or dry years. This way you can find out what the **climate** was like hundreds or thousands of years ago. The age of old building timber can also be worked out this way.

gewusst: The SLF in Davos is one of the best-known institutes for snow research in the world.
With tree rings you can sometimes work out to the exact year when a tree was felled.

teile.einleitung: Glyphosate is a chemical active substance against weeds, in other words a **herbicide**. It is one of the most widely used plant protection products in the world and has been fiercely debated for years.
wichtigste: Glyphosate is a weed killer (herbicide).
In plants it blocks the shikimate pathway.
Glyphosate acts on almost all green plants, it is not selective.
Monsanto brought it onto the market in the 1970s as “Roundup”.
Since 2018, Monsanto has belonged to the German company Bayer.
Expert bodies disagree about a possible cancer risk.
In 2023, the EU extended the approval by ten years.

abschnitte.text: In the plant, glyphosate inhibits an enzyme called **EPSPS**. This enzyme belongs to the **shikimate pathway**, a metabolic pathway with which plants make certain **amino acids**. Amino acids are building blocks for proteins. If they are lacking, the plant dies after a few days. Humans and animals do not have this metabolic pathway, and take up these amino acids with their food. Other possible effects are discussed, though, for example on bacteria in the gut.

Glyphosate is a **broad-spectrum herbicide**: it harms almost every green plant that it hits. That is why farmers often spray it before sowing or after the harvest, when no crop is standing in the field. This clears the soil of weeds without having to plough. It was also used for a long time on railway tracks and in gardens.

Later, Monsanto developed **genetically modified** varieties of soya, maize or cotton. They carry a gene for an insensitive enzyme and survive the spraying. The weeds next to them, on the other hand, die. In countries that grow such varieties, the use of glyphosate rose sharply as a result.

The International Agency for Research on Cancer (**IARC**) classified glyphosate in 2015 as “probably carcinogenic”. Authorities such as the European Food Safety Authority **EFSA**, on the other hand, concluded that no cancer risk has been proven when it is used correctly. After taking over Monsanto, Bayer had to deal with many lawsuits in the USA, which cost the company billions. In 2023, the EU Commission extended the approval until 2033, because the member states could not agree. In Switzerland, too, restrictions are being debated.

gewusst: The patent on the active substance expired long ago, which is why many companies make glyphosate today.
Glyphosate acts only through the green parts of plants, and plants hardly take it up through the soil.

teile.einleitung: A garden is a piece of land on which people grow and look after plants or simply relax. Vegetables, herbs, flowers and fruit grow here, and many small animals find a habitat. Anyone who gardens learns a lot about how nature works.
wichtigste: A piece of ground in the garden on which you plant vegetables is called a bed.
You water plants with a watering can, best in the morning or in the evening.
The earthworm is useful because it loosens the soil and makes it fertile.
The potato grows as a tuber under the ground.
In the compost, kitchen scraps and leaves slowly turn into new soil.
Beneficial animals such as ladybirds, hedgehogs and bees help in the garden.
In Swiss towns, many people rent an allotment garden.

abschnitte.text: A **garden** is a piece of land, usually fenced in, near a house. There are vegetable gardens, flower gardens, orchards and herb gardens. Old **farmhouse gardens** in Switzerland combine everything: vegetables, herbs and flowers grow in beds edged by small hedges. You can also make a small garden in pots on a balcony.

A **bed** is a piece of loose soil on which you plant vegetables or flowers. In spring you sow carrots (called “Rüebli” in Switzerland), radishes and lettuce, for example. Potatoes are put in the ground as tubers, and in autumn you dig up many new tubers. Anyone who grows the vegetables in a different place each year practises **crop rotation**, so that the soil stays healthy.

You dig over with the spade, smooth the soil with the rake, and loosen the ground and remove weeds with the hoe. Watering is done with the **watering can** or the hose, best early in the morning or in the evening, so that the water does not evaporate straight away. Rainwater from a water butt is ideal for plants. Vegetables need a lot of sun, so beds should not lie in the shade.

The **earthworm** eats dead plant parts and soil and leaves behind fine, fertile crumbs. Its tunnels loosen the soil so that air and water reach the roots. In the **compost**, worms, woodlice, fungi and bacteria break down kitchen scraps, leaves and grass cuttings. After about a year, dark, nutrient-rich compost soil forms from it.

Ladybirds and their larvae eat many **aphids**. Hedgehogs and toads hunt slugs and insects at night. Bees, bumblebees and butterflies **pollinate** the flowers of fruit trees and of vegetables such as courgettes. Anyone who makes a pile of branches or stones, wild flowers and a water basin gives these animals a home.

In towns such as Zurich, Basel or Bern there are many **allotment gardens**, small garden plots that you can rent. More and more schools have a school garden in which children sow and harvest themselves. In botanical gardens, for example in Bern, Zurich or Geneva, you can marvel at plants from all over the world. Natural gardens with native plants are important because they offer food to many animals.

begriffe.erklaerung: A piece of garden soil on which vegetables or flowers grow.
A heap of garden and kitchen waste that turns into soil.
An animal that helps in the garden, for example by eating pests.
Each year a different vegetable is grown in one spot.

gewusst: A single ladybird can eat several thousand aphids in its life.
Earthworms have neither eyes nor ears, but they sense light and vibrations with their skin.
The potato originally comes from the Andes in South America.

teile.einleitung: The Föhn is a warm, dry downslope wind that blows in the Swiss Alps. It blows from the mountains down into the valleys and can suddenly bring spring-like temperatures there in winter. Many people even feel it in their own bodies.
wichtigste: The Föhn is a warm and dry downslope wind on the lee side of a mountain range.
In Switzerland the south Föhn is best known, which blows into the valleys on the northern side of the Alps.
The air warms up as it descends, because it is compressed.
Typical of Föhn weather are a very clear, blue sky and good visibility.
Well-known Föhn valleys are the Reuss valley in Uri, the Glarus region and the St Gallen Rhine valley.
In Föhn conditions the fire risk is high, so in some places special fire bans apply.
In Switzerland the hairdryer is also called a Föhn, because it blows warm air.

abschnitte.text: The **Föhn** is a downslope wind, that is, a wind that blows from a mountain range down into the valley. It is warm, dry and often very stormy. Föhn winds exist in many mountain ranges of the world, but the name comes from the Alpine region. It probably goes back to the Latin word **favonius**, which was what the Romans called a mild west wind.

In a south Föhn, damp air flows from the Mediterranean towards the Alps and has to rise. As it does so, it cools, clouds form, and in Ticino it often rains or snows heavily. The air loses so much moisture and falls dry into the valley on the northern side. As it sinks, it is compressed and warms by about 1 degree per 100 metres of height, so it is warmer down below than it was at the same height earlier in the south. This process is called the **Föhn effect**.

In a Föhn, you often see a thick wall of cloud above the crest of the Alps, the **Föhn wall**. On the northern side the clouds dissolve, and a blue hole in the sky appears, the **Föhn window**. Sometimes smooth, lens-shaped clouds hover in the sky, which look like UFOs. In a Föhn, the mountains seem close enough to touch, because the air is so clear.

The Föhn blows especially often in the canton of Uri, for example in **Altdorf**, but also in the Glarus region, in the Haslital and in the St Gallen Rhine valley. In winter, the south Föhn can melt the snow there within hours, which is why it is also called the snow eater. If there is a north wind on the southern side of the Alps, it is called the **north Föhn**, which then brings dry, sunny weather to Ticino. On Lake Lucerne and Lake Walen, the Föhn can whip up high waves.

Because the Föhn is very dry and strong, a small spark can quickly start a big fire. In the **fire of Glarus** in 1861, a fire in a Föhn storm destroyed a large part of the town. That is why in some Föhn areas there are rules that forbid open fires during a Föhn. Föhn storms can also blow down trees and strip roofs.

Some people feel tired or irritable in a Föhn, or get a headache, which is called **Föhn sickness**. Scientists have not yet fully worked out why this is. For farming in the Rhine valley, the Föhn used to be important, because it helped maize and grapes to ripen. Because the hairdryer blows warm air like the wind, it is also called a Föhn in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wind that blows from mountains down into the valley.
A thick wall of cloud above the crest of the Alps in a Föhn.
A patch of blue sky on the Föhn side, where the clouds dissolve.
The windward side is the side the wind comes from, the leeward side is the side facing away from the wind.

gewusst: In a strong Föhn, it can be warmer in Altdorf in winter than in many places on the Mediterranean.
The Föhn is sometimes called the “oldest man of Uri”, because it has always blown through the Reuss valley.
Winds similar to the Föhn exist elsewhere too; in North America such a wind is called a Chinook.

teile.einleitung: With binoculars you can see faraway things up close. They are an important tool for watching birds and other animals in nature.
wichtigste: Binoculars make faraway things look close.
They usually have two tubes, one for each eye.
In “8x42”, the 8 means that they magnify eight times.
You focus them with a small wheel.
You must never look at the sun through binoculars.
With binoculars you can watch animals without disturbing them.

abschnitte.text: Binoculars usually have **two tubes**, one for each eye. So you see with both eyes at the same time, which is pleasant and comfortable. Inside the tubes are **lenses** and **prisms** made of glass. They magnify the image and turn it so that it appears the right way up.

On many pairs of binoculars it says, for example, **8x42**. The **8** means that the binoculars **magnify eight times**. A bird 80 metres away then looks as if it were 10 metres away. The **42** tells you how big the front lenses are in millimetres. Bigger lenses catch more light, so the image is brighter.

First you adjust the distance between the two tubes to your own eyes. Then you turn the small **focus wheel** in the middle until the image is **sharp**. You hang the **strap** around your neck. That way the binoculars cannot fall and are always ready. It is best to find the animal first with the naked eye and then raise the binoculars.
You must **never look at the sun** through binoculars. The lenses focus the sunlight very strongly. This can seriously injure your eyes at once and for ever. Even a short look is dangerous.

Binoculars are ideal for **birdwatching**. You do not have to go close and so you do not disturb the animals. In the **Alps** you can use them to spot **ibex**, chamois or marmots on the rocky slopes, for example. Birds of prey in the sky or ducks on a lake are also much easier to see.

gewusst: Binoculars with a magnification of about eight to ten times can still be held well without a tripod.
With stronger magnification the image shakes more, because every small movement of the hand is magnified too.

teile.einleitung: The raspberry is a popular red berry that grows in woods and gardens here. It is sweet, soft and has a delicate scent. A raspberry actually consists of many tiny little fruits.
