wichtigste: Most raspberries are red, but there are yellow varieties too.
A raspberry is made up of many small beads.
When freshly picked, it is hollow inside.
The canes of the bush have fine prickles.
Most raspberries ripen in summer.
Tea is made from dried raspberry leaves.

abschnitte.titel: A berry made of many beads
abschnitte.text: If you look closely at a **raspberry**, you see many small **beads**. Each of them is a little fruit of its own with a tiny **seed** inside. Together they make up the raspberry. Experts call something like this an **aggregate fruit**. The blackberry is built in the same way.

The beads sit on a small **cone**. When you pick the fruit, this cone stays on the plant. That is why a freshly picked raspberry has a **hole** inside and is **hollow**. With the blackberry it is different: there the cone stays in the fruit. That is a good way to tell the two berries apart.

Raspberries grow on long **canes**. These have many small, **fine prickles**. They prick less than the thorns of the blackberry. In Switzerland, wild raspberries can be found at the edges of woods and in forest clearings. In gardens, larger varieties are grown. A mild **tea** can be made from the dried **leaves**.

Most raspberries are ripe in **summer**. Some varieties bear fruit until **autumn**. Ripe raspberries are usually bright **red**. There are also varieties with **yellow** fruit. They often taste especially mild.

Raspberries are very **soft and delicate**. In big heaps, the ones at the bottom would be **crushed**. That is why they are carefully put into small punnets. Fresh raspberries keep for only a few days. But they freeze well and can be made into **jam**, syrup and cakes.

gewusst: A single raspberry is made up of several dozen tiny little fruits.
The raspberry is related to the rose, and both belong to the rose family.

teile.einleitung: **Gregor Mendel** was a monk and naturalist. With experiments on peas, he discovered the rules by which characteristics are passed on to offspring. He is therefore regarded as the founder of **genetics**.
wichtigste: Gregor Mendel lived from 1822 to 1884.
He was an Augustinian monk in the monastery in Brno.
He did his most important experiments with the garden pea.
He studied seven pairs of characteristics of the pea.
His work appeared in print in 1866.
Around 1900 his rules were rediscovered.
In 1868 he became abbot of his monastery.

abschnitte.text: Mendel came from a farming family in Silesia. In 1843 he entered the **Augustinian monastery** of St Thomas in **Brno** (in German, “Brünn”), which today lies in the Czech Republic. The monastery supported science. Mendel also studied natural sciences in Vienna and worked as a teacher. In 1868 he became **abbot**, that is, head of the monastery. After that he hardly had any time left for research.

In the monastery garden, Mendel crossed **garden peas** for years. He chose **seven pairs of characteristics**, for example round or wrinkled seeds and yellow or green colour. Mendel counted very precisely how many offspring showed which characteristic. In doing so he found fixed numerical ratios, for example **3 to 1**. From this he concluded that characteristics are determined by hereditary factors, which today we call **genes**.

Mendel presented his results in 1865, and in 1866 the paper “Experiments on Plant Hybrids” appeared. From it, **Mendel's laws** were later formed: the law of uniformity, the law of segregation and the law of independent assortment. During his lifetime, only a few researchers paid attention to his work. Around **1900**, several researchers rediscovered the laws independently of each other, among them **Carl Correns**, Hugo de Vries and Erich Tschermak.

The Swiss botanist **Carl Nägeli** advised Mendel to study **hawkweed** too. But the results did not fit those of the peas. Today we know why: hawkweed often makes its seeds without pollination, which is called **apomixis**. The offspring are then copies of the mother plant. Mendel could not know that at the time.

gewusst: Mendel failed the teacher's exam twice and still carried on researching.
For his experiments, Mendel grew thousands of pea plants.

teile.einleitung: A greenhouse is a house made of glass or transparent plastic film in which plants grow. It is used to let plants grow warm in any weather. This way you can grow tomatoes, cucumbers or flowers even when it is still cold outside.
wichtigste: A greenhouse lets plants grow warm in any weather.
Walls and roof are made of glass or transparent film.
Sunlight gets in and warms the air and the soil.
The warm air stays trapped in the house and cannot blow away.
In greenhouses, mainly vegetables, flowers and young plants grow.
In Switzerland, too, a lot of vegetables come from greenhouses.
Botanical gardens show plants from faraway countries in greenhouses.

abschnitte.text: A greenhouse is a building with transparent walls and a transparent roof. It is also called a **hothouse** or glasshouse. Small greenhouses stand in many gardens, while large ones belong to vegetable farms and nurseries. Simple forms are the **polytunnel** and the cold frame, a flat box with a glass lid.

Sunlight passes through the glass and warms plants, soil and air. The warm air cannot simply escape, because it is enclosed by the house. That is why it is often much warmer inside than outside, similar to a car standing in the sun. If it gets too hot, you open windows in the roof for **ventilation**.

In greenhouses, mainly warmth-loving vegetables grow, such as tomatoes, cucumbers, peppers and aubergines. Nurseries raise **seedlings** there, that is, young plants that later go outdoors. Cut flowers and houseplants are also often raised in the glasshouse. Because wind, hail and cold stay outside, the plants grow protected and evenly.

Large greenhouses are heated in winter and get extra light from lamps. Computers measure temperature, humidity and light and control windows and watering automatically. Some plants grow not in soil but in a nutrient solution, which is called **hydroponics**. Against pests, beneficial insects are often used, for example small parasitic wasps.

In the Bernese Seeland and in other vegetable-growing regions of Switzerland, there are many greenhouses. Thanks to them, there are Swiss tomatoes and cucumbers from spring to autumn. In Zurich Zoo stands the **Masoala Rainforest hall**, a huge greenhouse with a piece of rainforest from Madagascar. The botanical gardens in Zurich, Bern, Basel and Geneva also have tropical houses.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another word for greenhouse.
A simple, arched greenhouse made of plastic film.
A young plant that is later planted in its final place.
Growing plants without soil, in water with nutrients.

gewusst: The term greenhouse effect for the warming of the Earth is named after the greenhouse.
In southern Spain near Almería there are so many greenhouses that their roofs look like a huge white sea from space.

teile.einleitung: A fire pit is a place where you are allowed to light a fire safely. In Switzerland there are many of them in the woods, where families and school classes like to cook over a fire.
wichtigste: The fire should be small and easy to keep an eye on.
You collect dead wood from the ground.
Plastic and rubbish do not belong in the fire.
Water for putting it out should always be nearby.
When there is a fire ban, you do not light a fire.
Before you leave, you put the fire out completely.

abschnitte.text: A **fire pit** is often a ring of stones or a fixed barbecue spot. There the ground is protected, and the fire stays in its place. You do not light a fire directly **under trees**, because the branches can catch fire. The fire should be **small and easy to keep an eye on**. A big fire is harder to control and needs a lot of wood.

In the woods you collect **dead wood from the ground**. It is drier and burns better than fresh branches. Living trees and shrubs are left standing. Small, thin twigs help with lighting, and you add thicker branches later. **Plastic**, tins and other rubbish do not belong in the fire, because poisonous gases are produced.

abschnitte.titel: Cooking over a fire in Switzerland
abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, grilling over a fire is called **“bräteln”**. Particularly popular is the **cervelat**, a Swiss sausage. You cut it at the ends and put it on a stick. Twist bread made of dough is also often baked over the embers. It is best to cook over the embers, not in the tall flames.

When cooking over a fire, you should always have **water** nearby, so that you can put the fire out quickly. When it has not rained for a long time, the woods are very dry. Then municipalities or cantons sometimes issue a **fire ban**. In this case you light **no fire**, not even at a permanent fire pit. Otherwise a small spark can start a forest fire.

Before you leave the fire pit, you must put the fire out **completely**. You pour water on the embers and stir with a stick. Nothing may glow or smoke any more. You also take your own rubbish away with you. This way the fire pit stays clean and safe for everyone.

gewusst: Embers can stay hot under the ash for many hours, even when you no longer see any flames.
The cervelat is sometimes called the national sausage of Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: A raised bog is a wet, domed landscape of peat that lives almost only on rain and snow. It is one of the rarest and most sensitive habitats in Switzerland.
wichtigste: A raised bog is supplied with water only by precipitation, not by groundwater.
The name comes from the shape: the middle bulges upwards like a watch glass.
The main builders of a raised bog are the peat mosses.
The water in a raised bog is acidic and very poor in nutrients.
At the edge there is a wet zone, the lagg.
Switzerland has around 550 raised bogs of national importance, and they cover only about 0.03 per cent of the country’s area.

abschnitte.text: A raised bog has grown so high above its surroundings that it no longer reaches the **groundwater**. All of its water comes from **rain and snow**. That is why it is also called a rain-fed bog. Rainwater contains hardly any minerals. So a raised bog is a place very poor in nutrients.

The most important plants in a raised bog are the **peat mosses**. They keep growing at the top while their lower parts die. Because it is so wet and lacks air, the dead parts hardly rot. In this way **peat** forms, layer upon layer. Peat mosses also give off acid and make the water **acidic**.

In the middle the peat grows most strongly. That is why a raised bog bulges upwards like a **watch glass**. The name therefore has nothing to do with height above sea level. On the surface, drier hummocks, called **hummocks** or **bulten**, alternate with wet hollows, called **hollows** or **schlenken**. Around the bog lies the **lagg**, a wet edge zone where bog water mixes with water from the mineral soil.

Only a few plants can cope with acidic, nutrient-poor water. A well-known example is the **sundew**. It has leaves with sticky droplets that small insects get stuck to. From the animals it catches, it gets nutrients that are missing in the soil. Cotton grass and cranberry also like to grow in raised bogs.

The **federal inventory** of raised bogs of national importance lists around 550 bogs (as of 2025). Together they cover only about 1,600 hectares. That is about **0.03 per cent** of the country’s area. In the past, many bogs were drained or dug up for fuel peat. Today, bogs in Switzerland are protected by the **Federal Constitution**.

gewusst: Peat grows very slowly, often only about one millimetre a year.
Since the Rothenthurm Initiative was accepted in 1987, the Federal Constitution has protected bogs of special beauty and national importance.

teile.einleitung: In the middle of many flowers stands the pistil. Its lowest, thickened part is called the **ovary**. From it, the fruit with the seeds later develops.
wichtigste: The pistil consists of ovary, style and stigma.
The ovary is the thickened base of the pistil.
In the ovary lie the ovules, which become seeds.
The wall of the ovary becomes the fruit wall.
An ovary can be superior or inferior.
In the strawberry, the flower base helps too, and it is a false fruit.

abschnitte.text: The **pistil** is the female part of the flower. At the very top sits the **stigma**, which catches the pollen. Below it lies the **style**, a thin stalk. At the very bottom is the **ovary**. It is thickened and built like a small chamber. In it lie the **ovules**.

If pollen reaches the stigma, the flower can be fertilised. Afterwards the ovules grow into **seeds**. The ovary itself becomes the **fruit**. Its wall becomes the **fruit wall**. In the **cherry**, the fruit wall forms the skin, the juicy flesh and the hard stone.

If the ovary sits above the point where the flower envelope is attached, it is called **superior**. You can then see it well in the middle of the flower, as in the **tulip**. If it lies below the point where the flower envelope is attached, it is called **inferior**. This is the case in the **apple**. That is why at the bottom of an apple you can still see the dried remains of the calyx, which are often called the “fly”.

The ovary is formed from one or more **carpels**. In legumes such as the **pea**, it consists of a single carpel. From it the **pod** develops. Later it opens along two seams and releases the seeds. Other flowers have ovaries made up of three, five or even more carpels.

Sometimes other parts of the flower also take part in the fruit. In the **strawberry**, the **flower base** becomes the red, sweet flesh. The actual small fruits are the yellow dots on the surface. Because it is not only the ovary that takes part, such a thing is called a **false fruit**. The apple, too, counts as a false fruit.

gewusst: The small dots on the strawberry are its actual fruits.
The “fly” at the bottom of the apple is a remnant of the flower.

teile.einleitung: The buttercup (in German, “Hahnenfuss”, or “cock's foot”) is one of the best-known meadow flowers of Switzerland. In spring it colours whole meadows bright yellow. It looks pretty, but fresh it is poisonous.
wichtigste: The meadow buttercup has bright yellow flowers.
Its leaves are deeply cut and recall the foot of a cock.
The petals shine as if freshly varnished.
A flower usually has five petals.
Fresh buttercup is poisonous and acrid, dried in hay it is harmless.
Many people also call it “butter flower”.

abschnitte.text: The **meadow buttercup** (in German, “Scharfer Hahnenfuss”) grows on meadows and pastures, from the lowlands up into the mountains. In spring and early summer it flowers so abundantly that whole meadows glow yellow. Its flower usually has **five petals**. Because of the butter-yellow colour, many people call it **butter flower**. This name, however, is also used for other yellow flowers such as the dandelion.

The leaves of the buttercup are deeply cut and divided into several lobes. With a little imagination they look like the **foot of a cock**. That is where the plant gets its German name. The buttercup gives its name to a whole plant family, the **buttercup family** (in German, “Hahnenfussgewächse”).

Anyone who looks closely at a buttercup flower sees that it shines strongly. The petals look **freshly varnished**. The reason is a special layer in the petals that throws the light back like a mirror. Children sometimes hold the flower under the chin: then the skin glows yellow.

Fresh buttercup contains an **acrid, poisonous substance**. That is why cows do not eat it in the pasture and simply leave it standing. It is not edible for people either. The plant sap can **irritate the skin**, so you wash your hands after picking it. When it dries, the acrid substance is lost: in **hay**, the buttercup is harmless for the animals.
When the yellow petals have fallen, a small round **head** is left. It consists of many tiny **nutlets**. Each nutlet holds a seed. This is how the buttercup can multiply in the meadow.

gewusst: The shine of the buttercup flower comes from a special mirror-like layer that is rare in flowers.
On many pastures in summer you see islands of buttercup that the cows have not grazed.

teile.einleitung: In the summer of 2003, Switzerland and large parts of Europe experienced an extreme heatwave. For weeks it was hot and dry. At that time the highest temperature ever officially recorded in Switzerland was measured in Grono in the canton of the Grisons.
wichtigste: On 11 August 2003, 41.5 °C was measured in Grono, GR.
This is the highest official value in Switzerland (as of 2026).
The heat peaked in the first half of August.
A persistent high-pressure area determined the weather for many weeks.
According to estimates, several tens of thousands of extra people died in Europe.
The glaciers of the Alps melted exceptionally strongly.

abschnitte.text: **June 2003** was already very hot. But the greatest heat came in the **first half of August**. During this time several temperature records were broken. On **11 August 2003**, the thermometer in **Grono** in the Misox valley showed **41.5 °C**. This is the highest temperature ever officially measured in Switzerland (as of 2026). There were also especially many **tropical nights**, when the temperature did not fall below 20 °C.

For many weeks a **persistent high-pressure area** lay over central and western Europe. A high usually brings plenty of sun and little rain. Because it hardly moved, one hot day followed another. The soils dried out, and in many areas there was not enough water for farming.

Great heat is hard on the body, especially for **older people** and the sick. Experts estimate that **several tens of thousands of people** more died in Europe than in a normal summer. There were especially many deaths in **France**. The 2003 heatwave is regarded as one of the worst natural disasters in Europe. Afterwards, many countries introduced **heat warnings**.

The long heat made the **glaciers** of the Alps melt exceptionally strongly. The summer of 2003 brought one of the largest **ice losses** measured up to that time. The rivers also became very warm. In the **Rhine near Schaffhausen**, a large part of the **graylings** died. These fish need cool, oxygen-rich water.

Many experts see the summer of 2003 as a hint of how **climate change** can have an effect. Since then there have been further very hot summers in Switzerland. That is why heat warnings and protective measures are taken more seriously today. Important tips in hot weather are: drink plenty, look for shade and do not do strenuous exercise in the midday heat.

gewusst: The temperature record from Grono in 2003 still stands in Switzerland today (as of 2026).
In France, around 15,000 more people than usual died in August 2003.

teile.einleitung: Hay is dried grass with herbs. Farmers harvest it in summer and feed it to their animals in winter. In Switzerland, the hay harvest is called the “Heuet”.
wichtigste: Hay is cut grass that has been dried in the sun.
Making hay needs sunny, dry weather.
Cut grass is turned so that it dries faster.
Wet hay goes mouldy and can even catch fire by itself.
Hay is stored in the hayloft or pressed into round bales.
Straw is dry cereal stalks, not hay.

abschnitte.text: **Hay** is made of grass and herbs that have been **cut** and **dried** in the sun. Dry hay keeps for a very long time. That is why it is an important **winter feed**. In winter, hardly any grass grows outdoors. Then **cows**, horses, sheep and goats are given hay to eat.

In Switzerland, the hay harvest is called the **Heuet**. It takes place mainly in **early summer**. The Wümmet, by contrast, is the grape harvest in autumn. For the Heuet, the farmer needs **sunny and dry weather**. The cut grass has to lie in the meadow for a few days to dry. Rain would stop it from drying.

The cut grass is **turned** several times. This brings the damp underside to the top, into the sun and wind. That way the grass dries evenly and faster. In the past this was done by hand with a rake, but today it is mostly done with machines. Once the hay is dry, it is gathered together and brought in.

On a farm, hay is stored in the **hayloft**. In the barn it is usually above the stable. There the hay stays dry. Hay is often also rolled into large **round bales** with a baler. This makes it easy to transport and store. **Straw**, by the way, is something different: it is the dry stalks of cereals such as wheat or barley after threshing.

Hay must **not** go into the barn **wet**. Otherwise it starts to go **mouldy** and gets warm. In the worst case, it can even **catch fire by itself** and start a blaze. That is why farmers sometimes measure the temperature of freshly stored hay with a long probe. If it gets too hot, the fire brigade is called.

gewusst: A haystack can catch fire by itself without any spark, just from the warmth produced by tiny living things in the damp hay.
The fire brigade has special measuring probes for hot haystacks.

teile.einleitung: An altitudinal zone is a height band in the mountains with a typical plant world. Because it gets cooler with height, different zones follow one above the other in the Alps, from the valley to the summit.
wichtigste: Altitudinal zones arise because it gets cooler with height.
For every 100 metres of height, it gets about 0.5 to 0.7 °C cooler on average.
From bottom to top: colline, montane, subalpine, alpine, nival.
The topmost zone is the nival zone, with snow, ice and rock.
On south-facing slopes the zones usually lie higher than on north-facing slopes.
Above the snow line, the snow no longer melts completely in summer.

abschnitte.text: With every metre of height, the average temperature falls. On average it is about **0.5 to 0.7 °C** per 100 metres, so about 5 to 7 degrees for 1,000 metres of height. In addition, the **growing season** becomes shorter: spring begins later and winter earlier. Up high, only plants that cope well with **cold** can grow. This gives rise to zones of typical plants, one above the other, called **altitudinal zones**.

abschnitte.titel: From the hills to the mountain forest
abschnitte.text: The lowest zone is the **colline zone**, the warm hill country with deciduous woods, fields, fruit and vines. Above it follows the **montane zone**, the mountain forest zone with beeches, firs and spruces. Then comes the **subalpine zone**, the uppermost forest zone with spruces, larches and Swiss stone pines. It ends at the **tree line**, above which no trees grow.

Above the tree line lies the **alpine zone** with dwarf shrubs, grassland and the **alpine pastures**. Right at the top follows the **nival zone** with snow, ice and rock. Its name comes from the Latin “nix, nivis”, meaning snow. The boundary to it is formed by the **snow line**. Above it, more snow falls in a year than can melt in summer. There, **firn** and **glaciers** form.

The altitudinal zones do not lie at the same height everywhere. What matters is the **aspect**, that is, the compass direction a slope faces. In Switzerland, **south-facing slopes** get more sun and are warmer. That is why forest and plants usually reach higher up there than on **north-facing slopes**. In the warmer, inner Alpine valleys such as the Valais or the Engadine, too, the zones lie higher than at the edge of the Alps.

gewusst: A climb of 1,000 metres of height changes the climate about as much as a journey of several hundred kilometres northwards.
Even in the nival zone, a few flowering plants still grow, for example the glacier crowfoot.

teile.einleitung: A fruit is the part of a plant that encloses and protects the seeds. Cherries, apples, bananas and strawberries are fruits, but from the point of view of biology so are tomatoes, cucumbers and hazelnuts. Fruits are not only tasty, they also help the plant to spread its seeds.
wichtigste: A fruit develops from the ovary of a flower after fertilisation.
In the fruit lie the seeds from which new plants can grow.
The cherry grows on a tree and has a hard stone inside.
A ripe banana is yellow, while unripe bananas are green.
Botanists distinguish, for example, berries, stone fruits, nuts and pome fruit.
Picking and gathering ripe fruit is called the harvest.
The apple is the most important kind of fruit in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: Every fruit begins as a flower. After pollination and **fertilisation**, the petals fall off, and the **ovary** slowly grows into the fruit. Inside, the **seeds** ripen. On a cherry tree it takes about two to three months from the white blossom in April to the ripe red cherry.

In a **stone fruit** such as cherry, plum or peach, the seed sits in a hard stone. In **berries**, many seeds lie in the soft flesh, including blueberries, grapes, tomatoes and even the banana. Apples and pears are **pome fruit** with a core in the middle. Hazelnuts and walnuts have a hard shell around the seed.

The strawberry is not really a berry. The small yellow dots on its skin are the true fruits, tiny little nuts, and the red flesh is the thickened base of the flower. Botanically speaking, cucumber, pumpkin, pepper and tomato are fruits, but in the kitchen we call them vegetables. The difference between **fruit** and vegetables is therefore more a question of the kitchen than of biology.

For the plant, the fruit is a means of transport for the seeds. Sweet, coloured fruits attract animals that eat them and later pass the seeds out somewhere else. Other fruits fly with the wind, like the maple, or hook onto fur, like the burdock. This way plants can conquer new habitats.

In Switzerland, mainly apples, pears, cherries, plums, apricots and berries grow. The canton of **Thurgau** is known for its many apple trees and is therefore jokingly called “Mostindien” (Cider India). Apricots come mainly from the Valais, and cherries, for example, from the Basel region and from Zug. Bananas, oranges and pineapples need a warm climate and are imported from abroad.

Picking and gathering ripe fruit is called the **harvest**. Many fruits contain vitamins, for example vitamin C, as well as minerals and dietary fibre. Experts recommend eating fruit and vegetables every day. Fruit is also made into jam, juice, cider or dried fruit so that it keeps longer.

begriffe.erklaerung: The part of the flower from which the fruit grows.
A fruit with a hard stone around the seed, like the cherry.
A fruit with soft flesh and usually many seeds.
Fruits such as apple and pear with a core.

gewusst: Botanically, the banana is a berry, but the strawberry is not.
Bananas do not grow on a tree, but on a giant herbaceous plant.
You should not bite into the stones of cherries and apricots, because they contain a poisonous substance.

teile.einleitung: On mountain summits all around the world, researchers regularly count every small plant. The programme is called **GLORIA**. It shows how the plant life of mountains is changing because of climate change.
wichtigste: GLORIA stands for “Global Observation Research Initiative in Alpine Environments”.
The network is coordinated from Vienna.
At least four summits are studied in each region.
The summits range from the tree line up to the nival zone.
On permanent plots of one square metre, every plant species is recorded.
On many summits, warmth-loving species are increasing.

abschnitte.text: **GLORIA** is a worldwide network of research groups. They observe the **plant life on mountain summits** over many years. Mountain plants react sensitively to warmth. That is why they are well suited to recognising the effects of **climate change**. The network is coordinated from **Vienna**, by the University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences and the Austrian Academy of Sciences. There are GLORIA summits in the Swiss Alps too.

In the so-called **multi-summit approach**, each region includes at least **four summits**. They are staggered in height. The lowest lies near the **tree line**, the highest in the **nival zone**, that is, the zone of snow and ice. This way a whole **altitudinal gradient** is covered. You can compare how plants change at different heights.

Below each summit, the researchers set up **permanent observation plots**. They are squares with sides **one metre** long, in all four directions of the compass. Every plant species in them is noted, as well as how much ground it covers. After a few years, the count is repeated in exactly the same way. This makes even small changes visible.

Warmth-loving species from lower altitudes are moving upwards. Cold-loving species are becoming rarer. This change is called **thermophilisation**. A study in the journal **“Nature”** in 2018 examined around 300 European summits. It showed that the number of plant species on the summits is **increasing faster and faster**, in step with the warming.

The development is not the same everywhere. A GLORIA study from 2012 showed that in the northern and temperate mountains the number of species increased. In the mountains by the **Mediterranean**, on the other hand, it decreased. This is probably due to increasing **dryness**. For specialised summit plants, less and less room is left at the top, because there is nothing higher than the summit.

gewusst: More species on a summit sounds good, but it can push out rare specialists of the cold.
For their counts, the researchers climb the summits themselves and work there for days.

teile.einleitung: When there is still snow in the woods, a small shrub with pink flowers is already blooming: the **mezereon** (in German, “Gewöhnlicher Seidelbast”). It has a strong, sweet scent. But be careful: the mezereon is very poisonous.
wichtigste: The mezereon is a small shrub, usually about one metre tall.
It blooms as early as February or March.
The pink flowers sit directly on the bare twigs.
The flowers have a strong, sweet scent.
In late summer it bears red berries, which are very poisonous.
It grows in deciduous and mountain woods, in Switzerland too.

abschnitte.text: The mezereon is a **small shrub**, usually only about one metre tall. It grows in **deciduous woods** and **mountain woods**, in Switzerland too. In the woods it stands out mainly in early spring, when it is in flower and there is otherwise little green.

The mezereon blooms **very early in spring**, as early as February or March, often when there is still snow. The small flowers are **pink** to purplish red, rarely white. They sit densely **directly on the bare twigs**. The leaves grow only after flowering. The flowers have a **strong, sweet scent**. This way they attract insects early in the year.

In late summer the mezereon bears bright **red berries**. They look tempting, but are **very poisonous**. You must never eat them. For some birds, on the other hand, they are no problem, and they eat the berries and so spread the seeds.

All parts of the mezereon are poisonous, especially the **bark**, the **sap** and the berries. They contain a sharp poison. If the sap gets on the skin, it can **turn red and burn**, and sometimes blisters form. That is why it is best not to touch the shrub. In some cantons the mezereon is also protected.

gewusst: The mezereon often blooms when there is still snow in the woods.
Its flowers appear before the leaves, directly on the twigs.

teile.einleitung: A **genetically modified organism**, GMO for short, is a living thing whose genetic material has been changed in the laboratory. This change does not occur in a natural way. GMOs are used mainly in agriculture and in research and are strictly regulated in Switzerland.
wichtigste: In a GMO, the genetic material has been changed in a way that does not occur naturally.
Classical breeding by crossing does not legally produce a GMO.
Transgenic organisms contain genes from another species.
In 1994 the Flavr Savr tomato came onto the market in the USA as the first GMO food.
From 0.9 per cent accidental GMO content per ingredient, labelling is required.
The Cartagena Protocol regulates trade in GMOs across borders.

abschnitte.text: Under Swiss and EU law, a GMO is an organism whose **genetic material** has been changed in a way that does not happen through crossing or natural processes. **Classical breeding** therefore does not produce a GMO. If genes from another species are inserted, for example bacterial genes in maize, this is called **transgenic**. In **cisgenic** plants, the genes come from the same species or a species that can be crossed with it.

There are different methods. With the **gene gun**, the biolistic method, tiny particles of gold or tungsten are coated with DNA and shot into plant cells at high speed. In early GMO plants, **antibiotic resistance genes** were often used as markers. Only cells that had taken up the new gene together with the marker survived on a nutrient medium containing antibiotic. Today people try to avoid such markers.

The first genetically modified food was the **Flavr Savr tomato**, which came onto the market in the USA in 1994. It was meant to go soft more slowly, but it was not an economic success. In 1996 came **Roundup Ready soya**. It tolerates the weedkiller **glyphosate**, while the weeds die. Such **herbicide tolerance** is still among the most common genetic-engineering traits today.

In Switzerland, GMO plants may not be grown commercially because of the GMO moratorium. If traces of GMOs get into food by accident, a threshold of **0.9 per cent** per ingredient applies, as in the EU. If the share is above this, the product must be labelled. Internationally, the **Cartagena Protocol** regulates the cross-border movement of GMOs. It came into force in 2003, and Switzerland is also a party to it.

There is a lot of argument about GMOs. Supporters see chances for higher yields or plants that resist diseases. Critics worry about consequences for nature, about dependence on large seed companies and about the freedom of choice of consumers. The laws try to make research possible and at the same time to protect people and the environment.
